mfg1-electrical-l004.title: Do not overlook the 0.5 mm mark on a micrometer
mfg1-electrical-l004.exampleText:
The sleeve shows 6 mm and the following 0.5 mm line. The thimble, graduated in 0.01 mm increments, indicates 24.
1. Read the sleeve as 6.5 mm.
2. Read the thimble as 24 × 0.01 = 0.24 mm.
3. Calculate 6.5 + 0.24 = 6.74 mm.
The result is 6.74 mm. Missing the 0.5 mm line produces 6.24 mm, an error of 0.50 mm.

mfg1-surface-lesson-003.title: Evaluate film thickness at each location, not only the average
mfg1-surface-lesson-003.exampleText: For practice, assume an allowed thickness of 8–12 μm. Three specified points give 7, 10 and 13 μm. The average is (7+10+13)/3 = 10 μm, but two points are outside the range. Do not pass the item on the average alone; record each location and value. The 8–12 μm range is a teaching assumption, not a recommended process setting.

mfg1-surface-lesson-005.title: Distinguish the anode and cathode in electroplating
mfg1-surface-lesson-005.exampleText: In a training diagram, consider a solution containing copper ions and a soluble copper anode. Pair the anode reaction Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ with the workpiece-side reaction Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. This explains the basic reactions; it does not mean every bath composition or installation uses the same copper anode.

mfg1-surface-lesson-006.title: Relate current density and workpiece shape to thickness variation
mfg1-surface-lesson-006.exampleText: For calculation practice, a treated area of 2.4 dm² with a current of 7.2 A gives an average current density of 7.2 ÷ 2.4 = 3.0 A/dm². If only the area doubles to 4.8 dm² while current stays the same, it becomes 1.5 A/dm². These are practice figures, not recommended conditions for an actual bath.

mfg1-surface-lesson-007.title: Anodizing forms an oxide film from the substrate
mfg1-surface-lesson-007.exampleText: A newcomer describes an anodized item as having “a silver-coloured metal plated on top.” The instructor clarifies that this process forms an oxide film from the aluminium surface itself. Mark the workpiece on the anode side in the process diagram, then compare it with the cathode-side workpiece in electroplating.
mfg1-surface-lesson-007.structureTitle: Understand pores and the barrier layer conceptually
mfg1-surface-lesson-007.structureText:
A typical porous film includes a region with fine pores and a dense barrier layer next to the substrate. Some colouring methods use the pores, but colouring and corrosion-resistance evaluation are not the same.
Post-treatments such as sealing are selected for the required properties. Do not judge solely that an attractive colour is acceptable or that thicker is always better; evaluate the specified inspection items.

mfg1-surface-lesson-010.title: Determine concentration by neutralization titration
mfg1-surface-lesson-010.exampleText: Assume that 10.0 mL of hydrochloric-acid sample consumes 12.0 mL of 0.100 mol/L sodium hydroxide. With a 1:1 ratio, the standard solution supplies 0.100 × 0.0120 = 0.00120 mol. Acid concentration is 0.00120 ÷ 0.0100 = 0.120 mol/L. This is calculation practice, not a specification for an actual analytical method or control value.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-011.title: Distinguish work standards from QC process charts
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-011.exampleText: In an imaginary cutting process, the work standard specifies how to secure the material and which tool to use. The QC process chart requires checking cut length with a specified instrument at startup and every 30 minutes, segregating affected items and contacting the responsible person if a result is outside the range. Following the working sequence does not permit skipping the 30-minute checks. Conversely, performing the measurement does not justify omitting the securing method.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-011.structureText: A work standard specifies the work content, sequence, equipment, tools, and important conditions to maintain required quality despite changes in people or time. A QC process chart organizes what is controlled in each process, how often and by what method, and how abnormalities are handled. The working method and the control system play different roles even in the same process.

mfg1-electrical-l011.title: Distinguish variation from specifications
mfg1-electrical-l011.exampleText: Suppose a training example allows 9.90–10.10 mm. Three measurements are 9.80, 10.00, and 10.20 mm. Their mean is (9.80 + 10.00 + 10.20) ÷ 3 = 10.00 mm, but the two outer values are outside specification. A centered mean does not guarantee individual conformity. These three points also cannot establish adequate process capability.
mfg1-electrical-l011.structureText:
Upper and lower specification limits define the permitted range required for the product. A control chart instead arranges measurements in time order to examine stability and signs of change. Control limits and specification limits do not have the same purpose or method of determination.
Even while values remain within specification, a continuing shift in one direction may call for investigation. Conversely, an out-of-specification product cannot be shipped just because its value lies within control limits. Judge product acceptance and monitor the process separately.

mfg1-surface-lesson-011.title: Distinguish mass concentration from molarity
mfg1-surface-lesson-011.exampleText: For a practice solute with molar mass 40.0 g/mol, mass 4.00 g and final solution volume 0.500 L, mass concentration is 4.00 ÷ 0.500 = 8.00 g/L. Amount of substance is 4.00 ÷ 40.0 = 0.100 mol, giving molarity 0.100 ÷ 0.500 = 0.200 mol/L. This is a paper calculation, not a chemical-preparation instruction.
mfg1-surface-lesson-011.structureTitle: Read what is divided by what
mfg1-surface-lesson-011.structureText:
Mass concentration in g/L is solute mass per volume of solution. Molarity in mol/L is amount of substance per volume of solution. Equal numbers with different units mean different things. Read units as well as numbers on records and chemical labels.
The solute is the dissolved component, the solvent is the dissolving liquid and the solution is the resulting uniform liquid. Distinguish the final solution volume in the denominator from the volume of water added. Dissolving something in 1 L of water does not guarantee a final solution volume of 1 L.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-012.title: Choose QC tools to match the purpose
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-012.exampleText: One week’s appearance defects are recorded as 18 dents, 9 cases of dirt, and 3 cases of discoloration. There are 30 cases in total; Pareto cumulative percentages are 60% through dents, 90% through dirt, and 100% through discoloration. This supports investigating dents first, but a highly dangerous or severe defect must not be postponed simply because its count is low.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-012.structureTitle: Principle and decision criteria · Records and common mistakes
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-012.structureText:
Use a check sheet to collect data, a Pareto chart to prioritize categories by counts, and a histogram to examine distributions such as dimensions. A line graph helps show change over time, a control chart monitors process stability, and a scatter plot shows relationships between two quantities. A cause-and-effect diagram organizes possible causes. Decide what you want to judge before creating a chart.

A histogram shows a distribution and does not preserve the original time sequence. A visible relationship in a scatter plot alone does not prove causation. A control chart’s control limits are also different from specification limits used to accept products. Choose the chart and criteria that match the purpose, rather than drawing conclusions from appearance alone.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-013.title: Check SI units and prefixes before recording values
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-013.exampleText: To record a thickness of 0.8 mm in metres, use 1 mm = 0.001 m, giving 0.0008 m. A mass of 2.4 kg is 2400 g, and a time of 750 ms is 0.75 s. Converting the result back to the original unit helps detect a thousandfold error.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-013.structureTitle: Principle and decision criteria · Records and common mistakes
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-013.structureText:
The seven SI base units are metre m for length, kilogram kg for mass, second s for time, ampere A for electric current, kelvin K for thermodynamic temperature, mole mol for amount of substance, and candela cd for luminous intensity. Workplaces also use mm, g, and ms. Identical numbers with different units represent different quantities, so check the units in the instruction, display, and record field together.

Uppercase and lowercase letters matter. The unit m indicates length, while the first m in mm is the prefix meaning one thousandth. Mass in kg and force in N are different quantities. Do not rely on the conversational word “weight”; check whether the document asks for mass or force. Keep units in intermediate calculation steps as well.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-014.title: Distinguish inspection scope from nonconforming-item percentage
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-014.exampleText: From a fictional lot of 600 items, 60 are inspected according to the procedure and 3 are nonconforming. The percentage within the sample is 3 ÷ 60 × 100 = 5%. Using 3 ÷ 600 × 100 = 0.5% would incorrectly treat the 540 uninspected items as conforming. The lot’s acceptance must follow the specified acceptance number or other criteria, not the 5% alone.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-014.structureTitle: Principle and decision criteria · Records and common mistakes
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-014.structureText:
Incoming inspection checks whether purchased items meet specification; in-process inspection checks characteristics during manufacturing; shipping inspection checks whether completed products meet requirements. Full inspection covers every item in scope, while sampling inspection covers specified samples. Do not change sample size, selection method, or acceptance criteria for convenience.

One product with two scratches is still one nonconforming item. Do not confuse the count of scratches with the count of nonconforming items. Record whether the result covers all items or only a sample, the period, and the lot number. Sampling informs assessment of the lot’s condition; it does not guarantee that every uninspected item conforms.

mfg1-electrical-l012.title: Use a Pareto chart to consider improvement priorities
mfg1-electrical-l012.exampleText: For the same period and target, each defect is assigned one category: labeling errors 18, scratches 9, missing parts 3. Total: 30. Percentages: 60%, 30%, 10%. Cumulative percentages in descending order: 60%, 90%, 100%. Labeling errors and scratches account for 90%, but missing safety parts cannot be postponed merely because there are fewer of them.
mfg1-electrical-l012.structureTitle: Agree on counting rules first · Counts alone do not determine priority
mfg1-electrical-l012.structureText:
Before improvement, agree on what counts as one event, the collection period, target process, and categories. If one product has two defects, defect occurrences and defective products give different totals. Without a defined check sheet, collected figures may not be comparable later.
A Pareto chart orders category counts from highest to lowest and shows cumulative percentages. It helps identify categories accounting for many occurrences, but the labels in the chart do not by themselves prove root causes.

Sum all counts, then calculate each percentage as category count ÷ total × 100. Add percentages from the largest category to obtain cumulative percentages. Do not directly compare counts collected under different conditions.
Even infrequent defects may require priority if they could cause serious harm such as electric shock or fire. Identify frequent categories with the chart while separately assessing safety and customer impact. Verify improvements using the same definitions and conditions.

mfg1-electrical-l013.title: Read drawing scales and line meanings
mfg1-electrical-l013.exampleText: In a training drawing at 1:5, an actual width of 80 mm is drawn as 80 ÷ 5 = 16 mm. If the paper is reduced again when copied, a ruler may no longer show 16 mm. The dimension annotation of 80 mm remains the basis for the actual width. Do not change material width because the picture appears small.
mfg1-electrical-l013.structureTitle: Drawing size and actual size · Lines express visibility and purpose
mfg1-electrical-l013.structureText:
Full scale 1:1 draws the object at actual size, enlarged scale 2:1 at twice its size, and reduced scale 1:2 at half its size. Enlarging a drawing does not double the dimension value written on it. Read a dimension value as the actual dimension of the object.
Copying and screen display can alter drawing size. Do not treat a ruler measurement from a screen or printed drawing as the product dimension. Check written dimensions, units, notes, and revision, and clarify uncertainties before processing.

Thick continuous lines show visible outlines; thin continuous lines serve purposes such as dimension lines; thin chain lines show centers; dashed lines show hidden features. Similar-looking lines can mean different things depending on thickness and pattern. Do not mistake a hole centerline for a cutting outline.
An enlarged portion alone may not show hidden features or datum surfaces. Compare related views, sections, and notes to determine which surface and endpoint define each dimension before work.

mfg1-electrical-l014.title: Use layout and connection drawings for different purposes
mfg1-electrical-l014.exampleText: Even if layout terminal block TB2 is on the left, a connection instruction to TB1-3 does not permit connection to TB2 merely because it is nearby. Verify revision and equipment identification and hold the connection until the discrepancy is resolved. Physical layout, component identification, and destination must agree.
mfg1-electrical-l014.structureTitle: Choose a drawing for the question · Trace names and terminal numbers
mfg1-electrical-l014.structureText:
A layout drawing helps check where equipment goes and the space needed for installation or maintenance. A connection drawing helps check which equipment or terminal connects where. Positions on a drawing do not necessarily show the order in which current flows.
A system diagram helps understand the overall electrical system, while circuit or schematic connection drawings help explain operating relationships. Names and conventions may differ by workplace, so check titles, legends, and notes.

When drawings span several sheets, match equipment symbols, part numbers, and terminal numbers. Do not connect items simply because they are drawn close together. Similar names do not make different numbers or signals the same connection.
Old standards and industry conventions can coexist. Rather than memorizing only one symbol shape, check the standards and legend applicable to the drawing. Read contact behavior together with equipment state: an a contact closes when operated, while a b contact opens when operated.

mfg1-surface-lesson-012.title: Distinguish acidic oxides from basic oxides
mfg1-surface-lesson-012.exampleText: Sort cards marked CO₂, CaO and Al₂O₃ into reactions with bases, with acids and with both respectively. CO₂ is acidic, CaO basic and Al₂O₃ amphoteric. This is a knowledge exercise, not chemical mixing.
mfg1-surface-lesson-012.structureTitle: Classify by the reaction partner · Organize examples by reaction relationships · Keep classification separate from safety
mfg1-surface-lesson-012.structureText:
An oxide is a compound of oxygen and another element. An acidic oxide reacts with a base to form a salt; a basic oxide reacts with an acid to form a salt. Do not reverse the rule by assuming “acidic” means it reacts with an acid.
The corresponding passage in the original textbook was corrected; this unit follows the official errata dated October 1, 2026. Use corrected knowledge rather than copying the original sentence. Confusing phosphorus-oxide names and formulas are not used here.

Carbon dioxide, CO₂, is an acidic oxide; calcium oxide, CaO, is a basic oxide. On paper, match acidic oxides with the base side and basic oxides with the acid side. Reaction conditions and products are not identical in every case.
Aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃, and zinc oxide, ZnO, are amphoteric oxides that can react with both acids and bases. This helps explain relationships between surface oxides and treatment liquids, but does not authorize learners to select process chemicals independently.

A neutral-oxide classification does not mean safe. Carbon monoxide, CO, is an example of a neutral oxide but is a harmful gas. Do not use “neutral” to mean harmless.
Powders, gases and heated solids require different handling even among oxides. Do not classify an unknown material by experimenting with acids or bases; check its name, formula, SDS and approved procedure.

mfg1-surface-lesson-013.title: Distinguish dissolution and precipitation in a process
mfg1-surface-lesson-013.exampleText: White turbidity is found in a bath with a recorded liquid-mixing event. The worker does not independently transfer only the clear portion to the next bath. Report the liquids mixed, time, temperature and turbidity. Do not identify “silver chloride” by colour alone; responsible staff decide analysis and action.
mfg1-surface-lesson-013.structureTitle: Dissolving means becoming uniformly distributed · A reaction can form a sparingly soluble solid · Distinguish analysis from a production-bath abnormality
mfg1-surface-lesson-013.structureText:
A solution is formed when a solute dissolves uniformly in a solvent. In salt water, salt is the solute and water the solvent. Components that are no longer visible have not disappeared; a clear liquid can still contain them.
A solid remaining at the bottom may be incompletely dissolved, exceed solubility, or be a different contaminant. Do not identify composition or quantity from appearance alone; check liquid identity, temperature and mixing history.

Precipitation occurs when components react and a poorly soluble solid appears. With chloride ions Cl⁻ and silver ions Ag⁺, the relationship Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl represents formation of solid silver chloride. Both charge and atom counts balance.
A white solid is not necessarily silver chloride. Other reactions can produce similar-looking solids. Use an appropriate analytical method and procedure; do not identify a compound from observation alone.

Some analytical methods deliberately form and separate a precipitate to determine quantity. Unexpected precipitation in a production bath instead requires investigation of conditions or contamination. A useful analytical phenomenon is not automatically acceptable in production.
Less precipitate or clearer liquid does not prove all components are correct. Filter or add chemicals only within an approved process, and manage both solids and liquids by prescribed methods.

mfg1-surface-lesson-014.title: Estimate material mass from density
mfg1-surface-lesson-014.exampleText: Assume a solid practice aluminium plate of 100 mm × 40 mm × 5 mm and density 2.70 g/cm³. Its volume is 10 cm × 4 cm × 0.5 cm = 20 cm³, so mass is 2.70 × 20 = 54.0 g. Account for cutouts or holes in a real item. This calculation does not identify the material or authorize lifting.
mfg1-surface-lesson-014.structureTitle: Equal size does not mean equal mass · Convert length units first · An estimate does not replace identification or lifting authorization
mfg1-surface-lesson-014.structureText:
Density is mass per unit volume, expressed in units such as g/cm³. At equal volume, denser material has more mass. Distinguish density and its units from specific gravity, a ratio to a reference.
The basic calculation is mass = density × volume. For a hollow item or one with holes, subtract void volume from external volume. Do not assume external dimensions describe a completely solid rectangular block.

Converting mm to cm divides length by ten, but volume is affected in three dimensions: 1 cm³ = 1000 mm³. Align units before multiplying; do not directly multiply g/cm³ by mm³.
Representative values serve practice or estimation, while actual density can vary with alloy composition and temperature. Where material certification or drawings specify a value, check its applicability conditions.

If calculated and measured mass differ substantially, recheck units, holes, shape, quantity and material. Similar mass alone does not prove identical material or quality.
Do not use an estimate alone to lift a heavy item by yourself or judge lifting-gear capacity. Actual weight, centre of gravity, handling procedure and confirmation by responsible personnel are necessary.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-015.title: Distinguish tensile-test and hardness-test results
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-015.exampleText: A force of 10000 N on a specimen of cross-sectional area 25 mm² gives engineering stress of 400 N/mm² = 400 MPa. If a gauge length of 50 mm becomes 51 mm while loaded, extension is 1 mm and engineering strain is 1 ÷ 50 = 0.02, or 2%. These values at a single point must not automatically be called ultimate tensile strength or elongation after fracture.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-015.structureTitle: Principle and decision criteria · Records and common mistakes
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-015.structureText:
A tensile test applies tensile force to a specimen and examines properties from the force and extension. With original cross-sectional area A and force F, engineering stress is F ÷ A. With original gauge length L and extension ΔL, engineering strain is ΔL ÷ L; multiply by 100 for percent. Testing generally continues to fracture, so the specimen cannot be used unchanged as a product.

Hardness testing evaluates another property. Rockwell uses indentation depth, Brinell uses indentation diameter, and Vickers uses diagonal length. HRC, HBW, and HV relate to test methods and conditions, rather than being decorative labels. Do not extract only the number and compare different methods as though they share one scale; assess using the specified method and conditions.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-016.title: Match nondestructive inspection to the defect’s location
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-016.exampleText: Suppose visual examination of a weld reveals no obvious crack. This alone does not establish that there is no internal defect. Confirm the required inspection scope and method. Similarly, do not assume magnetic particle testing applies to a nonmagnetic material; ask the inspection specialist to verify compatibility between material and method.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-016.structureTitle: Principle and decision criteria · Records and common mistakes
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-016.structureText:
Nondestructive inspection investigates defects without destruction that makes the object unusable. Radiographic testing uses differences in transmission, and ultrasonic testing uses reflections and related signals to investigate the interior. Magnetic particle testing examines the surface or near surface of objects that can be magnetized; penetrant testing examines defects open to the surface. Detectable defects and applicable materials vary by method.

Sensory inspection uses sight, hearing, and other senses, but should align lighting, reference samples, and acceptance criteria rather than rely only on individual impressions. “No abnormality detected” is a result under specified conditions; no method necessarily detects every defect. Record the method, scope, and conditions together with the result.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-017.title: Align pre-measurement conditions and reading methods
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-017.exampleText: Two people measure the same shaft and obtain different readings. One reads the instrument from an angle; the other measures the hot shaft immediately after machining. Before taking an average, align the measurement method and temperature conditions and check again. Record both values, times, and object conditions; do not combine measurements from different conditions without qualification.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-017.structureTitle: Principle and decision criteria · Records and common mistakes
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-017.structureText:
Measurements are affected by the instrument, operator, temperature, setup, and other factors. Read the scale straight on because an oblique view creates parallax. Check calibration relating the indication to a reference, daily inspection records, and validity; a correct zero alone does not guarantee correctness across the full range.

A jig is an aid for holding the object or instrument steadily. A V-block can hold cylindrical objects, but improper clamping force or positioning can cause deformation or tilt. Decide the reference, measurement location, and holding method before measuring. Do not adjust an instrument found to be offset without authorization and continue using it.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-018.title: Use caliper measuring faces and the vernier correctly
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-018.exampleText: With a 0.05 mm least-reading vernier caliper, a main-scale reading of 18 mm and alignment at the fourth vernier division give 4 × 0.05 = 0.20 mm on the vernier. The total is 18.20 mm. Check the instrument’s least reading first so the fourth division is not interpreted as 0.4 mm. This is a calculation example; actual alignment must be read straight on at the instrument.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-018.structureTitle: Principle and decision criteria · Records and common mistakes
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-018.structureText:
Calipers have outside and inside jaws; models with a depth bar also measure depth. Choose the correct measuring faces and check cleanliness, smooth movement, play, gaps when closed, and zero. Clean the workpiece too, and handle burrs using the approved method. Squeezing harder does not necessarily improve accuracy.

For outside dimensions, hold the part steadily as near the root of the jaws as practicable and avoid reading while tilted. For inside and depth measurements, also check contact with the object. Digital display resolution and measurement accuracy are different. A fine display alone does not establish suitability for judging a required tolerance; use the specified instrument.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-019.title: Check micrometer measuring force and the half-millimetre mark
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-019.exampleText: For a 0.5 mm screw pitch and a thimble divided into 50 divisions per revolution, one division is 0.01 mm. If the sleeve shows 7.5 mm and the thimble shows 0.23 mm, the result is 7.73 mm. Reading only 7 mm and missing the half-millimetre mark creates a 0.5 mm error. First identify the last visible sleeve graduation.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-019.structureTitle: Principle and decision criteria · Records and common mistakes
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-019.structureText:
An outside micrometer grips the object between the screw-driven spindle and the fixed anvil. Clean the measuring faces and check zero or the datum using a reference suitable for the range. Let the instrument and object acclimatize to the specified environment to reduce temperature effects. The textbook gives 20°C as the reference. Rushing to measure a hot product makes dimensional comparison inappropriate.

After contact, use the specified constant-force device and do not overtighten. Follow the instrument instructions for how to use it and how many operations are required. Do not select a reading obtained by excessive tightening as the correct one; align posture and contact before reading. Do not add digits without authorization, and follow the procedure for recorded digits and units.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-020.title: Read drawings through scale and line types
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-020.exampleText: On a part drawing at 2:1, a feature is dimensioned as 12. The feature may appear about 24 mm long on the drawing, but the specified actual size is 12 mm. In a separate scale-calculation exercise stating “30 mm on the drawing at 1:5,” the actual size is 30 × 5 = 150 mm. Distinguish reading a dimension instruction from a scale-calculation exercise.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-020.structureTitle: Principle and decision criteria · Records and common mistakes
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-020.structureText:
A 1:1 scale is full size, 2:1 is an enlargement to twice the actual size, and 1:2 is a reduction to half size. Written dimensions indicate the object’s actual size regardless of scale. Screen magnification or print size may also change, so do not determine machining dimensions solely by measuring the screen or paper with a ruler.

Visible outlines use thick continuous lines; dimension and extension lines use thin continuous lines; hidden outlines use dashed lines; centres normally use thin chain lines with one dash and one dot. Mistaking a centre line for an outline changes the interpreted shape. Part drawings support machining, assembly drawings support assembly, and layout drawings show equipment positions; check the suitable drawing and revision for the task.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-021.title: Read dimensional tolerances and supplementary symbols
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-021.exampleText: An imaginary shaft has nominal size 20 mm, upper deviation +0.04 mm, and lower deviation −0.02 mm. The upper limit is 20.04 mm, the lower limit 19.98 mm, and the tolerance 0.06 mm. In a simple limit comparison, 20.03 mm is in range and 19.97 mm is outside. However, readings near a limit must follow the specified measuring method and decision rule; do not round for convenience.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-021.structureTitle: Principle and decision criteria · Records and common mistakes
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-021.structureText:
A dimension has a permitted range; the difference between its upper and lower limits is the tolerance. In a display adding signed deviations to a nominal dimension, the upper entry is the upper deviation and the lower entry is the lower deviation. Add them with their signs to obtain limit dimensions. Do not treat the two numbers as unsigned magnitudes and add or subtract by appearance.

φ denotes diameter, R radius, and t thickness. φ10 and R10 are not the same size; a circle with R10 has diameter 20. Tolerance-class uppercase letters are used for holes and lowercase letters for shafts; consult the appropriate table for numerical ranges. Do not infer the actual fit from the letter’s position alone; check the limit dimensions of both the mating hole and shaft.

mfg1-electrical-l015.title: Distinguish conducting, magnetic, and insulating materials
mfg1-electrical-l015.exampleText: In a transformer teaching model, the current-carrying winding, flux-carrying core, and insulation separating windings have different roles. Use a conducting material for the winding, an appropriate magnetic material for the core, and an appropriate insulating material for separation. Specifications determine actual grades and temperature ratings; this model explanation does not authorize substitute materials in real products.
mfg1-electrical-l015.structureTitle: Do not confuse the three roles · A material name alone does not guarantee insulation
mfg1-electrical-l015.structureText:
Conducting materials carry current; copper and aluminum are used for wires according to application. Magnetic materials use magnetic effects, as in transformer cores. Insulating materials resist current and separate conductors. Different materials fulfill these roles even within one component.
High conductivity does not make a material optimal for every condition. Also check weight, workability, temperature, mechanical strength, and joining method. Aluminum conducts electricity but cannot be treated as the same magnetic material as iron.

Insulating performance can change with overheating, dirt, damage, and aging. Check thermal class, operating temperature, environment, and required thickness against specifications. Do not assume safety just because something looks like plastic or rubber.
This lesson applies the October 1, 2026 errata. Remove “natural rubber” from the inorganic insulating examples on printed page 70 of the uploaded PDF; the inorganic examples are mica and ceramic. Do not memorize natural rubber as an inorganic material.

mfg1-electrical-l016.title: Read resistor markings and tolerance
mfg1-electrical-l016.exampleText: Orange–orange–brown–gold gives significant digits 33, multiplier 10¹, and tolerance ±5%. Thus 33 × 10 = 330 Ω, also written as 0.330 kΩ. Joining all color digits to make 331 Ω is incorrect: the third band sets a multiplying factor, not another digit.
mfg1-electrical-l016.structureTitle: Read the four bands separately · Nominal value and range
mfg1-electrical-l016.structureText:
For a common four-band marking, the first two bands are significant digits, the third is a multiplier, and the last is tolerance. The digit colors are black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, gray 8, and white 9. Gold tolerance is ±5%; silver is ±10%.
Do not apply this method unchanged to components with another band count or special markings. Check the specification if reading direction or band meaning is unclear. Do not infer the original value of a burnt component solely from its remaining colors.

Tolerance indicates the allowed deviation from a nominal value. For 330 Ω at ±5%, 330 × 0.05 = 16.5 Ω, giving a calculated range of 313.5–346.5 Ω. Actual incoming acceptance follows measurement conditions and component specifications.
Equal resistance does not imply equal power rating, operating temperature, or size. Reading the resistance from a color code does not establish that another resistor is a suitable replacement.

mfg1-electrical-l017.title: Calculate series and parallel circuits
mfg1-electrical-l017.exampleText: Connect the same 1 kΩ and 2 kΩ in parallel across 12 V: branch currents are 12 mA and 6 mA, total 18 mA. Equivalent resistance is (1000 × 2000)/(1000 + 2000) ≈ 666.7 Ω. The same components give very different total current when connected differently. These are ideal calculations; real connections require checks of supply capacity, component ratings, heating, and protection.
mfg1-electrical-l017.structureTitle: Identify what is common · Series example
mfg1-electrical-l017.structureText:
Two resistors in a single series path carry the same current. Equivalent resistance is R = R1 + R2; voltages are V1 = IR1 and V2 = IR2. Supply voltage equals their sum.
In parallel, both ends connect to the same two points, so each resistor has the same voltage. Branch currents are I1 = V/R1 and I2 = V/R2, and total current is their sum. For two resistors, R = R1R2/(R1 + R2); for positive resistances the result is smaller than the smaller resistor.

Calculate a 1 kΩ resistor and a 2 kΩ resistor in series across an ideal 12 V DC source. Equivalent resistance is 3 kΩ = 3000 Ω; current is 12 ÷ 3000 = 0.004 A = 4 mA. The 1 kΩ voltage is 4 V and the 2 kΩ voltage is 8 V; check 4 + 8 = 12 V. The larger resistance takes the larger voltage share.

mfg1-electrical-l018.title: Understand diode direction and rectification
mfg1-electrical-l018.exampleText: In an idealized single-diode explanation, passing only one side of AC produces intervals with and without current. Reversing the diode reverses which side passes. This illustrates directionality, not a procedure for direct connection to an AC supply. Real rectifier circuits also require appropriate ratings and other components.
mfg1-electrical-l018.structureTitle: Two terminals and direction · Rectification and mounting checks
mfg1-electrical-l018.structureText:
A diode is a semiconductor component with two terminals: anode A and cathode K. In a basic explanation, the anode-to-cathode direction is forward, while the opposite direction resists current. Do not assume it can be fitted either way just because it has two leads.
Actual components have forward voltage, allowable current, reverse voltage ratings, and other conditions. Do not assume reverse current is absolutely zero under every circumstance; use the part within specifications. Intended functions also vary by type, such as Zener diodes.

In AC, voltage direction changes repeatedly. Using diode directionality can select current corresponding to one direction, which is the basic idea of rectification. The resulting waveform is not necessarily a constant flat DC output immediately.
For mounting, match A/K on the circuit drawing with part polarity markings and board markings. Check the component documentation for band or mark meaning instead of judging from a similar shape. Hold and clarify a polarity mismatch before energization.

mfg1-electrical-l019.title: Prepare to protect electronic parts from static electricity
mfg1-electrical-l019.exampleText: Before assembly, ICs are in an ordinary clear bag and there is no verification record for the specified bench mat. Hold opening and have the responsible person check packaging specifications and workplace records. Do not improvise by attaching metal wire; handle parts only after an approved environment is ready. A clean appearance does not justify skipping the procedure.
mfg1-electrical-l019.structureTitle: Prevent damage you cannot see · Prepare components and the environment
mfg1-electrical-l019.structureText:
Static electricity can change characteristics or damage ICs and other electronic parts. Not feeling a discharge and seeing no external defect do not guarantee absence of damage. Arrange precautions before opening packaging, not just checks after work.
A bench, mat, clothing, floor, or shoes alone do not complete protection. Use the workplace-specified combination and verification method and confirm equipment and accessories are in good condition. Conductive static-control measures must also satisfy protection of people from electric shock.

Check required part and material numbers, quantities, deterioration, and damage before work. Identify and organize parts by type, provide adequate space and lighting, and keep unrelated packaging and waste off the static-controlled surface.
Use specified static-protective packaging for transport and storage. The presence of a bag does not mean every bag performs the same way. Clarify handling uncertainties before opening or transferring components. Do not begin with unanswered questions about the work instructions.

mfg1-electrical-l020.title: Reason about AND and OR in sequence control
mfg1-electrical-l020.exampleText: “Lamp L turns on when both A and B are on” specifies AND. At A = 1, B = 0 it stays off; at both 1 it turns on. Changing the wording to “at least one of A or B is on” specifies OR, so A = 1, B = 0 also lights it. Different conditions change output even with the same two inputs.
mfg1-electrical-l020.structureTitle: Distinguish sequence from conditions · Check all four combinations
mfg1-electrical-l020.structureText:
Sequence control advances stages in a predetermined order or procedure. It may use combinations of relays and other components or a PLC program. Separate when events happen from the conditions that produce an output.
Here, 0 means off and 1 means on in a teaching indicator-lamp example. AND outputs 1 only when all inputs are 1; OR outputs 1 when at least one is 1; NOT reverses an input. OR does not mean “only one or the other”: both inputs being 1 also produces 1.

For A/B combinations 00, 01, 10, and 11, AND outputs are 0, 0, 0, 1, while OR outputs are 0, 1, 1, 1. NOT of A alone gives output 1 at A = 0 and 0 at A = 1. Tables help expose confusion with everyday uses of “or.”
In basic examples using a/NO contacts that close when their inputs turn on, series contacts represent AND and parallel contacts represent OR. This explains logic; it is not sufficient by itself to design a real safety circuit. Failure behavior and safety standards need separate consideration.

mfg1-electrical-l021.title: Distinguish preventive from corrective maintenance
mfg1-electrical-l021.exampleText: In a teaching example, replacing a part every fixed number of hours is planned preventive maintenance; deciding service from increasing continuously monitored vibration is predictive maintenance; repair after a failure stops the unit is corrective maintenance. Different parts of the same machine may use different approaches. Workers report signs and respect the boundary where maintenance personnel make the decision.
mfg1-electrical-l021.structureTitle: When and on what basis to intervene · Replacement count alone does not show merit
mfg1-electrical-l021.structureText:
Preventive maintenance checks and services equipment before failure to reduce failure occurrence. It can include scheduled replacement based on service period or operating hours. Predictive maintenance monitors conditions such as vibration or temperature and uses signs of deterioration to judge service needs.
Corrective maintenance responds after a fault or failure. Selecting an approach requires considering failure impact, safety, downtime losses, monitoring cost, and replacement cost together. A cheap component is not automatically suitable to run until failure.

Early replacement may reduce unexpected stoppages but may also discard usable parts. Condition monitoring can reduce waste but requires defined targets, management thresholds, measurement methods, and systems. Collecting numbers alone does not establish predictive maintenance.
Record equipment identification, date/time, operating conditions, observations or measurements, differences from normal, and whom you informed. For an unusual sound, note when it occurs and the operating state rather than just “sounds odd”; this supports investigation.

mfg1-surface-lesson-015.title: Verify the identity of copper, aluminium and zinc alloys
mfg1-surface-lesson-015.exampleText: Two copper-coloured component types arrive in one box; one delivery document says brass and the other bronze. Do not group them by appearance. Separate part numbers and lots, then check material codes and work instructions. Zinc is a typical brass addition and tin a typical bronze addition, but that knowledge alone does not identify individual items.
mfg1-surface-lesson-015.structureTitle: The main component does not fully define an alloy · Check aluminium and zinc varieties too · Do not identify unknown material by trial
mfg1-surface-lesson-015.structureText:
An alloy combines a principal metal with other elements to adjust properties. Typical copper-based examples are brass with zinc, bronze with tin, and cupronickel with nickel. Actual alloys may have other additions, so a name alone does not reveal exact proportions.
Materials are selected according to priorities such as conductivity, strength and corrosion resistance. Different substrates affect pretreatment and finish; similar-looking items cannot automatically be processed together.

Aluminium alloys retain lightness while adjusting properties and are used in machining, forming or casting. A material designation such as ADC12 gives more specific identification than simply saying “aluminium.”
Zinc is used for coatings on ferrous materials and in die-casting alloys. A zinc-alloy substrate and a zinc surface film have different roles. Recording substrate, undercoat and outermost layer separately helps prevent mix-ups.

At receipt, compare drawings, material codes, lot labels and certificates. Do not identify unlabelled material solely by colour or weight, or by testing a reaction in acid. Identify unverified items and route them through an approved verification method.
When materials change, responsible staff check whether existing pretreatment remains suitable and whether required appearance or inspection methods are affected. Verifying material and having authority to change process settings are separate matters.

mfg1-surface-lesson-016.title: Control degreasing and activation in sequence
mfg1-surface-lesson-016.exampleText: A lot has finished activation but waits longer than planned because equipment stops. Do not decide “another acid dip will fix it.” Record stop time, holding condition, lot and completed stages. The responsible person checks surface condition and procedure before deciding the next action.
mfg1-surface-lesson-016.structureTitle: Cleaning stages have different roles · Maintain the activated surface condition · Pass preceding-stage information forward
mfg1-surface-lesson-016.structureText:
Before electroplating, degreasing removes oils and contamination, while activation removes oxides and prepares the surface. Calling both simply “washing” obscures the defect each stage prevents. Select liquids and methods for the substrate.
Control degreasing concentration, temperature and time. Residual contamination can repel liquid or impair adhesion, but absence of visible oil alone does not prove adequate degreasing. Use the specified verification method.

Activation uses chemicals and conditions suited to the substrate surface. Both insufficient and excessive treatment can cause problems; check concentration, temperature, duration and delay before the next stage. A stronger bath or longer immersion is not necessarily better and can be dangerous.
Rinsing after treatment removes the previous liquid and limits carryover to the next bath. Check rinse routing and cleanliness, and do not skip stages. Rinse water is also controlled waste and cannot automatically be discharged untreated.

Record part number, lot, bath, time and conditions so later adhesion defects can be investigated. Identify and report affected items if waiting unexpectedly increases, the wrong bath is used or conditions go out of range.
Returning an item to a previous stage without authorization loses traceability and risks overprocessing or mixing liquids. Responsible staff decide whether and how to reprocess according to material and quality requirements.

mfg1-surface-lesson-017.title: Investigate blistering and discolouration through process history
mfg1-surface-lesson-017.exampleText: A component looked normal immediately after drying but developed local discolouration by the next day. Provide the responsible person with the affected position, storage location, packaging and drying/rinsing records. Do not prematurely conclude storage caused it; also compare unaffected items held under the same conditions.
mfg1-surface-lesson-017.structureTitle: Describe the observed condition precisely · Trace possible contributing stages · Control product disposition while investigating
mfg1-surface-lesson-017.structureText:
Blistering is a raised film separating from the substrate. Discolouration is a colour change; an unplated area is one that should have received coating but did not. First record location, extent and shape on the item.
“Bad plating” is insufficient information for investigation. Standardize inspection conditions, retain photographs or location sketches, and link discovery time to the lot. Do not polish away the appearance or flatten the blister to conceal it.

Inadequate pretreatment, such as degreasing or activation, can contribute to blistering or unplated areas. Rinsing, storage, substrate and deposits can contribute to discolouration. Appearance alone does not confirm one cause.
Compare other items in the lot, positions on the same jig, processing records and storage conditions. Compare affected and unaffected items under consistent conditions rather than looking only at defective ones.

Even before identifying a cause, keep suspect items separate from acceptable goods. Identify and hold them, determine the potentially affected scope, and follow designated authority for shipment decisions. A worker cannot approve shipment merely because a defect looks small.
After corrective action, verify improvement using the same inspection method. A mark becoming invisible under different lighting or changing the recorded position does not prove improvement. Also check how reprocessing affects dimensions and performance.

mfg1-surface-lesson-018.title: Understand pretreatment and bath control in hot-dip coating
mfg1-surface-lesson-018.exampleText: Two same-shaped items differ: one looks dry and the other retains liquid in a recess. Do not judge them equivalent from visible flat areas alone. Follow drying and shape-specific checks. If uncertain, hold the item and explain the reason to the responsible person rather than immersing it.
mfg1-surface-lesson-018.structureTitle: Form a coating in a molten-metal bath · Degreasing, pickling, fluxing and drying · Do not control the process by temperature alone
mfg1-surface-lesson-018.structureText:
Hot-dip coating immerses a substrate in molten metal and forms a film through withdrawal, cooling and related stages. It differs from electroplating, which uses current to deposit metal from solution. Hot-dip galvanizing is a representative example.
Conditions vary with bath metal, substrate combination, shape and dimensions. Even for corrosion-resistant applications, thicker is not automatically better. Check required dimensions, appearance, alloy layers and other specified properties.

Removing oil and oxides is important for proper contact with molten metal. Flux treatment helps preserve the surface after pickling and assists reaction between substrate and molten metal. Use the specified liquid and sequence for the product.
Drying before immersion is important to reduce molten-metal splashing. Do not assume an item is dry when it is wet or retains liquid internally. Follow the prescribed checks and equipment requirements for its shape.

Temperature, immersion time, withdrawal, cooling and finishing influence the film. A normal equipment display does not authorize processing when material or pretreatment is unverified. Retain history and investigate preceding stages if an unplated area or another defect appears.
High-temperature baths, splashes and handling create serious hazards. A lesson on principles is not equipment-operation authorization. Learn exclusion zones, transport methods and emergency actions through training, and work only within your instructions.

mfg1-surface-lesson-019.title: Separate the mechanisms of electroless and dry coating
mfg1-surface-lesson-019.exampleText: A worker is about to apply electroless-bath conditions to an item specified for PVD. Because film-formation mechanisms differ, those settings cannot be transferred. Confirm process type, substrate, required pretreatment and equipment with the responsible person before proceeding.
mfg1-surface-lesson-019.structureTitle: Chemical plating without external current to the item · No external current does not mean no control · Distinguish PVD and CVD by formation mechanism
mfg1-surface-lesson-019.structureText:
Electroless plating forms metal films chemically rather than passing current from an external supply to the item as in ordinary electroplating. Methods include reducing-agent processes and displacement processes that react with the substrate. Do not treat their reactions as identical.
Some reduction processes require pretreatment such as applying a catalyst. In an autocatalytic process, the deposited film catalyses further reaction. Applying the method to a nonconductive substrate requires appropriate pretreatment and material compatibility.

Electroless processes still require concentration, temperature, pH and agitation control. A process that can produce relatively uniform films on complex shapes does not automatically solve inaccessible areas or unsuitable pretreatment.
Nickel-phosphorus, copper and gold processes are selected for applications and required properties. Do not decide a material change from a teaching example alone; check process instructions and quality requirements.

Dry PVD deposits material physically, using evaporation or sputtering. CVD forms a film through chemical reactions involving gaseous precursors. Both differ from ordinary wet plating by immersion in an aqueous bath.
“Dry” does not mean no hazardous substances or exhaust. Vacuum, high temperature, power, precursor gases and exhaust treatment require controls appropriate to the machine and method. Follow dedicated training and procedures for operation and maintenance.

mfg1-surface-lesson-020.title: Check wastewater segregation and treatment status
mfg1-surface-lesson-020.exampleText: Liquid at a treatment outlet has become clear, but analytical results are pending. Do not assume it is ready for discharge; keep it awaiting the prescribed confirmation. If another leak is found, do not add a different waste liquid without knowing its pH; report to the responsible person.
mfg1-surface-lesson-020.structureTitle: Rinse water still contains components · Do not mix different streams · Check treatment results separately from leakage
mfg1-surface-lesson-020.structureText:
Rinse water from plating or anodizing may contain chemicals and metals carried over from preceding stages. Clarity does not prove absence of harmful substances. Prevent unmanaged discharge to rivers or seepage into the ground.
Treatment requirements are not limited to pH. Control conditions depend on substances, concentrations and discharge destinations. The responsible environmental staff verify current permits and rules; this lesson does not set legal limits or authorize discharge.

Segregate wastewater and spent liquids into designated streams according to composition and treatment method. If labels or piping identification are unclear, hold the transfer and check rather than judging by colour. Classifying liquids as acidic or alkaline does not make every mixture permissible.
Some mixtures generate hazardous gas or heat. Learners must not mix small quantities to test them or dilute waste down a drain. Trained personnel follow prescribed methods for sampling, transfer and treatment.

Even after separating solids, a clear liquid may retain dissolved components. Judge treatment through required analysis and checks rather than appearance. Removed solids also require prescribed waste management.
A leak around floors or pipes can still affect the environment after drying. Report from a safe position to prevent escalation, recording location, time, suspected stream and visible conditions. Do not independently neutralize an unknown leak.

mfg1-surface-lesson-021.title: Record exhaust, noise and environmental controls
mfg1-surface-lesson-021.exampleText: After a complaint about night-time fan noise, the responsible staff organize operating times, work activities, noise and exhaust-equipment conditions. Workers report rather than stop the fan themselves. After corrective action, verify required exhaust performance as well as noise under comparable conditions.
mfg1-surface-lesson-021.structureTitle: One control can create another impact · Distinguish ambient conditions from discharge control · Plan, act, check and revise improvements
mfg1-surface-lesson-021.structureText:
Surface treatment requires controls for chemical mist, solvent vapour and dust according to the source and equipment. Exhaust and scrubbing equipment reduce worker and environmental exposure, but fans and similar machinery may create noise.
Stopping exhaust to reduce noise can increase a different hazard. Rather than lowering one number alone, consider equipment function, work conditions and surrounding impacts together. Operational changes require responsible staff evaluation and authorization.

Distinguish evaluating the surrounding environment from controlling substances and quantities leaving equipment. Check site conditions according to equipment scope, location and time. Specific legal limits and notifications must be managed from current sources.
Little odour does not prove safety. Do not judge gas concentration by smell; use prescribed inspection and measurement. Record discovery time and equipment status for unusual sound, exhaust changes, leaks or complaints too.

Environmental management identifies which activities cause which impacts and defines targets, actions and verification. Continual improvement is important in ISO 14001’s approach. Certification does not automatically make every emission or task compliant.
The 3Rs—reduce use, reuse and recycle—must preserve quality and safety. Do not mix chemicals or change waste classifications without authorization to save liquid. Record before-and-after results under comparable conditions to verify effects.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-022.title: Connect daily and periodic inspections
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-022.exampleText: This morning’s checklist includes leaks, unusual sounds, and cover condition. A completed periodic inspection yesterday does not remove the need to check for leaks this morning. If insufficient lighting prevents a check, record why it remains unconfirmed instead of marking it normal, and consult the responsible person about how to check and whether operation is permitted. A completion mark must reflect work actually performed.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-022.structureTitle: Principle and process role · Conditions and records to check
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-022.structureText:
Preventive maintenance is an approach to checking equipment condition to prevent failures and accidents, rather than only repairing it after a breakdown. Daily checks cover specified items before work and at other designated times to detect small changes early. Periodic inspections follow a plan and examine details that daily checks alone may not reveal. Performing one does not permit omission of the other.

Link equipment number, date and time, condition, and action in the inspection record. Comparable observations are more useful for tracking change than simply writing “same as usual.” Repair and internal inspection require authority and safety measures. Dismantling beyond the scope you can inspect is not evidence of greater diligence.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-023.title: Separate density from a material’s response to force
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-023.exampleText:
Consider a component of volume 20 cm³. Assuming densities of 2.70 g/cm³ for aluminum and 7.87 g/cm³ for iron, their calculated masses are 54.0 g and 157.4 g respectively. However, lower mass does not authorize replacement of a specified iron component with aluminum. Required strength, deformation behavior, temperature conditions, and other factors must also be checked. Density varies with the material and alloy.

Use the volume of the material itself in a density calculation. For a homogeneous paper model with ρ=2.5 g/cm³, an enclosing volume of 24 cm³ and a material-free cavity of 4 cm³, the material volume is 24−4=20 cm³ and the mass is 2.5×20=50 g. No other material is present. To infer cavity volume, subtract mass/density from the enclosing volume: a mass of 45 g gives 24−45/2.5=6 cm³. These model values do not identify a real material or certify a real part's integrity.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-023.structureTitle: Principle and process role · Conditions and records to check
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-023.structureText:
Density is mass per unit volume. Objects of the same volume can have different masses when their materials differ. Elasticity means deformation recovers after force is removed; plasticity means deformation remains. Hardness and toughness—the ability to resist fracture under impact and similar loading—are also different properties. “Light” or “hard” alone does not establish suitability for an application.

A bent sheet can spring back partly when force is removed. Separating elastic recovery from the plastic deformation that remains helps explain the final shape. Do not determine material grade solely by appearance, color, or how heavy it feels; check the material identification and records. Material substitution involves design and quality decisions.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-024.title: Distinguish steel heat treatments by purpose
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-024.exampleText: An imaginary tool-component process sheet specifies “temper under the specified conditions after quenching.” Do not assume the component is complete simply because quenching made it hard; confirm completion of the entire sequence, including tempering and inspection. Similarly, an instruction to soften material before further machining cannot be replaced with quenching because the names sound similar.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-024.structureTitle: Principle and process role · Conditions and records to check
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-024.structureText:
Heat treatment changes metal structure and properties through heating and cooling conditions. In typical steel treatments, quenching is used to increase hardness, while tempering adjusts hardness, toughness, and other properties after quenching. Annealing may soften the material to improve machinability. Not every metal hardens in the same way under identical heating and cooling.

Surface hardening improves surface properties, so the interior and surface are not necessarily in the same condition. Welding also creates a heat-affected zone around the melted area. Match the material, treatment purpose, temperature, time, cooling conditions, and inspection results. This lesson explains the concepts; it is not an operating instruction for setting heat-treatment conditions.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-025.title: Distinguish the motions of lathes, milling machines, and drill presses
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-025.exampleText: Consider a sequence that finishes a round bar’s outside diameter, then makes a flat mounting face and a hole. A lathe, milling machine, and drill press are possible choices, but the actual route is determined by the drawing, machine capability, and approved process sheet. Do not assume a round starting material must stay on a lathe throughout. A machining center has automatic tool-changing capability and can perform several operations.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-025.structureTitle: Principle and process role · Conditions and records to check
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-025.structureText:
Cutting removes material with a tool to form the required shape. A lathe mainly rotates the workpiece against a tool to machine features such as outside diameters. A milling machine rotates the tool and uses relative movement between tool and workpiece to produce flats and grooves. A drill press rotates a drill to make holes. Distinguishing what rotates helps explain machine roles and danger areas.

Cutting produces heat and chips. Cutting fluids and coolants help remove heat, reduce tool wear, and carry away chips, but adding fluid alone does not prove an unusual sound or poor finish has been resolved. Compare clamping, tooling, and cutting conditions with the records. The source figure numbers have corrections, so identify references by page and machine name.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-026.title: Distinguish grinding and polishing objectives
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-026.exampleText: Even if a shaft looks shiny, an outside diameter above the upper limit is not dimensionally acceptable. Conversely, an acceptable size does not establish that the required roughness has been met. Refinishing also removes material and changes size, so confirm the available machining allowance and approved disposition before proceeding.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-026.structureTitle: Principle and process role · Conditions and records to check
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-026.structureText:
Grinding removes small amounts of material using abrasive grains in a wheel and is used for hard materials or surfaces requiring high dimensional accuracy. Polishing conditions a surface with abrasives and similar media. Its purposes include appearance, roughness, and friction, but a shinier surface is not necessarily better for every application. Check drawing requirements for size and surface condition separately.

The wheel or polishing medium must suit the material, processing purpose, and equipment conditions. Do not substitute a similar-looking item without permission. Link the processed location with its inspection result and do not use gloss as a substitute for measurement. This lesson does not replace the education or qualifications required for wheel replacement or trial running.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-027.title: Compare how welding, casting, and plastic forming create shapes
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-027.exampleText: Compare three objectives: joining two sheets, making a body with complex spaces in a mold, and pressing a sheet into a bend. Welding, casting, and press work are possible choices respectively. However, do not select a method from shape alone; check material, required strength, production quantity, and later processes. Several methods can be combined, such as machining after casting.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-027.structureTitle: Principle and process role · Conditions and records to check
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-027.structureText:
Welding joins members using heat, pressure, or related means. Casting pours molten metal into a mold and solidifies it into shape. Plastic forming applies force to solid material and retains deformation to form a shape. These mechanisms differ from cutting, which removes material. Examples of plastic forming include press work, forging, and rolling.

A good-looking joint, a casting removed from its mold, or a pressed item that appears to have the correct shape does not alone prove that all requirements are met. Confirm process-appropriate internal, dimensional, and visual inspections. Consider heat-induced changes around a weld and springback after forming, and consult before changing methods outside your authority.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-028.title: Match roughness parameters and measurement conditions
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-028.exampleText: An imaginary instruction requires “Ra no greater than 0.8 μm,” but the result field only states “Rz 3.2 μm.” You cannot decide acceptance by comparing the numbers alone. The parameters differ, so confirm a result measured for the specified Ra under the required conditions. A separate acceptable outside-diameter result cannot substitute for roughness acceptance.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-028.structureTitle: Principle and process role · Conditions and records to check
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-028.structureText:
Surface roughness describes small surface irregularities and relates to friction, wear, lubrication, and appearance. Ra is arithmetic mean roughness and Rz is maximum-height roughness. Check the parameter, unit, and measurement conditions against the drawing requirement. A smaller roughness value is not unconditionally better for every function.

A stylus roughness instrument converts needle motion into a signal to examine irregularities. Location, direction, and surface contamination can affect the result, so follow the specified measurement method. Record parameter name, value, unit, and location, aligning the conditions for comparison. Take care not to damage a precision surface through the stylus or cleaning.

mfg1-electrical-l022.title: Distinguish coils from capacitors
mfg1-electrical-l022.exampleText: Two capacitors have the same capacitance, but one is rated 16 V and the other 50 V. Equal capacitance does not mean equal specifications. Check polarity, dimensions, temperature, permitted conditions, and operating voltage, and use the approved part number. A resistance reading across a coil also does not mean it functions like a capacitor or resistor.
mfg1-electrical-l022.structureTitle: Similar appearance, different functions · Separate the initial transient from the settled state
mfg1-electrical-l022.structureText:
A coil consists of wound wire; some use a magnetic core. Its distinctive feature is the relationship between current and magnetism. A capacitor separates conductors with insulation and stores charge. Size or terminal count alone does not establish whether a part serves as a coil, capacitor, or resistor.
Capacitors include electrolytic, ceramic, and film types with different capacitance, voltage rating, polarity, temperature, and other conditions. Equal capacitance alone does not justify substituting another type. For polarized types such as some electrolytic capacitors, compare documentation with mounting orientation.

In a basic ideal example, connecting a capacitor through a resistor to a DC source causes charging current, then no current in the fully charged steady state. This is an idealized explanation, not a safety guarantee that ignores real leakage or failure.
Charge may remain after power is switched off. A switch being off does not establish absence of hazardous energy. Do not invent a discharge method or waiting time; follow workplace procedures.

mfg1-electrical-l023.title: Transistor amplification and switching
mfg1-electrical-l023.exampleTitle: Limit the use of a ratio calculation
mfg1-electrical-l023.exampleText: At one teaching operating point, suppose base current is 0.10 mA and collector current is 8 mA. The ratio there is 8 ÷ 0.10 = 80. This does not establish a constant 80-fold ratio with other loads or unlimited collector current. Explain the result with its conditions, type, and maximum ratings.
mfg1-electrical-l023.structureTitle: Match the three terminals · Do not select by gain alone
mfg1-electrical-l023.structureText:
A bipolar transistor has base B, collector C, and emitter E. PNP and NPN types differ in structure and operating polarity. Do not assume all three-lead parts have the same pin order; check each part-number diagram. Similar packages may have different terminal arrangements.
In basic terms, the base input controls collector current. Amplifying small signal changes and switching current on and off have different purposes and operating conditions.

Current gain hFE is the ratio of collector current to base current under specified operating conditions. It is not a universal fixed multiplier; it changes with conditions and the part. Nor can the on state in switching be determined unconditionally from an amplification equation alone.
Parts have maximum terminal voltages, currents, dissipation, and other ratings. A part may control a signal yet overheat or fail beyond those limits. Check the usage conditions and specification restrictions together rather than treating ratings as unrelated numbers.

mfg1-electrical-l024.title: Organize ICs and analog and digital circuit functions
mfg1-electrical-l024.exampleText:
For a teaching system sending a continuous temperature-related voltage to a computer, consider: sensor analog signal → necessary signal conditioning → A/D conversion → digital processing. A supply regulator supports the power conditions but does not replace A/D conversion. Check actual signal ranges and supply voltage against the IC specifications.

Match each function to the required input and output. A/D converts a continuous sensor voltage to digital data; D/A converts digital data to an analog output. Memory retains data, logic ICs process logical conditions, and an MPU performs computing and control. A voltage regulator stabilizes the supply rather than converting or storing data. Amplification increases an input signal’s amplitude; oscillation generates a sustained periodic signal, not merely a larger external signal. In a paper communications model, modulation places information on a carrier and demodulation retrieves it. AM varies carrier amplitude, FM frequency, PM phase. These function names do not authorize interchangeable IC replacement; pinout, signal range and power specifications still matter.
mfg1-electrical-l024.structureTitle: Consider how signals are handled · Circuit names and purposes
mfg1-electrical-l024.structureText:
Analog signals represent continuously varying quantities, while digital signals use discrete values. Analog functions include op-amp amplification and voltage-regulator supply stabilization; digital functions include logic processing and memory. Similar-looking ICs can have very different functions.
A/D conversion turns an analog quantity into a digital value; D/A does the reverse. These functions bridge signal domains. Explaining input and output with arrows is more useful than memorizing their names as one group.

An amplifier takes a small signal and produces a larger one; an oscillator generates a periodic signal. Making an existing signal larger and generating a periodic signal are not the same operation.
Modulation reflects information onto a carrier, while demodulation extracts information from a received modulated wave. AM varies amplitude, FM frequency, and PM phase. Also distinguish information processing from stabilizing the power supply.

mfg1-electrical-l025.title: Computer functions and binary numbers
mfg1-electrical-l025.exampleText: If a scanned barcode does not update the part number on screen, a read beep alone does not prove input, processing, and display are all normal. Report separately the facts you can check within your role, such as input history, processing results, and display state. Preserve the current condition and job number before deleting data or changing settings.
mfg1-electrical-l025.structureTitle: Trace five functions · Read binary by place value
mfg1-electrical-l025.structureText:
Input receives external data or commands; memory stores data and programs; control decodes instructions and directs other units; arithmetic performs calculations and logic; output presents results externally. The CPU combines the central control and arithmetic functions.
A factory recording terminal similarly receives a barcode, stores part data, compares it, and displays the result. Do not mistake the screen for the whole computer; separate which function may have a problem.

Binary uses 0 and 1, with place weights 1, 2, 4, 8… from the right. Decimal 10 is ten, but binary 10 is 1 × 2 + 0 × 1 = 2. The same written digits mean different values in different bases, so identify binary or decimal explicitly.
For example, binary 1101 is 1 × 8 + 1 × 4 + 0 × 2 + 1 × 1 = 13. Add the weights of the occupied places to check. Do not join digits after skipping zeros or read it as decimal 1101.

Use unsigned-integer place values, not table lookup alone. From the right the weights are 2⁰,2¹,2²…; 10100₂=16+4=20₁₀, and 20=16+4 converts back to 10100₂. In six digits the leftmost weight is 2⁵=32, not six. Leading zeros preserve unsigned value: 00110₂=110₂=6. They may still matter in identifiers or fixed-width records, so do not delete them. Only 0 and 1 are binary digits; check an invalid entry instead of guessing. Carry gives 1+1=10₂ and, without a width limit, 111₂+1=1000₂. Unsigned four-bit values run 0–15: maximum15, sixteen states. Do not truncate or enter a five-bit result into a four-bit field without its specification; signed encodings need separate rules.

mfg1-electrical-l026.title: Distinguish printed-board manufacture from component assembly
mfg1-electrical-l026.exampleText: If neighboring copper patterns are connected on an unpopulated board, identify it as a pattern-formation issue before soldering. A solder bridge between terminals after mounting is a different condition and discovery stage. Even with the same suspicion of a short, record location, process, material, and observed facts rather than deciding the cause in advance.
mfg1-electrical-l026.structureTitle: Board structure and component mounting · Copper to retain and copper to remove
mfg1-electrical-l026.structureText:
A printed wiring board has conductor patterns formed on an insulating base. Its process state differs from a board with electronic components mounted and ready to function as a circuit. Avoid using the short name “board” so vaguely that before/after mounting is unclear.
Structures include single-sided, double-sided, and multilayer; forms include rigid, flexible, and combinations. Flexible does not mean any location can be folded any number of times. Check bending locations and conditions in the specifications.

In a process that removes unwanted copper foil, protect the required pattern and remove exposed unwanted copper using an etchant or another specified method. Resist provides protection; etching removes copper or other material. Exposure and development conditions depend on materials and methods, so do not apply one sequence to all boards.
Another method forms the required pattern by plating. In either case, inspect broken tracks, unwanted connections between neighboring patterns, dimensions, holes, and surfaces against process criteria. Board manufacture and later component mounting require separate control.

mfg1-electrical-l027.title: Check grease functions and lubrication conditions
mfg1-electrical-l027.exampleText: A bearing-grease container has an unreadable label, while the previous record specifies product G-A. Do not add similarly colored G-B. Hold use and confirm material identity. Once the correct material and tools are confirmed, the assigned person applies the specified amount and records it. If there is unusual noise, do not assume lubrication will necessarily fix it.
mfg1-electrical-l027.structureTitle: Why grease is used · More is not necessarily better
mfg1-electrical-l027.structureText:
Grease is a semisolid lubricant used in bearings and other moving contact surfaces. Lubrication reduces friction and wear; applying just any substance does not produce the same effect. The material must suit the location and operating conditions.
Documents may specify grease consistency. A measured penetration value and a product grade number do not necessarily use the same scale or numerical relationship, so do not judge suitability from a number’s size alone. Match the specified part number and the exact specification field.

Equipment procedures specify points, amount, interval, and application method. Too much, too little, or foreign matter can affect function. Use clean specified tools and check component condition and records. Do not mix different greases by visual similarity or color.
Similarly named products may serve mechanical lubrication, electrical contacts, or heat transfer. This lesson on mechanical lubrication does not authorize applying any grease to electronic components. Also confirm who is assigned and the required stopping conditions.

mfg1-electrical-l028.title: Trace starting and stopping in a self-hold circuit
mfg1-electrical-l028.exampleText: Record: initially coil off/lamp off; after start coil on/lamp on; after start release still on through the auxiliary contact; after stop off. Add separate rows for power loss and restoration. Explain states using an approved drawing or teaching setup rather than experimenting on real machinery. Adequacy of stop and safety functions requires separate verification.
mfg1-electrical-l028.structureTitle: While pressed and after release · Stop and loss of power
mfg1-electrical-l028.structureText:
In a basic teaching circuit, pressing a start a/NO contact energizes the relay coil and closes its own a/NO contact. Placing this auxiliary contact in parallel with the start contact leaves a path to the coil after the button is released. Continued energization through that path is self-holding.
A lamp remaining on does not necessarily mean the button is still pressed. Trace the contacts that complete the current path. Distinguish the initial open auxiliary contact from its energized state.

This example places a stop b/NC contact in series with the path. Stop operation opens it, de-energizes the coil, and returns the auxiliary contact, releasing the hold. This differs from a circuit that stops merely when the start button is released.
In the basic example with an ordinary non-latching relay and a released start input, losing power releases the hold, and restoration alone does not restart it. This is not an unconditional guarantee for real equipment: check circuit configuration, input states, and holding method.

mfg1-surface-lesson-022.title: Distinguish ammeter and voltmeter connections
