mfg1-surface-lesson-022.exampleText: A record says “voltage 12 A.” First verify the measured quantity and unit. 12 A denotes current; do not simply move that number to a voltage field in V. Check the original instrument, measurement time and worker, then follow record-correction procedures.
mfg1-surface-lesson-022.structureTitle: First decide what to measure · Understand connections through diagrams · Report changes with their conditions
mfg1-surface-lesson-022.structureText:
Current describes electrical flow in a circuit and is expressed in A. Voltage is the potential difference between two points and is expressed in V. Both relate to film formation in plating and anodizing, but they are not the same quantity. Confusing their record fields prevents sound normal/abnormal judgements.
Before measuring, confirm the circuit, AC or DC, expected range and instrument. A displayed number does not prove a valid measurement. Check range, units and instrument condition too.

In a typical circuit diagram, an ammeter is in series and a voltmeter is in parallel across the two points being measured. Connecting an instrument set for current measurement directly across a power supply can cause a short circuit or other serious hazards. Learning the principle does not authorize rewiring equipment.
For a clamp meter, select a compatible measurement mode and the correct conductor. Check DC/AC suitability and which conductor to enclose; do not assume any number of wires can be clamped together.

When readings differ from before, check comparison conditions such as location, operation, rack loading and contact. One display alone cannot identify instrument failure versus process abnormality. Within your responsibility, record time and observed facts and report them.
Measuring energized parts or changing connections requires specific training, protection and authority. Untrained people must not experiment on operating equipment; use circuit drawings or safe training materials.

mfg1-surface-lesson-023.title: Compare corrosion tests under consistent purposes and conditions
mfg1-surface-lesson-023.exampleText: Lot A was tested by neutral salt spray and lot B by CASS. Do not conclude B is inferior from time alone; first report that methods differ. Quality staff confirm which results can be compared against the same product requirements.
mfg1-surface-lesson-023.structureTitle: Corrosion resistance is tested in different environments · Specimens and observations are conditions too · Evaluate resistance to alkali
mfg1-surface-lesson-023.structureText:
Salt-spray testing examines changes in films and substrates exposed to salt-containing mist. Methods include neutral salt spray, acidic salt spray with acetic acid, and CASS with additional copper chloride. Different methods use different liquids and conditions, so always identify the test.
A longer unchanged period in one test does not mean proportionally longer outdoor life. Tests evaluate prescribed conditions; actual use adds wet/dry cycles, scratches, temperatures and other factors.

Align specimen preparation, positioning, presence of deliberate scratches, observation times and evaluated changes. Confirm whether the criterion is red rust, discolouration, film damage or another phenomenon, and record it. Do not combine distinct phenomena under “rust appeared.”
When comparing lots, check method and specimen conditions as well as duration. Results from different conditions cannot directly establish superiority. Specific settings and pass limits follow the designated standard edition and product requirements.

Alkali-drop testing is used, for example, to evaluate alkali resistance of anodized aluminium films. Apply the specified liquid and judge film changes or time to electrical continuity by the required method. It does not evaluate exactly the same property as salt spray.
Specimens may be exposed to chemicals or heat and no longer remain in their shipment condition. Follow the test operator’s procedure and identify them separately from unused products. Learners must not improvise test-liquid preparation.

mfg1-surface-lesson-024.title: Check inspection conditions for limit samples and colour matching
mfg1-surface-lesson-024.exampleText: A part matches the colour reference at the inspection bench but looks redder beside a window. Do not accept or reject it at the window alone. Return it to the specified light source and compare with the reference at the same position and angle. Review instrument colour measurements with quality staff if necessary.
mfg1-surface-lesson-024.structureTitle: Use a shared visual acceptance basis · Changing light changes perceived colour · Appearance does not guarantee other performance
mfg1-surface-lesson-024.structureText:
Visual inspection uses limit samples illustrating acceptable conditions to reduce individual judgement differences. They are not decorative examples for a vague resemblance check; they establish the defect and allowable boundary. Check part number, revision and storage condition too.
Lighting and viewing direction change how scratches, unevenness and small holes appear. Use the specified source, illuminance, background, distance and angle. Do not invent a favourable condition such as passing a defect because sunlight hid it.

Colour matching compares a product with references for target colour or intensity. The same item can look different under daylight, fluorescent light or LED light. Do not compare reference and item under different light.
Fatigue and individual variation matter, so combine visual checks with colorimeter or colour-difference measurements where required. Numerical readings also require appropriate position, optical conditions and reference. Neither human nor instrument inspection is universally sufficient.

Appearance, adhesion, hardness and solder-wettability tests have different purposes. A colour match does not prove sufficient adhesion. Check each required property using its specified method.
Hold and consult on borderline items instead of changing samples or lighting to obtain a pass. Recording the inspected position and conditions helps investigate differing judgements.

mfg1-surface-lesson-025.title: Use melting point and conductivity for their intended purposes
mfg1-surface-lesson-025.exampleText: Someone says, “It is aluminium, so it is fine up to 660°C.” This confuses a representative melting point with a service limit. Check the actual alloy, required strength, film and component specification; use approved specifications to judge allowable temperature.
mfg1-surface-lesson-025.structureTitle: Melting temperature is not allowable service temperature · Consider ease of electrical conduction · Compare several properties
mfg1-surface-lesson-025.structureText:
Melting point is the temperature at which a solid becomes liquid. Representative pure-metal values are about 420°C for zinc and 660°C for aluminium. Alloys may melt over a range; do not apply a pure-metal number directly to an alloy.
Below melting point does not necessarily mean safe service. Strength, dimensional stability, films and bonded joints may be affected well before melting. Use product and material specifications for service temperature.

Conductivity indicates how readily material conducts electricity, in S/m or similar units. Typical pure metals such as silver, copper, gold and aluminium differ, but comparison conditions, temperature and alloy composition change values. Do not determine conductivity from colour.
Even with one material, overall wiring or contact resistance changes with length, cross-section and contact conditions. Highly conductive material does not eliminate poor jig contact or an undersized conductor.

Select materials by combined conductivity, strength, corrosion resistance, weight and machinability. Distinguish aluminium’s low weight from its conductivity differing from copper. Changes require drawing and process approval.
Substrate and film properties also differ. A substrate melting point does not guarantee film heat resistance; an outer metal name alone does not establish electrical-connection performance.

mfg1-surface-lesson-026.title: Check compatibility of jigs, masking and tank materials
mfg1-surface-lesson-026.exampleText: The specified tape runs out and someone proposes a visually similar substitute. Compatibility must cover chemicals, temperature, processing time and removal, not just adhesive strength. If approval cannot be confirmed, hold its use and consult the responsible person.
mfg1-surface-lesson-026.structureTitle: A jig does more than hold · Protect areas that must not be treated · Tank materials also have conditions
mfg1-surface-lesson-026.structureText:
Jigs hold or transport items and may also conduct current. Attachment can cause scratches, dents, deformation or jig marks; poor contact may cause insufficient or uneven film. Check orientation and contacts against the standard.
Use and stripping can degrade jigs. Inspect contacts, deformation and coating damage rather than judging only by usage count. Follow material- and process-specific cleaning, stripping and replacement procedures.

Masking protects areas where film or chemical action is unwanted. Tapes, coatings and rubbers differ in thermal and chemical resistance. A similar-coloured tape is not necessarily a substitute. Check drawing boundaries and approved materials.
Lifting edges or tears can let liquid enter unintended areas. Do not confuse protected areas with contacts needed for current. Record removal and verification after processing too.

Tank materials must suit chemical type, concentration, temperature and mechanical conditions. Names such as PVC, PP, FRP or metal do not establish compatibility with every acid or high temperature. Check manufacturer specifications and selection basis.
Report leaks, cracks, discolouration or lifted lining. Independently transferring liquid to another container or repairing with unverified material can cause leaks or chemical mixing.

mfg1-surface-lesson-027.title: Distinguish dissociation from metal ionization tendency
mfg1-surface-lesson-027.exampleText: An analysis sheet says “strong electrolyte,” and a worker explains that the liquid must therefore be concentrated. Strength refers to dissociation extent, not the concentration value itself. Verify component, concentration, temperature and method separately, then correct the explanation.
mfg1-surface-lesson-027.structureTitle: Separate into ions in solution · A metal’s tendency to release electrons · Do not mix materials to test properties
mfg1-surface-lesson-027.structureText:
An electrolyte separates into ions in aqueous solution and carries electrical charge. Positive cations and negative anions are involved. Not every dissolved substance dissociates to the same extent.
Strong versus weak electrolyte concerns the degree of ion separation under the conditions. It does not mean concentrated versus dilute. Read concentration and dissociation extent as separate properties.

Ionization tendency is a guide to a metal releasing electrons and becoming ions. Zinc and iron, for example, differ. Do not treat electrolyte dissociation degree and metal ionization tendency as the same quantity.
Actual corrosion also depends on environment and films. An oxide film can protect aluminium, so a ranking alone cannot determine an observed corrosion rate.

Solution composition, temperature and concentration also affect conductivity. Good conduction does not necessarily mean the target component has the right concentration. Confirm a method appropriate to the analytical purpose.
Metal-chemical reactions can release gas. Do not put metals into acid or energize unidentified liquids to test a ranking. Learn the mechanism through diagrams and records.

mfg1-surface-lesson-028.title: Consider deposited mass through charge and current efficiency
mfg1-surface-lesson-028.exampleText:
For practice, constant 2.0 A for 3 minutes means 3 × 60 = 180 seconds, so Q = 2.0 × 180 = 360 C. In a separate practice condition, theoretical mass 1.00 g at 80% efficiency gives 1.00 × 0.80 = 0.80 g. The two examples check calculations; they do not define a constant or operating conditions for the same bath.

For this paper model use deposited mass m=kItη. The supplied k is an electrochemical equivalent and η is the current efficiency for the target metal. Fictional k=0.20 mg/C, I=1.0 A, t=5 min=300 s and η=75%=0.75 give Q=300 C, theoretical mass60 mg and estimated mass45 mg. These are not an actual element's constant or bath conditions. At the same k, I and η, a target90 mg requires90/(0.20×1.0×0.75)=600 s=10 min. If k, I, time and η stay fixed, doubling area alone leaves total mass45 mg, while mean current density I/area halves. This does not guarantee local thickness or quality. Never assume constant real-process efficiency or change operating current or time without authorization.
mfg1-surface-lesson-028.structureTitle: Consider duration as well as current · Not all current produces the intended deposit · Longer time does not necessarily improve quality
mfg1-surface-lesson-028.structureText:
For constant current, charge Q equals current I multiplied by time t. Using A and seconds gives charge in C, coulombs. Equal current with different duration gives different charge. Do not mix minutes and seconds.
A varying-current process cannot simply apply one constant value over its whole duration. Use a treatment consistent with actual records, such as time segments. Distinguish settings from measured records.

Faraday’s law relates electrode-reacted substance quantity to charge. Actual baths have side reactions, such as hydrogen generation; not all supplied current necessarily deposits the desired metal.
Current efficiency represents the share used for the intended deposit. When estimating actual mass by multiplying theoretical mass by efficiency, use 0.80 for 80%. Efficiency depends on bath and conditions, so do not use the example as a fixed production value.

Estimated total deposit mass is separate from acceptable thickness uniformity, appearance and adhesion. More total material after longer processing does not necessarily remove local unevenness or defects.
If deposit is below expectation, check current, time, area, contact, bath conditions and measurement method and report it. Do not independently compensate by increasing current or duration.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-029.title: Read voltage, current, and resistance in a DC resistor circuit
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-029.exampleText: In a paper-based DC resistor circuit, assume 24 V across 12 Ω. The current is I = 24 ÷ 12 = 2 A. At the same 24 V, a resistance of 24 Ω gives 1 A. The example concerns a simple circuit with fixed resistance. Do not use this result directly as a motor’s starting current or an AC device’s current.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-029.structureTitle: Principle and process role · Conditions and records to check
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-029.structureText:
Voltage is measured in V, current in A, and resistance in Ω. Under applicable conditions, the voltage across a resistor and its current obey V = I × R. With the same voltage across a fixed resistor, a larger resistance gives a smaller current. This does not mean that an entire machine may always be calculated as a single resistor.

On a circuit diagram, a voltmeter connects in parallel across the part being measured; an ammeter connects in series so the branch current passes through it. This is study of what the connections mean. Connecting an ammeter directly across a power source can cause a dangerous short circuit. Actual measurement requires the operator’s applicable qualifications and training, suitable instrument ratings, procedures, and work authorization.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-030.title: Distinguish plastic molding by product shape
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-030.exampleText: Consider a complex small case, a hollow container, and a long tube with a repeating cross-section. Injection, blow molding, and extrusion are possible choices, but a hollow shape does not necessarily mean blow molding. A tube is also hollow, yet has a continuous constant cross-section. Decide from material, quantity, molding conditions, and the approved process as well as shape.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-030.structureTitle: Principle and process role · Conditions and records to check
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-030.structureText:
Injection molding shapes flowing resin in a mold. Blow molding uses air to produce hollow forms, while extrusion continuously pushes material through a die to make long products of constant cross-section. Compression molding shapes material by pressure within a mold. Reinforced plastic combines resin with reinforcement such as fibers. Materials and solidification mechanisms differ between methods.

Some materials solidify through cooling, while others cure through a chemical reaction. An open mold alone does not establish a safe touching temperature or completion of curing. The specified process includes removal, cooling, and inspection. Record resin name, material lot, equipment, and conditions; do not mix materials or change conditions without permission.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-031.title: Match coating purposes with application methods
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-031.exampleText: An outdoor component has uniform color on the visible front but missed coating on the rear. If corrosion protection is a purpose, an attractive front alone does not justify acceptance. Compare the specified surfaces, film condition, required thickness, and inspections with the instruction. Do not simply add another layer on your own; confirm the reprocessing method with the responsible person.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-031.structureTitle: Principle and process role · Conditions and records to check
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-031.structureText:
Coating does more than add color: it protects the substrate, improves appearance, and can provide functions such as insulation or heat shielding. Brush coating spreads paint with a tool; spray coating atomizes it onto the surface. Electrostatic coating uses forces from electric charge, while electrodeposition forms a film electrically in a bath. Similar names do not mean identical processes.

A functional paint does not provide its performance at every thickness or under all conditions. Align the paint, substrate, application, and drying or curing conditions. Both finish inspection and chemical handling are necessary; color alone does not identify the contents. Check equipment grounding, ventilation, and other requirements under the procedure for that coating method.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-032.title: Choose packaging for protection, identification, and transport
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-032.exampleText: Finished metal parts packed together in a box may contact one another and become scratched during transport. In addition to a strong outer box, check instructions for individual partitions and protection. Before putting different specifications together, verify whether mixed packing is permitted and whether labels and quantities remain identifiable. Do not count similar-looking items together.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-032.structureTitle: Principle and process role · Conditions and records to check
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-032.structureText:
Packaging protects products from scratches, dirt, moisture, and other hazards, communicates identification, and facilitates transport and storage. Individual wrapping supports separate protection and control; corrugated boxes group items together. Shrink film contracts under heat, but wrapping alone does not guarantee complete impact or moisture protection.

After packing, match the specified product name, specification, quantity, lot, and other information to the contents. A readable label and a correct label are separate checks. Consider package weight, stacking, and handling during opening, and observe storage conditions. Heat-shrink processes also require checking heat effects on the product and packaging material.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-033.title: Compare hot- and cold-rolling conditions
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-033.exampleText: Suppose a hot-rolled sheet measures differently while hot and after cooling. Account for thermal dimensional change and check in the specified measurement state. Cold rolling can produce precise dimensions and surfaces, but requires larger forces and can harden the material through working. Neither hot nor cold rolling is superior under every condition.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-033.structureTitle: Principle and process role · Conditions and records to check
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-033.structureText:
Rolling is plastic forming in which material passes between rolls and pressure changes its shape, for example by reducing thickness. Hot rolling heats the material to make deformation easier; cold rolling is introduced here as processing without applied heating. Cold rolling still generates heat during work and does not mean “cold, therefore safe.” Check the process against required thickness, material, and temperature conditions.

In an example plan reducing thickness from 6.0 mm to 4.5 mm, the reduction is 1.5 mm. Relative to the original thickness, it is 1.5 ÷ 6.0 × 100 = 25%. This calculation does not specify an allowable reduction in one pass. Actual pass count and conditions depend on equipment capability, material, and the approved process.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-034.title: Trace the roles of rolling oil and post-treatment
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-034.exampleText: Suppose linear scratches are found on a rolled sheet. Oil supply is one item to check, but roll and material-surface conditions also need investigation. Record the location, discovery time, affected scope, and oil/equipment records, then report to the responsible person. Do not increase supply without permission and declare the issue resolved simply because later sheets look better.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-034.structureTitle: Principle and process role · Conditions and records to check
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-034.structureText:
Rolling oil controls friction between the rolls and material to help the process run smoothly. It also carries away heat and helps reduce seizure and surface scratching. More oil is not necessarily better; oil type and supply conditions must follow equipment and product instructions. Do not try to address a defect only by changing the amount.

After rolling, properties may be adjusted by annealing or the surface may be treated to match the application. Reaching the required thickness is different from completing the required hardness and surface condition. Check the process sheet for post-treatment and inspections, and keep rolled-only items distinguishable from post-treated items.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-035.title: Check aluminum extrusion temperature, dies, and handling surfaces
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-035.exampleText: A line repeatedly appears at the same location along the product’s length. Die damage or deposits are possible checks, but foreign matter on the runout table receiving the product also needs investigation. Record the line’s position and continuity, and establish with the responsible person where it was introduced. Do not hold a moving product down or clean a hot die on the spot to investigate.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-035.structureTitle: Principle and process role · Conditions and records to check
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-035.structureText:
Aluminum extrusion pushes a heated billet through a die to produce a long product with a cross-section corresponding to the die opening. Applications include window frames and heat-dissipating fins. Specified cooling, straightening, and cutting follow extrusion. Product condition depends not only on die shape but also on material, temperature, and speed.

An excessively low billet temperature raises forming load; excessive temperature can also lead to problems such as surface cracks. Do not assume that simply raising temperature is better. Follow the specified range matching material, shape, and speed. Link the die number, material lot, temperature, speed, and receiving-surface condition in records, and ask the designated person to perform repairs or change conditions.

mfg1-electrical-l029.title: Motor types and control purposes
mfg1-electrical-l029.exampleText: Moving a conveyor at constant speed differs from stopping a table at a set location. Focus on speed for the first and position for the second while also checking torque and load conditions. Do not respond to a position error by merely raising speed; report command, detection, and mechanical observations within your role.
mfg1-electrical-l029.structureTitle: Energy and types · What servo control matches
mfg1-electrical-l029.structureText:
A motor converts electrical energy into mechanical rotation. There are DC and AC types; AC types include induction and synchronous motors. Equal voltage markings do not establish identical supply type, frequency, or connection.
Induction motors include squirrel-cage and wound-rotor types. Do not equate rotating-field speed with actual rotor speed. This lesson avoids memorizing a speed formula as actual RPM and instead emphasizes checking ratings, operating conditions, and control method.

Servo control can stop at a specified position, match a speed, or control turning torque. Feedback returns detected results from devices such as encoders to correct the difference from a command.
Simply rotating is not sufficient for a positioning system. Distinguish whether position, speed, or force must be met. Changing mounting or control settings can change machine behavior even with the same motor.

mfg1-electrical-l030.title: Transformer turns ratios and losses
mfg1-electrical-l030.exampleText: For a calculation example, V1 = 100 V, N1 = 500 turns, N2 = 100 turns gives V2 = 100 × 100/500 = 20 V. This is an ideal-ratio value, not a wiring instruction. Check actual ratings and destinations on the nameplate and drawings. A lower secondary voltage does not remove primary-side danger.
mfg1-electrical-l030.structureTitle: The relationship between windings · No load does not mean no loss
mfg1-electrical-l030.structureText:
A common transformer uses a core and multiple windings to change voltage through changing magnetic flux. For an ideal AC transformer, voltage ratio corresponds to turns ratio: V2/V1 = N2/N1.
Fewer secondary turns step voltage down; more step it up. Primary does not always mean high-voltage side. Nor can an ordinary AC transformer be used identically by applying DC directly. Check frequency, capacity, connections, and voltage rating.

Even without a secondary load, applying primary voltage causes losses such as core loss. Current through winding resistance also causes copper loss. No secondary load does not mean the primary is safe or consumes no power.
The ideal ratio omits actual losses and voltage variation. A matching voltage does not allow unlimited load; remain within capacity, temperature, and other limits. Match insulation type and construction to the application too.

mfg1-electrical-l031.title: Circuit-breaker roles and abnormality response
mfg1-electrical-l031.exampleText: If a breaker trips during operation and there is a burnt smell, follow stop, evacuation, and reporting procedures instead of resetting to investigate. Record equipment number, time, operating state, indications, and smell. Do not substitute a different device, such as trying to interrupt fault current by opening a disconnector.
mfg1-electrical-l031.structureTitle: Opening does not mean identical capability · Check what is protected and under what conditions
mfg1-electrical-l031.structureText:
A circuit breaker interrupts load or short-circuit current within its ratings and application. Interrupting large current can create an arc between contacts, making arc extinction important. Having a contact-opening mechanism does not by itself mean fault current can be safely interrupted.
In this teaching distinction, load switches handle load current, while disconnectors isolate a circuit with no current flowing. Do not group all devices as “switches”; identify function from nameplates, drawings, and operating procedures.

A wiring circuit breaker protects wiring against overcurrent from overloads or short circuits. Its presence does not establish protection of people against every leakage or shock condition. Check required protective functions and selection conditions for the equipment.
After a breaker operates, check the stopped area and people’s safety and report abnormality information. Repeatedly resetting without knowing the cause may worsen a fault or cause danger from restarting.

mfg1-electrical-l032.title: Separate solar-cell and storage-battery roles
mfg1-electrical-l032.exampleText: “It generated during the day, so the solar cell alone delivers the same power at night” is incomplete; nighttime use needs another storage or supply arrangement. “It works in an outage” also requires checking system functions and conditions. No generation does not mean no voltage in equipment or storage batteries.
mfg1-electrical-l032.structureTitle: Generation and storage are different · The device linking DC and AC
mfg1-electrical-l032.structureText:
A solar cell converts light energy into electricity. Insufficient light reduces generation, and without light at night it cannot generate as during daytime. Although called a “cell,” it differs from a storage battery that stores generated energy for later nighttime use.
Adding storage can save generated energy for later within system conditions. Capacity, charging/discharging, remaining charge, and available functions have limits. Solar panels alone do not guarantee every appliance will always work during an outage.

Solar-cell output is DC. In a system serving ordinary AC equipment, a power conditioner performs functions such as DC-to-AC conversion, adjustment for generation conditions, and abnormality detection.
Do not confuse generation, storage, and conversion as one box’s function. Actual connections require compatibility, protection, grid-related, and outage-behavior checks. This lesson explains system roles, not installation or grid-connection procedures.

mfg1-electrical-l033.title: Distinguish pressure, flow, and direction in hydraulics
mfg1-electrical-l033.exampleText: “Moves the wrong way,” “correct direction but slow,” and “insufficient force” are different observations in a teaching cylinder. Record them separately as direction, speed, and force information. Classification alone does not prove a particular valve failed. Confirm causes through approved checks before changing settings or disassembling.
mfg1-electrical-l033.structureTitle: From oil to motion · Do not confuse three controls
mfg1-electrical-l033.structureText:
Hydraulics uses oil flow and pressure to move machinery. Components include a pump, actuators converting hydraulic energy to force or motion, and valves controlling flow. Do not simplify a pump as independently creating constant pressure at any load; consider the circuit and load conditions.
A cylinder gives linear motion, while a hydraulic motor gives rotary motion. Trace where oil flows and which device moves, rather than only recognizing lines in a diagram.

Pressure-control valves adjust pressure, related to actuator force. Flow-control valves adjust flow, related to speed. Directional valves change the flow path and motion direction. Slow movement does not necessarily call for higher pressure.
Actual force and speed also depend on load and circuit conditions. Do not assume turning one adjustment screw solves everything. Report commanded values, pressure/flow state, and the specific motion difference within your assigned role.

mfg1-electrical-l034.title: Protect logistics quality with industrial packaging
mfg1-electrical-l034.exampleText: A planned box holds six control parts. The quantity is six, but the label shows another part number. Do not ship based on quantity alone; match identification, packaging specification, documents, and destination and request correction. For a do-not-stack box, also check storage and stacking arrangements follow the instruction. A neat-looking box does not justify skipping checks.
mfg1-electrical-l034.structureTitle: Being in a box is not enough · Logistics quality is more than avoiding damage
mfg1-electrical-l034.structureText:
Industrial packaging preserves product quality during storage and transport. Choose materials suited to shape, weight, fragility, humidity, temperature, and transport method. A large strong outer box can still allow damage if the product moves inside or load presses on terminals.
Clarify each material’s purpose, such as cushioning for shock and fixing material for movement. Electronic products may also need moisture and static protection. Reducing material use still requires meeting protection requirements.

Alongside product quality, meet the promised date and ensure correct item, quantity, and destination. Match product numbers, quantities, and identifiers on packaging and documents. Correct contents sent to the wrong destination do not meet logistics quality.
Handling, keep-dry, and do-not-stack marks tell handlers how to treat cargo. A label alone does not protect it; confirm actual storage and handling follow it. Do not guess the meaning or applicability of a mark.

mfg1-electrical-l035.title: Injection molding and fiber-reinforced plastics basics
mfg1-electrical-l035.exampleText: Glass-fiber board material and carbon-fiber components need not have the same electrical properties. Do not substitute based merely on a black appearance or fiber content. Even if molding produces the same shape, appearance may not reveal a wrong material; match identification and loading records.
mfg1-electrical-l035.structureTitle: How heat changes the material · Conditions determining shape and quality
mfg1-electrical-l035.structureText:
Thermoplastics use softening with heat and hardening on cooling. A cured thermoset cannot simply be remelted and reshaped in the same way. Check material name, lot, drying, and other conditions; do not mix different resins without authorization.
Injection molding heats resin, fills a mold, then applies holding pressure and cooling as specified before opening and removing the product. Injection unit, clamping unit, and mold serve different functions. Hazards include strong clamping force as well as hot resin.

Resin flows through sprue, runner, and gate into the product cavity. Temperature, pressure, amount, speed, cooling, and foreign matter affect the result. When a molding defect appears, record time, location, quantity, and conditions rather than changing one setting without permission.
FRP combines resin with fibers such as glass or carbon. Properties depend on fiber type, orientation, content, and resin. Do not generalize that every FRP is stronger than metal or electrically insulating; check application-specific specifications.

mfg1-surface-lesson-029.title: Organize conversion-coating types and their underlayer roles
mfg1-surface-lesson-029.exampleText: A drawing specifies phosphating before painting, but someone proposes similarly coloured blackening instead. Check required adhesion, corrosion resistance and specified process, not colour. Do not change treatment without approval; discuss the specification differences with responsible staff.
mfg1-surface-lesson-029.structureTitle: Form a film by reaction at the surface · Chromium treatments and other pretreatments · Do not confuse colour with corrosion resistance
mfg1-surface-lesson-029.structureText:
Conversion treatment uses chemical reaction at a metal surface to create a film with properties different from the substrate. Roles include corrosion protection, paint adhesion and lubricity. Calling every process metal plating confuses purpose and sequence.
Phosphating forms a phosphate-based film and is used, for example, as a paint pretreatment on steel. Check bath/substrate combinations; similar product names do not authorize substitution between chemical systems.

Chromate-related processes differ in chromium species and process system. Do not assume hexavalent and trivalent types have identical hazards or performance; check chemicals and product requirements. Nor does every system necessarily have identical self-healing properties.
Zincate forms a zinc film as a pretreatment before plating aluminium alloys and similar materials. Oxide removal and displacement-film formation help later adhesion. Distinguish its role from simply applying a thick main zinc coating.

Blackening is an example of forming a black oxide film on steel. Dark colour does not establish film thickness or corrosion resistance. Verify quality including required post-treatment and service conditions.
Each chemical has specific hazards and controls. Match environmental and customer substance requirements to current specifications; textbook inclusion does not mean perpetual permission to use it. Do not mix unverified process liquids as substitutes.

mfg1-surface-lesson-030.title: Separate coating methods from paint control requirements
mfg1-surface-lesson-030.exampleText: Only the base of a two-component paint remains, and someone proposes another product’s hardener. Both being “two-component” does not establish compatibility. Match product, specified hardener, ratio and expiry requirements; do not mix if they cannot be confirmed.
mfg1-surface-lesson-030.structureTitle: Application and curing are different viewpoints · Powder still requires safety controls · Match paint labels to the procedure
mfg1-surface-lesson-030.structureText:
Painting uses a paint film for protection, appearance, slip resistance and other functions. Spraying applies atomized paint; dipping immerses the item. Baking concerns heat curing, so it is not a completely parallel classification to application method.
Electrostatic painting uses electrical attraction; electrodeposition forms a film in a bath using DC. Electrodeposition includes anionic and cationic types. Using electricity does not make every method’s polarity or equipment identical.

Powder coating applies powdered paint and forms a film through heating or related processes. Even without solvent, dust, ignition, heat and charging hazards require material- and equipment-specific controls. Do not conclude “no solvent means no ventilation.”
Check substrate heat compatibility, pretreatment, thickness and drying/curing conditions. Higher temperature does not necessarily produce a better film faster; consider overheating defects.

Water-based versus solvent-based, resin family and one- versus two-component are separate classifications. Two-component products require the specified pairing, ratio and usable time. This lesson does not establish a universal mixing ratio.
Durability depends on formulation, pretreatment, cure and environment, not resin name alone. Avoid claims that water-based means harmless or a resin always lasts longest; check SDS and product specifications.

mfg1-surface-lesson-031.title: Read plating functions from the application
mfg1-surface-lesson-031.exampleText: Two similar-looking parts differ: one needs decoration, the other solder joining. Check layer structure and joining-property tests rather than colour. Passing decorative requirements does not mean passing solder wettability.
mfg1-surface-lesson-031.structureTitle: Corrosion protection has several mechanisms · Separate appearance from function · Connect layer structure and inspection
mfg1-surface-lesson-031.structureText:
Zinc-based films can protect ferrous substrates by corroding first: sacrificial protection. Nickel or chromium films can act as barriers to oxygen and water. Evaluate actual performance for the material combination and environment.
A film does not permit ignoring scratches or pinholes. Different protective mechanisms mean different effects of defects. A coating name alone does not guarantee the same protection on every substrate.

Decorative chromium emphasizes appearance, while hard chromium targets properties such as wear resistance. The same chromium name does not imply equal specifications, thickness or inspection. Similar appearance does not authorize substitution.
Gold and silver plating have decorative and electrical-contact applications. Tin or nickel/gold can serve electronic parts requiring joining. Confirm each layer’s purpose from drawings and process instructions.

Copper provides conductivity in wiring and through-holes; alloy plating can target other properties such as magnetism. Good gloss alone does not prove required electrical or mechanical performance.
Record principal function, undercoat/outermost layer and inspection method together. When applications change, do not substitute a similarly coloured plating without authorization; materials, process and quality staff verify suitability.

mfg1-surface-lesson-032.title: Separate rectifier, agitation and filtration functions
mfg1-surface-lesson-032.exampleText: Bath temperature is in range, but the filter unit sounds unusual. Do not assume all is well from temperature alone. Report equipment, sound change, time and flow condition. Do not open the running filter to investigate.
mfg1-surface-lesson-032.structureTitle: Check power and workpiece handling · Reduce temperature and concentration differences · Filtration has a limited removal scope
mfg1-surface-lesson-032.structureText:
A rectifier converts AC to DC and supplies current required for plating. Match current capacity, control method and waveform to the process. Correct settings do not guarantee current reaches the item as intended if contacts or wiring are faulty.
Holding methods include racks, rotating barrels and continuous reel-to-reel processing. Quantity, shape, contact and transport differ, so do not transfer conditions directly between methods.

Agitation reduces local concentration or temperature differences and may use air or mechanical methods. Temperature control uses heaters, coolers or heat exchangers. These are different functions requiring separate checks.
A normal temperature indication can coexist with nonuniform conditions away from the sensor if circulation or agitation stops. Check unusual sounds, flow or bubbles as prescribed; do not independently alter flow or method.

Filter circulation separates targeted particles through filter media. It does not remove every dissolved component. A clearer liquid does not automatically have correct composition or concentration.
Opening or replacing filters or pumps involves residual chemicals, pressure and restarting hazards. Do not open covers during operation. Trained personnel follow maintenance procedures covering shutdown, isolation and residual-material handling.

mfg1-surface-lesson-033.title: Distinguish anodizing post-treatment from performance evaluation
mfg1-surface-lesson-033.exampleText: Two products have equal thickness: an outdoor coloured part and a machine part exposed to wear. Do not call them equivalent from thickness alone. Confirm required tests, such as light resistance for the former and wear resistance for the latter. Follow each product’s instructions for whether and how to seal.
mfg1-surface-lesson-033.structureTitle: Film formation is followed by other stages · Check equipment and thermal conditions · Thickness alone is not a performance evaluation
mfg1-surface-lesson-033.structureText:
Anodizing may be followed by colouring, sealing and drying as required. Colouring changes appearance through methods such as introducing colour into pores; sealing closes pore openings, limits dye leaching and contributes to corrosion resistance. They are not one identical operation to deepen colour.
Sequence and applicability depend on film and use. Hard coatings involve trade-offs with wear resistance, so do not give every product the same sealing conditions. Confirm the specified process and settings.

Electrolytic and post-treatment baths differ in chemistry and temperature. Control tank materials, jigs, power, agitation and temperature for each stage. Material suitable in another bath may not suit a hot sealing solution.
Heat during drying or use affects film, dye and thermal-expansion differences with the substrate; under some conditions it can cause cracks or performance changes. Do not use a textbook example temperature as a universal limit; follow product specifications and approved conditions.

Depending on use, evaluate corrosion, light, wear and electrical-insulation properties as well as thickness. Colour remaining vivid under light and material resisting friction are different requirements.
Do not interpret representative withstand-voltage values as permission to use the actual item as protective insulation against electric shock. Evaluate specified tests, shape, defects and use conditions. Trained personnel conduct electrical tests.

mfg1-surface-lesson-034.title: Match buffs and compounds to the process purpose
mfg1-surface-lesson-034.exampleText: A soft finishing buff is unavailable and someone proposes a cloth buff used in roughing. Being cloth does not mean free of coarse particles. Check history and cleanliness; do not transfer it to finishing without approved preparation.
mfg1-surface-lesson-034.structureTitle: Buff material and structure change behaviour · Consider particles and supply form · Prevent carryover between stages
mfg1-surface-lesson-034.structureText:
Stiff-fibre buffs such as sisal are used for coarse scratches or unevenness. Cloth, rayon, felt, wool and sponge differ in stiffness, shape retention and conformity. Softer does not mean suitable for every stage.
Some nonwoven buffs contain abrasive particles. Even with identical outer shape, material and structure change results. Verify part number, purpose and condition rather than choosing a substitute merely because its dimensions fit.

Solid and liquid compounds differ in delivery, splashing and cleaning controls. Particle material and fineness matter too. Names such as red, white or green bars are clues, but colour alone does not establish every product’s composition or use.
Typical processing moves from coarse scratch removal to fine finishing. Grit and roughness guidelines are not automatically equivalent across product systems. Match product specifications to approved combinations.

A buff or tool retaining coarse particles can create new scratches during finishing. Separate storage, identification and cleaning of roughing and finishing tools, and identify compounds too. Do not simply return a tool dropped on the floor.
Use specified inspections, replacement or servicing for wear, clogging or unevenness. Do not skip speed compatibility and damage checks. Follow safe procedures for adjustment and installation.

mfg1-surface-lesson-035.title: Match polishing machines and holding methods to the work
mfg1-surface-lesson-035.exampleText: After scratches appear on robot-polished parts, a worker approaches the buff inside a stopped cell. A stop indication does not authorize entry. Check prescribed stopping, isolation and entry procedures. Responsible personnel inspect tools and holding, then inspect the first item before restarting production.
mfg1-surface-lesson-035.structureTitle: Machine form changes handling · Roles of belts and robots · Distinguish stopped machinery, entry and quality checks
mfg1-surface-lesson-035.structureText:
Bench or pedestal machines bring the item to a fixed rotating tool. Handheld machines move a powered tool to the item and may use electricity or compressed air. Both require controls for rotating-part contact, ejected items and posture.
Small parts, large items and complex surfaces differ in holding and tool access. Being hand-sized does not mean no fixture is needed. Use specified jigs, support and posture; responsible staff select machinery for material and shape.

Belt grinding uses a continuous abrasive belt, for example to prepare flats and corners. It is not the same tool as a soft rotating buff; check cutting action and contact hazards separately.
Robots repeat movements and help stabilize posture and conditions. Unsuitable programming, positioning, holding or tool wear still changes quality. Automatic operation does not waive inspection.

A robot appearing stopped can restart or retain stored energy. Do not enter its enclosure without authorization or defeat interlocks. Trained personnel perform setup, tool changes and maintenance in an approved safe condition.
Changing machines changes contact and feed even for the same appearance target. Perform trials, first-piece checks and specified inspections; production quantity alone does not establish stability. Record quality results and tool history.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-036.title: Separate pH records from oxidation and reduction
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-036.exampleText: A workbench container bears only a pH number, without an ingredient name or measurement date. Even a near-neutral number does not identify harmless water. Keep the container identified, do not use it, and check the original record with the responsible person. Practice organizing sample records; do not experiment by mixing acids and alkalis.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-036.structureTitle: Organize two different viewpoints · Explain electron transfer separately
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-036.structureText:
pH indicates the acidity or alkalinity of an aqueous solution. In introductory examples involving dilute solutions near room temperature, neutrality is compared with approximately pH 7. Do not omit temperature and solution conditions and claim that every solution must lie between 0 and 14. Link the reading to solution identification, temperature and measurement method.

Oxidation and reduction can also be explained through electron transfer: losing electrons is oxidation; gaining them is reduction. Rusting iron and combustion illustrate oxidation, but some reactions have no visible change. A low pH observation does not mean the same thing as a statement that a substance lost electrons.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-037.title: Distinguish the 3Rs by process stage
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-037.exampleTitle: Connect circulation with design and records
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-037.exampleText: A circular economy links design, repair, reuse and resource recovery instead of only a one-way use-and-discard flow. A larger collection amount alone does not prove less waste was generated. Record generation and collection separately, and propose improvements without omitting protective packaging or safe segregation.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-037.structureTitle: Think before disposal · Classify factory examples
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-037.structureText:
Reduce prevents waste generation, reuse uses an item repeatedly, and recycle uses waste as a resource. These are not different names for the same task. Reducing unnecessary packaging and collecting used packaging to turn it back into material act at different stages.

Ordering only the required number of dividers prevents surplus. Inspecting and cleaning approved returnable trays for use again is reuse. Collecting non-reusable metal offcuts by material type for recovery is recycling. Reuse still requires conditions preventing contamination, damage and mixed part numbers.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-038.title: Check a standard’s scope and edition against inspection requirements
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-038.exampleText: The edition referenced by an inspection sheet differs from the document on the workbench. Do not choose the newer-looking document yourself or judge from old memory alone. Confirm the edition specified for the product with the responsible person. Record document number, edition, scope and decision; do not change unconfirmed requirements yourself.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-038.structureTitle: Read what the standard addresses · Separate management systems from individual acceptance
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-038.structureText:
Standards provide agreed requirements for quality, dimensions, performance and test methods. ISO is an organization concerned with international standardization; JIS means Japanese Industrial Standards. Standards covering products or labels address different subjects from standards covering an organization’s management system.

ISO 9001 concerns quality management, and ISO 14001 concerns environmental management. Information about an organization’s system does not replace required inspection of a particular part’s dimensions, damage or material. Instrument labels or marks likewise do not replace checks of condition, inspection status and measurement conditions.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-039.title: Separate impact, bend and fatigue evaluation
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-039.exampleText: A prototype support bracket raises concerns both about cracking after forming and repeated loads in service. Do not mark both as checked from a post-bend observation alone; organize suitable tests with the responsible person for each requirement. A textbook angle given for one material must not become an acceptance condition for every material.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-039.structureTitle: Loads are applied differently · Examine bending and repetition separately
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-039.structureText:
Impact tests examine energy absorbed when a specimen breaks under a sudden load. A pendulum apparatus uses the difference in its swing heights before and after fracture. Comparisons require matching specified specimen, temperature, notch and test-method conditions.

Bend tests inspect the outside and other specified parts of a specimen for cracks after bending under set conditions. Fatigue tests evaluate factors such as cycles to failure under repeated loading. Passing one slowly applied load does not prove survival under long-term repetition.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-040.title: Relate a dial indicator’s difference to its reference dimension
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-040.exampleTitle: Add the difference to the reference
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-040.exampleText: In a paper exercise, the reference is 30.00 mm and the specified signed difference is −0.04 mm. The part measures 30.00 − 0.04 = 29.96 mm. Record reference, sign, unit and measurement location together. If the reference setting shifts, do not conveniently edit numbers; follow the procedure to check the cause and affected parts.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-040.structureTitle: Read the indication as a reference difference · Check direction and full revolutions
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-040.structureText:
A dial indicator amplifies contact-point movement. In comparative measurement, set it against a reference such as a gauge block, replace that reference with the part, and read the difference. Do not mistake the small displayed difference for the part’s entire dimension.

Align plunger movement with the change being measured and check for loose mounting or sticking. If the instrument has a short hand, include complete revolutions instead of reading the long hand alone. Confirm pushing direction, pointer rotation and positive/negative meaning from the instrument and setup instructions, not familiar appearance alone.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-041.title: Select comparative instruments for the measurement geometry
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-041.exampleText: Ordinary measuring faces cannot touch the intended position of a groove deep inside a hole. Do not record the visible entrance diameter as the groove diameter. Ask the responsible person about suitable contact geometry and reference. Record instrument, reference and position, and leave unmeasurable locations explicitly unverified.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-041.structureTitle: Reaching the location is not enough · Combine reference and measuring direction
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-041.structureText:
A lever-type indicator has a contact point that pivots like a lever. A cylinder gauge has a shape for comparative bore measurement. A dial caliper gauge has inside/outside-caliper-like contacts for hard-to-reach locations such as grooves. Check correct contact with the target surface as well as suitable range and resolution.

Comparative measurement requires setting against a specified reference. Learn the roles of gauge blocks and master rings, but do not treat a similarly named limit ring as a bore-setting reference automatically. For lever instruments, a mismatch between contact movement and the intended change causes error; verify the specified orientation.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-042.title: Separate master gauges from GO/NO-GO decisions
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-042.exampleTitle: Threads and storage have their own instructions
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-042.exampleText: Thread plug gauges serve internal threads; thread rings serve external threads. Apply the specified entry or turn-count criteria for thread NO-GO gauges rather than transferring a smooth-hole rule unchanged. Protect measuring faces and record reference dimension, gauge number, inspection state and result. Do not improvise burr removal or repair.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-042.structureTitle: Check the reference’s role · Do not judge from one side
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-042.structureText:
Gauge blocks provide length references and master rings provide references such as bore size. Limit gauges check whether holes or shafts meet specified limits, generally using GO and NO-GO sides together. Even ring-shaped gauges have different roles as setting masters and acceptance gauges.

In a basic smooth-hole example using the specified plug limit gauge, check that the GO side passes and the NO-GO side does not. If GO fails to enter, do not immediately blame machining alone: follow procedures to check part/gauge identification, contamination, damage and temperature. Never change the decision by forcing the gauge.

mfg1-electrical-l036.title: Check screw/tool compatibility and tightening conditions
mfg1-electrical-l036.exampleText: Plain washers, spring washers and screws with captive washers have different configurations. Do not substitute types indiscriminately or omit specified washers. Self-tapping screws form an internal thread as they are driven into an appropriate pilot hole; this does not mean they suit every material or hole. If specified parts are missing, report the part number and shortage for confirmation.
mfg1-electrical-l036.structureTitle: Do not substitute tools merely because they look similar · Follow the torque specification
mfg1-electrical-l036.structureText:
Use a slotted screwdriver matching the slot width for slotted screws and a suitable cross-head driver for cross recesses. Use a hex key for hex-socket bolts and a suitable spanner or ring spanner matching the width across flats for hex bolts and nuts. The nominal thread diameter and the width across flats do not necessarily have the same value. If a tool is loose, do not keep pressing it harder; check size and wear.

A torque wrench controls the specified tightening torque. Do not choose settings from bolt appearance or operator strength alone. Check the component, unit, setting and tightening sequence against drawings and work standards. Tighter is not always better: both insufficient and excessive tightening cause problems. Check the management status of tools requiring calibration or pre-use checks.

mfg1-electrical-l037.title: Choose chassis-working tools by their purpose
mfg1-electrical-l037.exampleText: When cutting metal with a hacksaw and hand-finishing with a file, check remaining burrs and interference with parts as well as the cut face. Burrs are protrusions created by cutting or drilling metal and other materials and can cause injury or assembly faults. Before machining, prepare tools, clamping and chip collection, and avoid using tools outside their intended purpose.
mfg1-electrical-l037.structureTitle: Locate features before making shapes · Cutting, drilling and threading
mfg1-electrical-l037.structureText:
A chassis supports equipment components. A scriber marks dimensions and positions on metal; a punch makes an indentation at a hole centre. For layouts that may change, do not immediately scratch permanent lines: make temporary marks by the appropriate procedure and check them. Align reference surfaces and orientation, then confirm components will fit before proceeding.

Drills make holes and pilot holes for tapping; hole saws make relatively large mounting holes. Taps cut internal threads and dies cut external threads. End mills operate in milling machines and cut with peripheral or end cutting edges. Even tools described as cutting tools differ in compatible material, shape, machine and required dimensions.

mfg1-electrical-l038.title: Align references for comparison and height measurement
mfg1-electrical-l038.exampleText: A surface plate supplies a reference plane for measurement or assembly; it does not itself display dimensions. Some metal rules use the graduated end as their starting point. Distinguish this from reading a caliper reference line, and check wear, dirt, positioning and required measurement accuracy.
mfg1-electrical-l038.structureTitle: Detect changes with a dial indicator · Distinguish height from depth
mfg1-electrical-l038.structureText:
A dial indicator mechanically magnifies small probe movements and displays them with a pointer. It is used for runout, flatness and dimensional comparison. Check the division and full-revolution values for the model; do not infer an absolute dimension solely from pointer motion. After setting the reference, compare under the same contact conditions and record both direction and amount of pointer movement.

A height gauge measures or marks heights from a reference surface. A reading mechanism resembling a vernier caliper does not give it every caliper function. Do not universally treat it as a hole-depth instrument: choose an instrument suited to the intended dimension. Dirt on the reference or base changes the measuring posture, so check before use.

mfg1-electrical-l039.title: Check the quantities and conditions measured by electrical instruments
mfg1-electrical-l039.exampleTitle: Light and magnetic field are different quantities
mfg1-electrical-l039.exampleText: A lux meter measures illuminance related to light reaching its receiver; a gaussmeter measures magnetic flux density using a Hall element or similar sensor. Bright light and a strong magnetic field are different evaluations. Sensor orientation, location and outside influences affect results, so match conditions for comparisons. Record both the unit and instrument name to prevent mix-ups.
mfg1-electrical-l039.structureTitle: Measuring component values with an LCR meter · Thermocouples use temperature difference
mfg1-electrical-l039.structureText:
An LCR meter measures coil inductance L, capacitor capacitance C, resistance R, impedance and related quantities. Its targets and methods differ from a tester reading resistance or voltage. Check component type, connection, test frequency and other conditions against specifications rather than judging acceptance from a number alone. Whether a component can remain connected to a circuit also depends on the instrument and procedure.

A thermocouple combines different metals and uses thermoelectric voltage arising from a junction temperature difference. Reference-junction treatment matters as well as the temperature at the measurement side. Check agreement of type, compensating leads, polarity and instrument setting. Do not guarantee an operating range from thermocouple type alone: judge it from product specifications and operating conditions.

mfg1-electrical-l040.title: Follow preparations for drilling and tapping in order
mfg1-electrical-l040.exampleText: Hold a hand tap in a tap wrench and maintain the proper orientation to the workpiece. Handle chips in the order and manner suited to the tool type. Do not force the tap through if resistance suddenly increases. Check pilot hole, tool, lubrication and chips to prevent breakage or defective threads. Afterwards inspect burrs and threads and keep chips out of equipment.
mfg1-electrical-l040.structureTitle: Check centres before machining · Distinguish pilot holes from internal threads
mfg1-electrical-l040.structureText:
Measure mounting-hole locations from the specified reference surface. Temporarily mark centre lines and outlines, place the actual device to check interference and orientation, then use a punch or other prescribed method. A hole made at the wrong location is not easily undone. Enlarge large holes in stages from a pilot hole as needed and clamp the workpiece securely.

Tapping forms an internal thread inside a pilot hole. The pilot diameter is not simply the nominal thread diameter: check tables matching the specified thread diameter, pitch, material and machining method. Follow the procedure for centre drilling, pilot drilling, chamfering, cutting-fluid use and other required preparations. Do not apply one hole diameter to every material based only on an approximate ratio in a reference.

mfg1-electrical-l041.title: Select file cross-sections and cutting directions
mfg1-electrical-l041.exampleTitle: Use small file sets for details
mfg1-electrical-l041.exampleText: Needle-file sets combine small files for detailed hand finishing. Their various sections suit confined areas and fine features. Do not force a large file into a narrow space and damage surrounding areas; finish only the necessary area gradually. When deburring drilled or cut features, check effects on assembly and specified dimensions rather than stopping at appearance alone.
mfg1-electrical-l041.structureTitle: Match cross-section to the intended shape · Cut on the push stroke
mfg1-electrical-l041.structureText:
Metalworking files cut and abrade metal by hand and come in flat, half-round, round, square, triangular and other shapes. Flat faces, round holes, curves, grooves and sharp corners present different contact surfaces. Do not select a tool merely because it fits: distinguish the surface to remove from surfaces to retain. Half-round files provide both flat and curved working surfaces.

Ordinary metalworking file teeth are arranged to cut when pushed forward. Instead of equal pressure in both directions, apply suitable pressure forward and release it on return. Clamping, handle condition and clogged teeth also affect results. Check dimensions during work to avoid removing too much.

mfg1-electrical-l042.title: Organize charge, magnetic fields and Fleming’s rules
mfg1-electrical-l042.exampleTitle: Left hand for force; right hand for induction
mfg1-electrical-l042.exampleText: Fleming’s left-hand rule gives the force direction on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field: thumb for force, first finger for field and middle finger for current. The right-hand rule gives induced electromotive-force direction when a conductor moves in a field: thumb for motion, first finger for field and middle finger for induced electromotive force. With a closed circuit it also helps determine induced-current direction. Rather than memorizing merely opposite hands, distinguish given conditions from the quantity sought.
mfg1-electrical-l042.structureTitle: Charge signs and separation · Fields and forces produced by current
mfg1-electrical-l042.structureText:
Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. In an ideal point-charge model, force magnitude is proportional to the product of charges and inversely proportional to separation squared. With unchanged charges and medium, doubling separation reduces force magnitude to one quarter. Signs help determine direction; explain magnitude and direction separately.

Electric current, as well as magnets, creates a magnetic field. In an idealized pair of parallel conductors, currents in the same direction attract and opposite currents repel. Force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field depends on field and current directions. Do not treat current, field and mechanical force as one quantity: draw their arrows separately.

mfg1-surface-lesson-036.title: Prevent mix-ups through reporting, communication, consultation and 5S
mfg1-surface-lesson-036.exampleText: A jig from another process was mixed into the cleaning-jig shelf. Record its number and location, identify it using the prescribed hold method and consult the responsible person. Tell the next operator it is under review. Do not discard it as part of sorting or move it to an empty shelf where it becomes harder to trace.
mfg1-surface-lesson-036.structureTitle: Separate facts from judgments · Combine tidying with identification · Make storage clear to everyone with the three fixed rules
mfg1-surface-lesson-036.structureText:
Reporting conveys progress or results; communication shares necessary information with those concerned; consultation seeks advice on matters you cannot decide. When reporting a surface-treatment abnormality, state the conclusion first, followed by the process, time, affected lot and confirmed values.
Separate an assumption such as “I think the chemical is the cause” from an observation such as “The label is unreadable.” Check that the listener understood and repeat the instructions received.

5S means sorting, setting in order, cleaning, maintaining cleanliness and discipline. Separate unnecessary items from necessary ones, decide how to arrange necessary items, remove dirt, and maintain that condition and the rules. Even if a chemical container seems unnecessary, do not discard it without the prescribed decision.
If cleaning reveals an abnormality, do not merely remove the dirt and finish. Record the location and possible leak, keep away from the hazardous area and notify the responsible person.

The three fixed rules specify location, item and quantity. A designated shelf alone does not establish control if its contents or quantity are wrong. Compare the label with the actual item and restore the specified condition after use.
Do not distinguish similar containers or jigs by color alone; check names, identification numbers and suitability for the process. Substituting another item without permission can affect both quality and safety.

mfg1-surface-lesson-037.title: Record 4M changes and verify improvements with PDCA
mfg1-surface-lesson-037.exampleText: In a hypothetical record, 10 of 200 items were defective before action and 4 of 80 afterward. The count fell, but both defect rates are 5%. Record the denominator rather than concluding that the rate fell to less than half. This is a calculation exercise, not an acceptable defect rate for a real process.
mfg1-surface-lesson-037.structureTitle: Do not focus on quality alone · 4M and facts at the workplace · Keep an evaluation after implementation
mfg1-surface-lesson-037.structureText:
QCD stands for quality, cost and delivery; QCDS adds safety. Faster, cheaper processing is not a good improvement if it fails performance requirements or increases danger.
Define the improvement goal with numbers or observable conditions, and decide first what must be maintained. Do not skip inspections or safety procedures to meet a deadline.

4M means people, machinery/equipment, materials and methods. When defects increase, arrange changes such as operator handovers, equipment checks, material lots and treatment procedures in time order. A changed factor is a clue, not proof of the cause.
The three-actuals principle checks the actual place, actual item and actual facts. Compare records with real conditions and separate observations from hypotheses. Checking the actual item does not authorize approaching hazardous equipment.

PDCA is a cycle of plan, do, check and act. Set goals and methods, implement within the approved scope and compare results under matching conditions. Feed the evaluation into the next plan or standard during the improvement stage.
Implementation alone does not demonstrate effectiveness. State differences in sample sizes or periods, and consider chance or other changes. Obtain the prescribed approval for changes.

mfg1-surface-lesson-038.title: Distinguish work standards from QC process charts
mfg1-surface-lesson-038.exampleText: A hypothetical plan requires designated samples from every lot. A morning measurement does not authorize skipping a different afternoon lot. Even with a correct measurement method, check whether frequency and coverage are insufficient and consult the responsible person.
mfg1-surface-lesson-038.structureTitle: The purpose of standardization · Read the control plan · Do not fill gaps with your own method
mfg1-surface-lesson-038.structureText:
Standardization shares rules and criteria to reduce variation in work. Work standards specify procedures, equipment, tools and precautions. Even experienced workers must not assume another product type or a revised procedure is unchanged.
Before work, check the product, process, document number and revision. A legible document for another process is not a valid basis.

A QC process chart summarizes control items, methods, frequency, responsibilities and actions for abnormalities for each process. Read not only what to measure but also when, who checks it and what to do when a value is outside the limit.
Even if you understand coating-thickness measurement, using the wrong lot or timing may fail the control plan. Work standards and QC process charts complement each other with different information.

Ask for clarification when frequency or criteria cannot be read or two documents conflict. Do not rely only on memory or choose the more convenient criterion.
For abnormal values, take prescribed action and keep product identification and records. If a standard needs changing, submit reasons and findings through the prescribed process; operators must not rewrite it without permission.

mfg1-surface-lesson-039.title: Choose QC tools according to what you need to investigate
mfg1-surface-lesson-039.exampleTitle: Choose the method from the purpose
mfg1-surface-lesson-039.exampleText: To examine treatment time and coating thickness, pair both values for each item in a scatter diagram. Consider a time-ordered graph for weekly counts and a Pareto chart for prioritizing defect types. Choose by the question to answer, not visual appeal.
mfg1-surface-lesson-039.structureTitle: Define categories before collecting data · Distinguish distributions from time order · Do not confuse relationships with causes
mfg1-surface-lesson-039.structureText:
A check sheet records defect types and other data using consistent categories. Changing category names or counting methods between days makes comparison difficult. Avoid double counting and record the total examined, period and process.
A Pareto chart arranges items in descending order of count or another measure and shows the cumulative proportion. High-count items are candidates for investigation, but this is no reason to ignore rare, serious safety issues.

A histogram groups values into intervals and displays counts to show spread and distribution shape. A control chart instead monitors time-ordered changes using control limits and other information. Remember that a histogram hides measurement order.
Control limits assess process variation; they do not mean the same thing as product specification limits. Points inside the lines do not prove that every product meets specifications.

A scatter diagram plots paired observations to examine a relationship. Seeing a relationship does not prove that one variable causes the other. Check other conditions and biases in the records.
A cause-and-effect diagram organizes possible factors behind a problem. Use 4M and other groupings to expand candidates, but factors on the diagram remain unverified hypotheses. Choose bar or line graphs according to the purpose as well.

mfg1-surface-lesson-040.title: Compare corrosion of iron, copper, aluminum and zinc
mfg1-surface-lesson-040.exampleText: White deposits were found on a zinc coating over iron. Do not immediately conclude that white means harmless or that the iron must have red rust. Ask quality personnel to check coating condition and requirements. Do not merely polish away the appearance and proceed to shipping approval.
mfg1-surface-lesson-040.structureTitle: Covering iron and the role of zinc · Copper and aluminum surfaces · Check the environment and specification
mfg1-surface-lesson-040.structureText:
Iron and steel corrode in environments involving moisture, oxygen and other factors. Blocking the environment with paint differs from protecting iron through preferential corrosion of zinc.
The zinc in zinc plating is itself consumed. Do not assume a coating provides permanent protection; check the environment, scratches, remaining coating and specification together.

Copper can form relatively stable surface films depending on the environment, but may discolor and can be affected by sulfides and other substances. “Copper withstands every chemical” is incorrect.
Aluminum’s natural oxide film protects its surface, but is thin and may be damaged by the environment or treatment. Do not regard it as having the same thickness or performance as an anodic oxide film produced by a controlled process.

Zinc can also be affected by corrosion under acidic, alkaline or other conditions. Confirm the post-treatment against required performance, material and applicable specification. Do not treat representative process names in this material as chemical recipes for workplace use.
If discoloration or rust is found, record material, position, storage conditions, wetting and lot. Authorized personnel decide conformity, reprocessing and chemical selection.

mfg1-surface-lesson-041.title: Use Ohm’s law with units and stated conditions
mfg1-surface-lesson-041.exampleText: Suppose an ideal resistor carries 30mA at 120mV. Convert to E=0.120V and I=0.030A: R=0.120/0.030=4Ω. The check 4Ω×0.030A=0.120V returns the original value. These numbers are for paper exercises, not equipment settings.
mfg1-surface-lesson-041.structureTitle: Write one relationship three ways · Align prefixes before calculating · Distinguish a resistor model from a plating tank
mfg1-surface-lesson-041.structureText:
For current I through resistance R and voltage E across it, E=RI, I=E/R and R=E/I. Units are volts V, amperes A and ohms Ω. Decide what to find first, then organize given values and units.
At constant resistance, increasing voltage increases current. At constant voltage, increasing resistance decreases current. Always state which quantity is held constant.

The prefix m means one thousandth. 200mA is 0.200A and 80mV is 0.080V. Entering numbers without units can create a thousandfold error. Convert to V and A first and include units such as Ω in the answer.
After rearranging a formula, check using the original relationship. If a calculated value disagrees with a measurement, check units, assumptions and the object’s condition; do not rewrite it to a convenient value.

These calculations assume a resistor for which Ohm’s law applies within the range considered. Electrode reactions, contacts and solution conditions also affect a plating tank’s power readings; the whole tank cannot always be treated as a constant resistance.
A change in voltage and current readings alone does not identify solution concentration or a single cause. Investigate prescribed monitoring items using equipment procedures. There is no need to change real equipment settings to study calculations.

mfg1-surface-lesson-042.title: Organize current and voltage in series and parallel circuits
mfg1-surface-lesson-042.exampleText: Ideal 6Ω and 3Ω resistors in parallel give 6×3/(6+3)=2Ω. At 6V, branch currents are 1A and 2A, totaling 3A. Connecting the same resistors in series gives 9Ω and is a different circuit. These are paper examples, not instructions to modify wiring.
