mfg1-surface-lesson-042.structureTitle: Current is shared in series · Parallel branches share terminal voltage · Check junction and loop balances
mfg1-surface-lesson-042.structureText:
In a series circuit with resistors along one path, the same current flows through each resistor. Equivalent resistance is R=R1+R2. Voltage drops depend on resistance; two resistors do not necessarily have equal voltages.
Ideal 4Ω and 8Ω resistors in series give 12Ω. At 24V across the circuit, current is 2A and the voltage drops are 8V and 16V.

In a parallel circuit with branches between the same two nodes, each branch has the same voltage. Current divides according to branch resistance. Equivalent resistance follows 1/R=1/R1+1/R2; for two resistors, R=R1R2/(R1+R2).
Positive finite resistances in parallel give an equivalent resistance smaller than the smaller resistor. Identify the nodes rather than confusing this with series addition.

Kirchhoff’s current law states that the sum of currents entering a junction equals the sum leaving it. The voltage law states that the signed sum of voltage changes around a closed loop is zero. With one source and resistors, source voltage corresponds to the sum of voltage drops.
Choose current directions and a loop direction first, and use consistent signs for the source and drops. If values do not balance, also check how the diagram was read and the measurement conditions.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-043.title: Check drawing paper and lettering, then choose a drawing suited to the task
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-043.exampleTitle: Match the purpose of the work to the drawing
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-043.exampleText: A detail drawing is for machining individual parts, an assembly drawing is for putting parts together, and a layout drawing shows matters such as equipment installation positions. Looking only at the hole dimensions of a part will not tell you where to install the equipment. Confirm the type of drawing and the object needed for the task, and ask the person responsible about missing information.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-043.structureTitle: Paper size and orientation · Read the character height
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-043.structureText:
For the mechanical drawings covered in this textbook, A-series paper is preferred, in a size that clearly shows the object. Normally the long edge is horizontal; A4 may also be used in portrait orientation. A larger sheet does not make the information more accurate. On copied or reduced drawings, check that the lines and lettering remain clearly readable.

The size of lettering on a drawing is specified by its character height. The textbook lists 3.5, 5, 7 and 10 mm for kanji, and 2.5, 3.5, 5, 7 and 10 mm for kana, letters and numbers. If a decimal point or part of a digit is illegible, do not guess and start work; request a legible approved drawing. Do not confuse enlargement or reduction during printing with a change to the stated dimension values.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-044.title: Match viewing directions to view positions in third-angle projection
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-044.exampleTitle: Compare the same feature in three views
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-044.exampleText: Imagine on paper a part with a hole on its top and a step on its side. The top view alone cannot establish the hole depth, so relate it to the front view or the sectional-view instructions. A projection-method symbol near the title block is another clue. If the arrangement does not match, do not mirror a view yourself; ask about the projection method and viewing direction.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-044.structureTitle: Look at a solid object from several directions · The front view is chosen for shape and purpose
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-044.structureText:
A projection view represents the shape of a solid object on a plane. In third-angle projection, the top view, seen from above, is placed above the front view, and the right-side view, seen from the right, is placed to its right. First check the front view and the stated projection method so you do not confuse left and right on the paper with the direction from which the object is viewed.

The front view is also called the principal view and clearly communicates shape and function. It is chosen with considerations such as the orientation in use for an assembly drawing, or the orientation during the main machining operation for a detail drawing. Avoiding too many hidden lines also matters. Do not assume without checking that the largest view is the front view.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-045.title: Distinguish cut material from internal space in a sectional view
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-045.exampleTitle: Not everything is drawn as cut in the same way
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-045.exampleText: Some portions may be left unsectioned if cutting them would add no useful explanation and would instead make the drawing harder to understand. You therefore cannot conclude that every unhatched area is hollow. If the cutting position or the part concerned is unclear, check the assembly drawing, detail drawing and indicated extent of the section before explaining the internal shape.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-045.structureTitle: It does not mean the object was actually cut · Distinguish hatching from a hole
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-045.structureText:
A sectional view represents the inside of an object by imagining a cut and removing the portion in front. It can make internal holes and steps easier to understand than using many hidden lines. It is a way of communicating shape, not a machining instruction to cut the actual product.

The cut surface of material is generally hatched. For a cylindrical part, distinguish the material exposed by the cut from the space inside the bore. Do not mistake every hatched area for a hole, or treat the diagonal lines themselves as instructions to machine grooves. Check the dimensions and the other projection views together.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-046.title: Read the required length from dimension lines and values
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-046.exampleText: Ordinary mechanical drawings may use millimetres for length without adding “mm” to every dimension value. Angles, however, use degrees or other angular units, so the same number can have a different meaning. Check the drawing’s unit specification first. If different dimensions are given for the same feature, do not choose whichever suits you; identify the conflicting area and ask for clarification.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-046.structureTitle: Read the finished-part requirement · The roles of two kinds of line
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-046.structureText:
Dimensions give the information needed for a part’s function and manufacture and normally specify its finished dimensions. Repeating the same dimension unnecessarily can cause conflicting values after a change. Even if the drawing is printed large, read its stated dimensions rather than measuring the paper with a ruler as a substitute for the requirement.

A dimension line corresponds to the indicated length or angle and has arrowheads or other end marks. Extension lines help show which positions the dimension runs between. Edge length, chord length, arc length and angle are not the same thing. Do not extract only the number; follow the end marks and extension lines to establish the feature concerned.

In a basic length-dimension drawing, also check the angle where the extension lines from the two ends meet the dimension line. The basic source example uses right angles. Angular and arc dimensions use different line geometry, so do not replace every arrangement with the same straight-line layout. On your own plate sketch, mark where the two types of line meet at right angles.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-047.title: Connect detail and reference dimensions to machining information
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-047.exampleTitle: Keep the meaning of the parentheses
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-047.exampleText: A reference dimension is a value provided for reference, with its number in parentheses. It may show a value obtainable from other dimensions. Omitting the parentheses when copying can change the understood role of the dimension. Do not independently substitute a parenthesized value as the sole basis for machining or acceptance; check the underlying instructions and inspection plan.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-047.structureTitle: Read the symbol together with the feature · Check machining conditions as well as hole diameter
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-047.structureText:
Radius is indicated by R, diameter by φ, and plate thickness by t, for example. Symbols may sometimes be omitted when the dimension-line direction or end marks make the meaning clear. Do not decide the dimension type solely because a symbol is not visible; check the feature and both ends of the dimension line. For example, R6 means radius 6 and φ6 means diameter 6; they do not specify the same shape.

When different hole-making methods need to be distinguished, the nominal tool size and machining method are also specified. Do not treat a drilled hole and a finishing reaming operation as the same process simply because their nominal diameters match. A through hole may be shown without a depth dimension, but the absence of a visible depth alone does not prove that every hole is through; compare the other views and instructions.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-048.title: Check the feature and datum of a geometrical tolerance
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-048.exampleTitle: Do not substitute your own reference
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-048.exampleText: A datum is a reference used when considering a geometrical tolerance. The attachment position on the drawing may differ for surface and axis indications. Do not add an unnecessary reference to a characteristic such as flatness, which concerns form on its own. If the reference surface or axis cannot be identified, do not finalize the measuring method; ask the person responsible about the feature, reference and applicable standard.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-048.structureTitle: A dimension range does not tell you every requirement · Read the frame in order and trace the feature
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-048.structureText:
Even if a diameter or length is within its specified range, requirements for surface flatness, axis orientation or position may not be met. Geometrical tolerances indicate characteristics such as straightness, flatness, roundness, parallelism, perpendicularity and position. Different types evaluate different properties, so one dimensional measurement does not mean everything has been checked.

A geometrical-tolerance frame gives the characteristic symbol, tolerance value and datum references where needed. For a paper example saying “parallelism, 0.08, B,” read not only 0.08 but also what must be parallel to reference B. Also check, through details such as the arrow attachment position, whether it applies to a surface or an axis.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-049.title: Trace the features specified by surface-texture and welding symbols
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-049.exampleTitle: Check which component needs edge preparation and the supplementary instructions
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-049.exampleText:
Edge preparation is the form made at a component’s end for welding. A bent arrow may indicate which component is to receive the preparation, but an unbent arrow may be used when the component is already clear, for example. Do not decide which side to machine solely from whether the arrow is bent; check the basic symbol, component, dimensions and supplementary instructions together. Reading symbols does not authorize you to omit work qualifications or safety procedures.
A bent arrow identifies the member to be prepared with a groove. The bend may be omitted when that member is clear or either member is acceptable. An unbent arrow alone does not mean no groove is needed; check the member and applicable drawing convention.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-049.structureTitle: Do not extract only the surface-texture number · Separate weld type from weld position
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-049.structureText:
Surface condition affects machine performance and includes waviness and roughness. Drawings add a parameter such as Ra or Rz and its value to a symbol, indicating the relevant surface directly or with a leader line. The same number means something different with a different parameter. Do not reuse a value from another surface; also check the machining-related symbol, relevant surface and measurement conditions.

A welding symbol is built around a reference line and basic symbol, with necessary dimensions and supplementary instructions added. Basic symbols distinguish square, V and single-bevel groove welds, fillet welds and other types. In the notation shown in this textbook, a basic symbol below the reference line indicates the arrow side, and one above it indicates the other side. On an actual drawing, also confirm the applicable standard and notation system; do not turn the drawing over and decide the position yourself.

mfg1-electrical-l043.title: The two exam sections and your study plan
mfg1-electrical-l043.exampleTitle: Understand the original Japanese before practicing
mfg1-electrical-l043.exampleText:
Read terms, units, and negative wording through to the end. Do not record, remove, or share exam-site questions or answers; this app uses newly written practice questions. Record why you struggle and move to timed practice after you can explain the material.
In study, separate difficult Japanese from unclear technical understanding. If researching a specialist term does not resolve it, ask a supervisor or colleague to confirm its meaning. Reread to connect the language with the skill until you can judge without looking up the meaning every time. The guide’s total of80minutes is test time, not a measurement of learning time. Check the end of a sentence, including any negation, before answering.
Do not take out or share even part of test information. Private SNS is no exception. The guide describes invigilators and surveillance cameras at the venue. Alongside invalidation of results for misconduct, its examples of measures include loss of eligibility for future tests and reporting to the Immigration Services Agency. This explains the guide’s cautions; it does not predict a current individual sanction.
mfg1-electrical-l043.structureTitle: Manage the two times separately · Relating the category to work
mfg1-electrical-l043.structureText:
The uploaded textbook describes the July 2026 format: theory has 30 true/false questions in 40 minutes; practical has 10 multiple-choice judgment and planning questions in 40 minutes. The respective passing rates are 65% and 60%, and each section must meet its own threshold. When this app scores practice questions equally, it uses at least 20 theory answers and 6 practical answers correct. This does not guarantee the official exam’s unpublished point allocation or minimum correct-answer counts.
The following records the guide as of July2026. The assessment checks skills requiring knowledge or experience. Its level is described as equivalent to Grade3 of the trade skills test, allowing a certain level of work without special development or training. It uses computer-based testing (CBT), in Japanese with readings on kanji. In principle, the stated eligibility is foreign nationals aged17 or older on the test date, or18 or older for Indonesian nationals, who intend to work in Japan after passing. These are facts recorded in that edition. Do not use this record alone to decide current application eligibility.

Electrical/electronic assembly study includes machining, maintenance, packaging, plastics, and circuit boards as well as wiring and circuits. Passing the exam is different from qualifications, training, and company authorization to operate a particular machine. Check the official application guidance for eligibility and what to bring.
Treat the listed work as a map of the study scope. Machining, finishing, inspection and maintenance include conventional turning, milling, numerically controlled turning, machining centers, jig and tool finishing, die and mold finishing, machine assembly finishing, machine inspection and mechanical maintenance. Electrical and electronics work includes electronic equipment assembly, rotating electrical machine assembly, transformer assembly, distribution and control panel assembly, switching control device assembly, rotating electrical machine winding manufacture, printed circuit board design and printed circuit board manufacture. Forming and packaging include compression molding, injection molding, inflation film molding, blow molding, industrial packaging, hand lay-up molding, bead-process expanded polystyrene molding, manufacture of plastics molding materials and film processing. The film processes listed are dry lamination, extrusion lamination, slitting, bag making and flat yarn. Inclusion in this table is not proof of unconditional authorization to perform an individual task.

mfg1-electrical-l044.title: Safety and health responsibilities and responses to abnormalities
mfg1-electrical-l044.exampleText: If sound, smell, or vibration differs from normal, follow your assigned procedure for stopping, evacuation, and reporting. Do not touch unfamiliar machines without authorization or throw tools to others; return them to their designated place. Do not skip procedures simply because danger is not visible.
mfg1-electrical-l044.structureTitle: A system that protects people and health · Know workplace roles
mfg1-electrical-l044.structureText:
Heat, heavy objects, machines, and chemicals present different hazards. Occupational safety and health covers disease prevention as well as injuries. Combine the company’s management responsibilities with workers’ compliance to reduce danger to everyone nearby.

The safety and health committee discusses issues; safety managers and occupational physicians have their own specialist roles. Requirements are not identical at every workplace. Confirm whom to consult, emergency contacts, and the chain of command in your own workplace.

mfg1-electrical-l045.title: Use 5S and the three fixed conditions to detect shortages and mixing
mfg1-electrical-l045.exampleTitle: Tidying is not authorization to discard
mfg1-electrical-l045.exampleText: Do not discard unidentified or held items yourself; identify them and ask the responsible person. If another item is in terminalB’s shelf location, merely moving it to a vacant space does not prevent recurrence. Compare labels and records and investigate why it was mixed in.
mfg1-electrical-l045.structureTitle: Distinguish five actions · Specify location, item, and quantity
mfg1-electrical-l045.structureText:
Sorting separates needed from unneeded things and removes the latter. Setting in order places needed items for convenient use; cleaning removes dirt. Standardized cleanliness maintains sorting, order, and cleaning, while discipline makes agreed behavior habitual.

The three fixed conditions specify location, item, and quantity. Mark not just the shelf position but also the part number and permitted quantity there. Upper and lower limits help reveal shortages, excess stock, and mixed items.

mfg1-electrical-l046.title: Confirm training and select protection for the task
mfg1-electrical-l046.exampleText: Safety footwear addresses hazards such as falling objects; protective glasses address flying material. Gloves can protect or create entanglement hazards, depending on the task. Keep gloved hands away from a rotating drill press, and confirm chemical-compatible protection and ventilation for chemical work. For transport, check weight, visibility, route, and specified aids, avoiding suspended loads and their surroundings. Near casting work, distinguish heat from dust and check heat-illness measures and suitable dust protection.
mfg1-electrical-l046.structureTitle: Learn before a new assignment · OJT is not leaving someone to learn alone
mfg1-electrical-l046.structureText:
On hiring or a change of duties, confirm hazards, equipment, protective equipment, procedures, startup checks, and emergency responses. The qualifications, skills courses, or special education needed for hazardous work depend on the actual conditions. The task name alone does not establish whether you may do it.

Check the instructor’s explanation and demonstration, practice within the approved scope, and receive feedback. Do not pretend to understand after merely watching; explain essential steps in your own words. Receiving OJT does not automatically replace statutory training or qualifications.

mfg1-electrical-l047.title: Read prohibition, warning, and evacuation signs separately
mfg1-electrical-l047.exampleText: Extinguisher, AED, and evacuation signs help locate equipment and destinations. Do not treat a wide-area evacuation location, evacuation building, and tsunami refuge as identical; match the disaster type with workplace routes. When using an AED, follow its voice guidance and emergency responders’ instructions.
mfg1-electrical-l047.structureTitle: Actions that are forbidden · Recognize the presence of danger
mfg1-electrical-l047.structureText:
Red prohibition signs include no smoking, no flames, no entry, do not touch, and not for drinking. Read a general prohibition symbol with its accompanying target. Confirm what is restricted, such as people entering versus vehicles entering.

Yellow warning signs include electric shock, slipping, steps, falls, and overhead obstacles. A warning rather than a prohibition does not automatically grant free entry. Check the area, work conditions, and accompanying instructions, and describe hazards specifically.

mfg1-electrical-l048.title: Connect SDS information and chemical labels to work
mfg1-electrical-l048.exampleTitle: Do not guess what an unknown liquid is
mfg1-electrical-l048.exampleText: Do not identify an unlabeled decanted liquid by color or smell; suspend use. Vapor can accumulate in tanks handling organic solvents, so cleaning is not a task to undertake independently. Decanting, mixing, and spill response require approved procedures.
mfg1-electrical-l048.structureTitle: Pictograms are clues to hazards · Read the necessary sections before use
mfg1-electrical-l048.structureText:
Flame, corrosion, health hazard, environmental hazard, and exclamation-mark symbols indicate different hazards. One container may present several. Do not infer all concentrations, protection, or first aid from the picture alone; match the product identification on the label and SDS.

An SDS includes hazards, handling and storage, exposure prevention, first aid, and spill response. Operate local exhaust or ventilation and confirm compatible protective equipment and waste-liquid containers. Follow the responsible person’s guidance for health management such as special medical examinations.

mfg1-electrical-l049.title: Near misses and improvement through OSHMS
mfg1-electrical-l049.exampleText: Anticipate machine failure, human error, and natural disasters, and continue reducing danger as far as possible. Check that a measure has not created a new hazard. Combine actions selected in hazard prediction with changes to equipment or processes.
mfg1-electrical-l049.structureTitle: Report small warning events · Improve as an organization
mfg1-electrical-l049.structureText:
Learn Heinrich’s 1:29:300 as a way of considering serious accidents, minor accidents, and near misses. It does not guarantee these counts at every site or mean that work is safe until 300 events. Record dangerous approaches or almost-falling objects even without injury.

OSHMS repeatedly plans, implements, evaluates, and improves safety and health management. Evaluate effects and remaining risks, assign responsibility and deadlines, and revise. Producing records alone does not complete the activity.

mfg1-surface-lesson-043.title: Check training scope and KYT action goals
mfg1-surface-lesson-043.exampleText: Before moving parts with a new cart, use a diagram to check changes in level and intersections. Propose an action such as stopping before the intersection and proceeding after checking both sides. The responsible person checks equipment and route measures and the training scope. Do not enter an operating transport route to look for hazards.
mfg1-surface-lesson-043.structureTitle: Recheck when the work changes · Confirm OJT learning after explanation and demonstration · Carry the four KYT stages through to action
mfg1-surface-lesson-043.structureText:
For unfamiliar equipment or materials, or changed procedures, do not decide your work scope from past experience alone. Training covers hazards and harmful effects, safety devices and protective equipment, work procedures, checks before starting, workplace organization, and communication and evacuation during accidents. Ask the person responsible about unfamiliar words or procedures before working.
Hazardous or harmful work may require confirmation of qualifications, skills courses or special training, depending on the work conditions. A name alone does not mean the same training is sufficient for everyone. Check the specific statutory category and authority through valid workplace documents and the responsible person.

OJT teaches knowledge and skills through actual work. Receive the instructor's explanation and demonstration, perform within the authorized safe scope, and then receive advice and correct mistakes. Having watched once is different from being allowed to work independently.
Do not continue an unconfirmed operation by guessing because the instructor has left. Agree in advance on what you may do, stopping conditions and whom to ask, and record checks of understanding and skill.

In KYT, identify unsafe actions and conditions from workplace pictures or actual conditions, select important hazards, consider specific measures, and summarize them as team action goals. Listing hazards alone does not confirm that measures were implemented.
“Be careful” does not say who will do what. Specify the person, situation, action and checking method. Discussion and pointing-and-calling cannot replace necessary engineering measures such as guards or isolation.

mfg1-surface-lesson-044.title: Separate risk evaluation from the effectiveness of measures
mfg1-surface-lesson-044.exampleTitle: The same measure still needs checking
mfg1-surface-lesson-044.exampleText: After changing flooring to prevent slipping while transporting containers, the responsible person checks places where liquid remains and how carts move. Record conditions before and after improvement, and confirm that the flooring also suits the chemicals and cleaning method. The installation date alone does not mark completion.
mfg1-surface-lesson-044.structureTitle: Identify hazards and consider their effects · Implementation and effectiveness are different · Continue reviewing through OSHMS
mfg1-surface-lesson-044.structureText:
Risk assessment identifies hazards and considers priorities using factors such as likelihood and severity. Even for the same number of operations, a fall and a splash of hot liquid can cause different harm. Use the workplace's evaluation method; do not invent statutory scores from the learning material.
A near miss is an event that felt dangerous even though no injury occurred. Treat Heinrich's ratio as a way of learning from minor events, not as a number guaranteeing accident probabilities in every workplace.

Consider removing the hazard itself or reducing it through equipment and work methods, together with necessary training and protective equipment. Saying “pay attention” does not complete a measure. Implement what the responsible person approved, and share remaining hazards and stopping conditions.
Check effectiveness under the same conditions after implementation. A nonslip mat can create a new trip hazard if its edge lifts. Examine whether the original hazard decreased and whether new hazards increased.

OSHMS sets safety and health goals and plans, implements them, evaluates results and improves them. Writing documents or providing training alone does not confirm effectiveness. Compare actual conditions with records.
Do not assume accidents can never occur. Manage residual risk by anticipating equipment failure, human error and disasters. Do not ignore small abnormalities, but do not enter a hazardous area to investigate their causes.

mfg1-surface-lesson-045.title: Connect prohibition, warning and evacuation signs to action
mfg1-surface-lesson-045.exampleText: A chemical-storage entrance has a no-flames sign, while another passage has a no-entry sign. Do not treat both simply as “caution”; check the prohibited activities or items and the area you cannot enter. Ask about unclear evacuation directions during normal operations rather than searching for the first time during an actual alarm.
mfg1-surface-lesson-045.structureTitle: Read prohibitions and warnings differently · Check chemical labels together with the SDS · Check equipment locations and evacuation destinations
mfg1-surface-lesson-045.structureText:
Prohibition signs identify actions not allowed in that place or situation. Distinguish no entry, no flames, do not touch and do not drink. Do not guess from red alone; read the shape and text together.
Warning signs indicate hazards such as electric shock, slippery floors, changes in level, overhead hazards and falls. A sign does not remove the hazard. Before passing through or starting work, check the designated route and safety procedures.

Flame, corrosion, health hazard, environmental hazard and exclamation-mark pictograms are clues to hazards. Identical pictograms do not necessarily mean identical protective equipment or storage conditions. Compare the product name, precautions, SDS and workplace procedures.
Seeing only one pictogram does not mean there are no other hazards. Suspend use and check if a label is missing, unclear or inconsistent with its container.

Fire-extinguisher and AED signs mark installation locations. Evacuation sites, evacuation buildings and tsunami evacuation destinations can have different purposes. Use the workplace evacuation plan to check routes and assembly locations suited to the anticipated disaster.
Knowing an AED or extinguisher sign does not mean you should operate it in every situation. In an emergency, follow procedures including reporting and evacuation, and the responsible person's instructions. Do not return to a dangerous location.

mfg1-surface-lesson-046.title: Check standards' scope and SI units
mfg1-surface-lesson-046.exampleText: If an instrument displays 250 mA, convert it to 0.250 A in a field requiring A. Do not write 250 A; show the conversion basis. If the applicable standard's edition is unreadable, ask the responsible person for the valid document rather than independently choosing a convenient latest edition.
mfg1-surface-lesson-046.structureTitle: Do not judge from a standard's name alone · JIS and measuring-instrument management · Distinguish the seven base units
mfg1-surface-lesson-046.structureText:
Standards are common agreements on matters such as quality, safety, performance, dimensions and test methods. ISO includes standards for products and services and for organizational management systems. ISO9001 concerns quality management and ISO14001 environmental management. They do not automatically guarantee every performance characteristic of each product.
Check the edition, subject, scope and product requirements as well as the standard number. Do not use an old edition or conditions for another application without authorization.

JIS means Japanese Industrial Standards. Check what the marking or certification covers. A JIS mark alone does not guarantee the instrument's current calibration, absence of damage or suitability for the target.
Using a conforming instrument and obtaining a conforming product are different. Check measurement conditions, results and required values, then use the designated decision method.

The SI base units are length m, mass kg, time s, electric current A, thermodynamic temperature K, amount of substance mol, and luminous intensity cd. Read indications such as temperature °C, voltage V and resistance Ω with their quantities. Do not treat illuminance and luminous intensity as the same quantity.
The prefix m means one thousandth and k means one thousand times. Although the letter is the same, standalone m means metre while m in mA means milli. Record the quantity and unit, not just the number.

mfg1-surface-lesson-047.title: Think about the 3 Rs and circular use through the process flow
mfg1-surface-lesson-047.exampleText: Classify resizing packaging to the necessary dimensions as reduction; repeatedly using approved, suitable returnable boxes as reuse; and sending sorted offcuts to an approved collector as recycling. Record effectiveness and approval conditions separately.
mfg1-surface-lesson-047.structureTitle: Distinguish three actions · Consider circularity from design onward · Preserve quality and safety conditions
mfg1-surface-lesson-047.structureText:
Reduce means reducing waste generation itself, reuse means using an item repeatedly after its first use, and recycle means reprocessing it as a resource. Ordering only the required amount, appropriately reusing containers and collecting by material have different purposes.
Putting something in a collection box does not by itself mean generation decreased. Separately record quantities generated and reused, collection destinations and other information.

A circular economy considers the circulation of value and resources through design, use, repair, reuse and recycling, beyond a one-way make-and-discard flow. It considers reducing waste and pollution, circulating products and materials, and regenerating nature.
Factories also consider packaging and jig life and ease of disassembly and collection. Recyclability alone does not make an unnecessary increase in use a good improvement.

When reusing chemical containers, check material, residues, labeling, cleaning method and approval for reuse. Mixing different liquids without authorization to increase the collected amount is not a 3 R activity.
Use the same product quantities and periods for before-and-after comparisons, and check changes in water, chemicals, energy and waste. Also examine whether saving in one place increases defects or wastewater burdens elsewhere.

mfg1-surface-lesson-048.title: Organize acids, bases and salts by name and properties
mfg1-surface-lesson-048.exampleText: Even if both container names include salt, do not assume they can replenish the same tank. Compare product number, composition, concentration and designated process. Hold and check any mismatch. This is identification practice, not an assignment to mix chemicals.
mfg1-surface-lesson-048.structureTitle: The scope of acid and base explanations · Neutralization and salt formation · Separate salt classification from solution properties
mfg1-surface-lesson-048.structureText:
This basic unit considers acids associated with hydrogen ions and bases associated with hydroxide ions in aqueous solution. Acid or base strength concerns the degree of dissociation; it is not the same as concentrated versus dilute.
Broader definitions also exist. Do not apply this aqueous explanation to every substance without qualification. A name or appearance alone does not establish that contact is safe.

In acid-base reactions, consider how hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions form water. Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide can be written HCl+NaOH→NaCl+H₂O. Check atom counts and charges on both sides.
The resulting salt and liquid pH depend on the combination and quantities. Saying “neutralized” does not necessarily mean pH 7 and harmless. Adjusting an actual tank follows a separate approved procedure from analytical calculation.

Study salts as compounds formed by reactions involving acids and bases. Acid salts, basic salts and normal salts are classified using chemical formulas and related information; their names alone do not determine solution pH or hazards. Even a normal salt does not always give a neutral aqueous solution.
A familiar name such as sodium chloride is not evidence that other metal salts have the same safety. Check composition, concentration, the SDS and waste-liquid category.

mfg1-surface-lesson-049.title: Distinguish redox from neutralization through electron changes
mfg1-surface-lesson-049.exampleText: If a report says a metal ion released electrons to become metal, check the electron's position in the half-reaction. For a cation becoming metal, electrons are on the left: this is reduction by electron gain. Compare with a neutralization equation and explain electron transfer and oxidation-number changes separately.
mfg1-surface-lesson-049.structureTitle: From individual definitions to the whole reaction · Combine two half-reactions · Distinguish neutralization
mfg1-surface-lesson-049.structureText:
Consider oxidation as losing electrons and reduction as gaining them. Electrons released by one side pass to the other, so oxidation and reduction occur together. A reaction can be redox through electron transfer even when no oxygen transfer is visible.
Earlier electroplating lessons addressed reduction of metal ions at the cathode. This unit asks a different question: follow which substance supplies electrons and which receives them across the whole reaction.

In a paper example, Fe→Fe²⁺+2 e⁻ is oxidation and Cu²⁺+2 e⁻→Cu is reduction. Combining them gives Fe+Cu²⁺→Fe²⁺+Cu, with electrons canceling. Check total charge as well as atom counts on both sides.
This is a reaction-reading example. Actual reaction behavior also depends on surface films, concentrations and the environment. Do not use the equation as a reason to put metal into an unknown liquid.

In H⁺+OH⁻→H₂O, the oxidation numbers of the elements considered here do not change. Do not call every acid-base reaction redox. Gas or color changes alone cannot establish the classification.
An oxidizing agent accepts electrons from the other substance and is itself reduced. A reducing agent donates electrons and is itself oxidized. Do not reverse its own change because of the impression given by its name.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-050.title: Read specific gravity as a density ratio and keep units distinct
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-050.exampleTitle: Copy numbers from a material table
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-050.exampleText: The source gives metal examples including aluminum 2.68 and iron 7.87. Alloys and conditions can differ, so do not replace these with density values from another source without authorization. When discussing a lighter part, check required strength, shape, temperature and material approval as well as specific gravity.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-050.structureTitle: Check the reference · Calculate an equal-volume comparison
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-050.structureText:
Specific gravity is treated as the ratio to the density of a reference substance. This source uses water at 4°C, with specific gravity 1, as the reference for solids and liquids. Distinguish this ratio from density values carrying units such as g/cm³. Records with different references or temperatures are not identical merely because their numbers look alike.

In a paper example, the masses of equal volumes of a specimen and reference water are specified as 84 g and 30 g. Their ratio is 84÷30=2.8. This differs from simply dividing the masses of objects with different volumes. These numbers are for learning, not inspection results certifying a material grade at work.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-051.title: Choose how to position a steel rule and a protractor
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-051.exampleText: Separate a request for an end length from a request for the angle of a sloping face. If the two reference faces are unclear, show the drawing and ask. Do not substitute an easier-to-see face. Record the instrument, target, contact faces and unit.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-051.structureTitle: Read length with a steel rule · An angle is a relationship between two faces
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-051.structureText:
A steel rule measures length. Align the end of the object with the reference position and read the scale from directly in front. Check chipped ends or dirty graduations. Do not assume it can guarantee precision tolerances merely because it is read like a paper ruler. Select the instrument specified by the requirement.

A protractor generally combines a graduated angle plate with a blade. Place the base and blade against the two planes whose angle is required, then read the scale. If one side is lifted or touches a different face, a readable number is still not the target angle.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-052.title: Separate the references of height gauges and depth gauges
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-052.exampleTitle: Check the increment for each instrument
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-052.exampleText: Analog and digital displays are available. The source shows vernier examples with scale increments of 0.05 mm or 0.02 mm; this does not apply to every instrument. Match instrument specifications, zero or datum setting, target location and temperature conditions before comparing results.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-052.structureTitle: The surface plate is the height reference · Depth starts from the upper reference face
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-052.structureText:
A height gauge is used on a surface plate to measure heights from that plane. Check that the measuring contact moves perpendicular to the reference face, and that the gauge base and plate have no foreign matter. Do not treat a tilted support as the same reference.

A depth gauge measures depth from a reference face. Seat it stably against that face and check that the measuring face reaches the target correctly. If it has not reached the bottom of a groove, do not record a value chosen to match the drawing depth.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-053.title: Check safety responsibilities and everyday communication
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-053.exampleTitle: Greetings and reports serve different purposes
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-053.exampleText: Morning greetings and words such as “work safely” help people cooperate. A nod alone, however, is not a report of a machine abnormality. Report the target, facts and actions clearly, and check that the other person understood.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-053.structureTitle: Do not leave everything to one person · Know specialist roles
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-053.structureText:
The source describes three aspects of occupational safety and health: standards for preventing harm, a system of responsibilities, and voluntary activities. Both the company and workers have roles. Naming a responsible person alone does not remove a hazard. Check whom you should consult and the emergency communication route.

A safety and health committee discusses safety and health issues; safety managers, occupational physicians and others have specialist roles. Confirm specific establishment and appointment requirements at the workplace. This lesson does not determine legal applicability by itself. Direct health concerns to the designated contact as well.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-054.title: Check training categories and the work you may perform
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-054.exampleTitle: Match records to the permitted work
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-054.exampleText: Know the training name, equipment covered, permitted activities and confirming person. If you learned operation but not internal adjustment, do not proceed to adjustment simply because it is the same machine. Stopping to ask about unfamiliar work is also part of learning safely.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-054.structureTitle: Changed work requires new checks · Do not treat every qualification and course as the same
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-054.structureText:
When joining a workplace or moving to a new task, learn the hazards of machinery and raw materials, protective equipment, safety devices, procedures, pre-start checks, housekeeping and evacuation in an accident. Experience operating the previous machine does not mean a new machine can be operated under the same conditions.

Forklifts, robot setting and maintenance, slinging and similar work require checking qualifications or training appropriate to the task and conditions. Do not describe one course as meeting every requirement. Confirm the requirements for the work and equipment with the responsible person. Reading the textbook or passing a mock exam does not replace workplace permission.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-055.title: Take near-miss reports beyond counting incidents
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-055.exampleText: A cart wheel stopped at a step and the load tilted. Report the time, step location, loading arrangement and evacuation already taken. Share who will check each countermeasure. Counting reports alone does not mean the problem has been addressed; check for recurrence and other hazards after action.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-055.structureTitle: No injury does not mean no information · The ratio is not a fixed forecast
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-055.structureText:
A near miss is an event in which a danger was noticed even though no accident resulted. Examples include an object nearly falling or someone nearly slipping. Record the location, action and surrounding conditions as well as the outcome to help investigate causes. Do not omit a record just because nobody was hurt.

The source presents Heinrich’s concept as 1 serious accident,29 minor accidents and 300 near misses. This is an educational ratio encouraging attention to small warning signs, not a prediction formula that must produce the same numbers in every workplace. Consider the potential severity when responding.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-056.title: Distinguish suspended-load hazards from fastening-tool hazards
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-056.exampleTitle: Do not hammer a bolt that will not enter
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-056.exampleText: Before using an impact wrench, check that the thread and part are compatible. If a bolt is difficult to insert, hammering its head can damage the threads. Do not force tightening. Follow the procedure to ask about the part number, alignment, foreign matter and damage.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-056.structureTitle: Stay out from under suspended loads · Angles change the forces
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-056.structureText:
A crane load can fall because of a wire-rope or attachment problem. Stay out from under the load and outside designated danger areas; follow access control and signals. Slinging and operation require the necessary qualifications, training and assigned scope. A nearby bystander must not independently start helping.

As the angle between wire ropes widens, the force on the ropes may increase even for the same load. Do not decide a safe angle or lifting method by appearance. Check the specified load, gear and plan. Do not calculate an actual lifting capacity from this lesson and change the arrangement independently.

mfg1-electrical-l050.title: Design, manufacturing, logistics quality, and 4M
mfg1-electrical-l050.exampleText: Man means workers, Machine equipment, Material materials, and Method procedures. Do not blame people alone for increased defects: compare material lots, tool condition, changed settings, and training. If several things changed together, record their respective times and scopes.
mfg1-electrical-l050.structureTitle: Start with customer requirements · QCD and safety
mfg1-electrical-l050.structureText:
Quality concerns how well performance, safety, reliability, and other customer requirements are met, not just the manufacturer’s convenience. Design quality is the intended characteristics; manufacturing quality is how well they are realized; logistics quality concerns items, quantities, timing, and condition until delivery.

Q means quality, C cost, and D delivery. Even when considering safetyS alongside them, do not remove safety devices to meet deadlines. Reworking defects affects time and trust as well as material cost.

mfg1-electrical-l051.title: Verify causes with the three actuals and PDCA
mfg1-electrical-l051.exampleText: Under the same inspection method,6 defects in 200 becoming 2 in 200 means a rate reduction from 3%to 1%. If materials or production conditions also changed, however, the measure alone is not yet proven to be the cause. Report facts, inferences, and further checks separately.
mfg1-electrical-l051.structureTitle: Actual place, item, and facts · Connect planning with evaluation
mfg1-electrical-l051.structureText:
The three actuals emphasize where the issue occurs, the item involved, and verified facts. Do not settle a cause from reports alone; examine the location and item within approved safe boundaries. This does not mean touching a dangerous object directly.

Plan sets the target and method, Do implements them, Check compares results against the target, and Act feeds findings into the next cycle. A single implementation does not guarantee effectiveness; align comparison periods, quantities, and other conditions.

mfg1-electrical-l052.title: Compare work standards with QC process charts
mfg1-electrical-l052.exampleText: Once per lot is not the same as once per hour. Checks may also be required for first pieces, tool changes, or changed settings. Identify and hold defects and investigate the affected scope, including when results were last normal.
mfg1-electrical-l052.structureTitle: Reproduce the same work · What, when, and how to control
mfg1-electrical-l052.structureText:
Work standards specify sequence, method, equipment, tools, and key points. Check the latest revision, applicable part number, and machine. Do not overwrite standards with your own improvement: obtain approval and communicate the change before applying it.

A QC process chart states the process, controlled characteristics, methods, frequency, responsibility, and abnormal responses. Check not only “caliper” but also measurement position, specification, sampling conditions, and record destination. The chart and work standard have different purposes and complement each other.

mfg1-electrical-l053.title: Separate counts, relationships, and possible causes with QC tools
mfg1-electrical-l053.exampleText: A cause-and-effect diagram organizes possible causes using 4Mor similar categories. A Pareto chart helps select high-count categories, but do not ignore rare severe safety events. Verify proposed causes through measurements and comparisons rather than assigning blame without evidence.
mfg1-electrical-l053.structureTitle: Define before collecting · Distribution is different from relationship
mfg1-electrical-l053.structureText:
A check sheet specifies items, period, target, and counting rules. Choose bar, line, or pie graphs to match the purpose. When totals or denominators differ, comparing counts alone can mislead; check proportions too.

Histograms show distributions, control charts show a process over time, and scatterplots show relationships between two variables. Correlation in a scatterplot does not prove one variable causes the other. Check conditions and outliers.

mfg1-electrical-l054.title: Check the scope of ISO, JIS, and certification
mfg1-electrical-l054.exampleText: A JIS mark concerns conformity of the specified product. A marked instrument’s reliability can still change through falls, wear, dirt, or calibration status. Do not substitute the mark for pre-use checks or the product’s inspection result.
mfg1-electrical-l054.structureTitle: Products and management systems · Scope and edition
mfg1-electrical-l054.structureText:
ISO includes standards for products and methods as well as organizational management systems. ISO9001 concerns quality management, and ISO14001 environmental management. Organizational certification does not mean every product unconditionally passes.

JIS means Japanese Industrial Standards. Basic, method, and product standards concern different targets. Check edition, scope, contract, and drawing requirements as well as the number. International alignment does not guarantee every requirement is identical.

mfg1-electrical-l055.title: Connect SI base units and prefixes to calculations
mfg1-electrical-l055.exampleText: 1 mm²=10⁻⁶m²: the length conversion factor cannot be applied unchanged to area.30 minutes is 0.5 hours;1.2 kW for 30 minutes uses 0.6 kWh. Align units before substitution and attach a unit to the result.
mfg1-electrical-l055.structureText:
The SI base units are length m, mass kg, time s, electric current A, thermodynamic temperature K, amount of substance mol, and luminous intensity cd. Voltage V, resistance Ω, and power W are derived units. Do not confuse mass kg with force N, or temperature K with Celsius.

k means 1000 times, m means one thousandth, and μ means one millionth. 2.4 kΩ = 2400 Ω, 750 mA = 0.750 A, and 2200 μF = 2.2 mF. Lowercase m and uppercase M are different prefixes, so preserve their case.

mfg1-electrical-l056.title: Do not confuse pH, oxidation-reduction, and specific gravity
mfg1-electrical-l056.exampleText: For solids and liquids, specific gravity is a ratio to the density of reference water and has no unit. Density, expressed inkg/m³or similar units, is different. At specific gravity 2.5, equal volumes have 2.5 times the reference water’s mass; differing volumes change the mass comparison.
mfg1-electrical-l056.structureTitle: Acidity and alkalinity · Think in terms of electrons
mfg1-electrical-l056.structureText:
pH is a dimensionless indicator of acidity or alkalinity in aqueous solution. In ordinary dilute-solution examples around 25°C, near 7 is neutral. This does not mean every liquid must have a pH from 0 to 14 or that neutral pH is 7 at every temperature.

Oxidation can be described as losing electrons, and reduction as gaining electrons. Combining with oxygen or losing oxygen are representative reaction examples. Oxidation and reduction occur together; do not judge process progress by color alone.

mfg1-surface-lesson-050.title: Check reaction equivalents before converting concentration notation
mfg1-surface-lesson-050.exampleText: When NaOH at 0.40 mol/L is used in a one-equivalent neutralization, it is 0.40 equiv/L. Its factor differs from complete sulfuric-acid neutralization. Write both equations, compare required amounts, and explain that concentration calculation and permission to replenish an actual tank are different.
mfg1-surface-lesson-050.structureTitle: Decide what the reaction counts · Check the factor from the equation · Compare the method document and analysis sheet
mfg1-surface-lesson-050.structureText:
Molar concentration is amount of substance per solution volume. The older notation normality counts equivalents for a specified reaction. Even for the same substance, the equivalent value can change with the reaction definition, so the symbol N alone provides insufficient conditions.

For complete neutralization H₂SO₄+2 NaOH→Na₂SO₄+2 H₂O,1 mol sulfuric acid corresponds to 2 mol sodium hydroxide. Under these conditions,0.30 mol/L sulfuric acid is 0.60 equiv/L. Simply dividing mol/L by the acid's valence does not match this reaction balance. The original learning text contradicts its example, so do not use that sentence as a calculation rule.

Check conversion conditions against the reaction: electron numbers for redox, reacting hydrogen ions for neutralization, and so forth. To avoid misunderstanding, state mol/L together with the specific reaction equation. Do not simply replace N with mol/L while keeping the number; ask the responsible person about the reaction and definition.

mfg1-surface-lesson-051.title: Understand pH measurement with glass and reference electrodes
mfg1-surface-lesson-051.exampleText: If a portable meter's value will not stabilize, report calibration status, electrode contamination, temperature and measurement time rather than recording only a favorable instant. The operator must not fix it by adding a different internal liquid without authorization.
mfg1-surface-lesson-051.structureTitle: Relate potential difference to pH · Separate the change from its conditions · Applications and preparation
mfg1-surface-lesson-051.structureText:
A glass-electrode pH meter uses a reference electrode to measure a potential difference associated with sample conditions and relate it to pH. A display alone does not establish suitability; check calibration, electrode condition and temperature. Internal electrode structure and liquid are model-specific, so a general diagram does not authorize disassembly or refilling.

The relationship between potential difference and pH depends on conditions such as temperature. Do not treat approximately 60 mV per pH unit as an exact constant at all temperatures. Follow specifications for calibration solution and temperature, and obtain the designated inspection if abnormal.

Fixed, benchtop and portable instruments have different applications. Check sampling, cleaning, electrode storage and sample suitability through the procedure. Test-paper color charts are product-specific; do not use the textbook chart as a universal decision chart.

mfg1-surface-lesson-052.title: Distinguish DC, AC and circuit symbols from diagrams
mfg1-surface-lesson-052.exampleText: If a drawing specifies DC but the meter is on an AC range, do not use the value directly for process decisions. Check the supply type, instrument compatibility, responsible person and procedure. Do not alter actual wiring for learning.
mfg1-surface-lesson-052.structureTitle: DC is not necessarily constant · Read symbols and connections together · Conductors and insulators also have conditions
mfg1-surface-lesson-052.structureText:
Study DC as current flowing in one direction. Some examples are constant, but DC magnitude can also vary with time, as in pulsation after rectification. AC changes direction periodically.50 Hz means 50 cycles per second, distinct from merely counting 50 polarity changes.

Resistors, capacitors, earth connections, batteries and AC supplies have different symbols. Long and short battery lines help identify polarity. Follow junctions and wiring extents as well as symbols. Check drawing rules where lines cross without a connection indication.

Metals are typical conductors, while rubber and resins are typical insulators, but contamination, moisture, damage and voltage can change the hazard. A material name alone does not guarantee shock protection. An earth symbol on the drawing and a sound actual earth connection are also different.

mfg1-surface-lesson-053.title: Consider current and magnetic-field directions with a stated viewpoint
mfg1-surface-lesson-053.exampleText: Mark the viewpoint and current arrows on a diagram. Explain the right-hand rules for straight conductors and coils and the left-hand motor rule separately. There is no need to touch a running motor or wiring to copy a hand position.
mfg1-surface-lesson-053.structureTitle: Consider the space around a straight conductor · The correspondence changes for a coil · Separate force from induction
mfg1-surface-lesson-053.structureText:
Current in a straight conductor creates a magnetic field around it. Point the right thumb along conventional current; the curled four fingers indicate the magnetic-field direction. Before saying clockwise, specify which side of the conductor you are viewing.

For a coil, curl the right fingers along the current's circulation and use the thumb for the internal magnetic field. Do not confuse this with the straight-conductor rule in which the thumb indicated current. Electric fields relate to charges and magnetic fields to magnets or currents; applications include motors.

In Fleming's left-hand rule, the index finger represents magnetic field, the middle finger conventional current and the thumb force. Use it for current experiencing force in a magnetic field. In the right-hand rule, the index finger represents magnetic field, the middle finger induced current and the thumb conductor motion. Use motion and field to consider induced-current direction. Do not swap hands; align the phenomenon and viewpoint.

mfg1-surface-lesson-054.title: Identify steels and nonferrous metals using material designations
mfg1-surface-lesson-054.exampleTitle: Similar weight does not identify a material
mfg1-surface-lesson-054.exampleText: Two samples with similar masses are not necessarily the same metal or alloy. Check measurement error, cavities, shape and quantity too. Identify unknown-material items and send them for the responsible person's confirmation.
mfg1-surface-lesson-054.structureTitle: Separate main constituents from alloying elements · Read the conditions of property tables · Connect alloys to surface treatment
mfg1-surface-lesson-054.structureText:
Study iron-based materials as materials mainly containing iron, with carbon and other elements. Steel, cast iron and different alloys vary in composition, workability and strength. Nonferrous metals are metals other than iron and steel, including copper, aluminium, zinc and nickel. Nonferrous does not mean identical magnetism or corrosion behavior.

For equal volumes, greater density means greater mass. Density alone, however, cannot establish strength or material identity. Compare low melting point, high conductivity, corrosion resistance and workability separately according to purpose. Do not apply representative values to all alloys without qualification.

Aluminium alloys such as duralumin, die-casting materials such as ADC 12 and zinc alloys differ in composition and production. A material change also affects pretreatment and adhesion, so compare drawings, material designations and lot certificates.

mfg1-surface-lesson-055.title: Separate adhesion, hardness and solder-wettability tests
mfg1-surface-lesson-055.exampleText: Even if a contact component passes color and thickness checks, do not omit specified solder-wettability confirmation when joining performance is required. Operators must not improvise heating conditions; ask quality personnel about the sample and method.
mfg1-surface-lesson-055.structureTitle: Adhesion concerns the interface · Distinguish hardness and solder wettability · Do not mix samples back with products
mfg1-surface-lesson-055.structureText:
Adhesion tests investigate how firmly a coating attaches to its substrate. Tape peeling, bending, filing and thermal shock apply different effects and do not necessarily produce identical results. Check the specified method, sample and decision criteria.

Hardness tests investigate resistance to indentation and related effects. Methods include micro-Vickers, Rockwell and Brinell. The responsible person selects a method suited to load, surface condition and film thickness. Solder wettability evaluates how solder spreads over a surface and similar behavior; hardness or color cannot substitute for it.

Bending, scratching, heating or chemical action during a test may prevent return to the original shipping condition. Follow sampling plans and identification requirements. Do not mix tested items with unused conforming items. Judge method suitability and product conformity using the specified criteria.

mfg1-surface-lesson-056.title: Separate pollution categories and sources of chemical information
mfg1-surface-lesson-056.exampleText: If a customer asks about contained substances, organize the item number, edition, composition information, supplier evidence and applicable conditions for the responsible person. Do not assume the SDS alone satisfies all requirements; check necessary documents and analyses. Learning material does not replace specific legal compliance decisions.
mfg1-surface-lesson-056.structureTitle: Consider multiple impact pathways · Product substances differ from workplace emissions · Do not reduce REACH to registration
mfg1-surface-lesson-056.structureText:
Distinguish water, air and soil pollution, noise, vibration, ground subsidence and offensive odors. Clear wastewater or weak odor does not establish that the whole factory has no impact. Record floor leaks and waste movements too, and consider prevention and reduction.

RoHS is an EU system restricting certain hazardous substances in electrical and electronic equipment. It is not the same as workplace wastewater control values. The responsible person checks current requirements, including covered products, materials and exemptions. Do not declare compliance from a chemical name alone.

REACH is an EU system covering registration, evaluation, authorization and restriction of chemicals. Communication and use conditions also apply according to roles. It does not mean registering all product information permits every use. Check current information for specific obligations based on substance, quantity and supply-chain role.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-057.title: Do not confuse protection against dust with protection against gas
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-057.exampleText: Wearing protective equipment does not solve poor ventilation or a broken guard. When dust increases, withdraw to a safe position and report the source, ventilation, protective equipment and work conditions. Do not choose equipment of unknown protective performance merely by its color or shape.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-057.structureTitle: Particles and gases are different · Match eye and body protection to the task
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-057.structureText:
A dust respirator is intended to filter particles such as dust. Do not assume it removes harmful gases in the same way. Gases require checking protective equipment suitable for the substance, while oxygen deficiency is a separate hazard. Ask the responsible person about the type, applicable conditions and fitting checks.

Protective glasses guard the eyes against flying material and similar hazards. Tasks such as gas cutting also require the specified protection against harmful light. Match sleeves and gloves to the process, observing prohibitions such as no gloves at a rotating drill press. Do not apply one example outfit to every task.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-058.title: In a fire, prioritize reporting, evacuation and suitable initial action
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-058.exampleText: Initial firefighting is limited to the workplace procedure and to trained personnel who have checked a safe escape route and equipment conditions. Power operation is also limited to what can be done from a safe, authorized position; do not approach the fire to switch it off. If flames or smoke spread, evacuate rather than persist in firefighting.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-058.structureTitle: Alert others first · Read the fire class and extinguisher suitability
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-058.structureText:
On discovering fire or smoke, alert others through the workplace emergency procedure and secure a safe evacuation route. In normal conditions, check not only extinguisher locations but also whom to call, the assembly point and the conditions for evacuation. Do not return to investigate a place obscured by smoke.

The source describes ordinary fires involving wood or paper, oil fires and electrical fires as classes A, B and C. Applying water to oil or energized parts is dangerous. Read the extinguisher’s suitability marking rather than assuming every extinguishing agent suits every fire.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-059.title: Check handling, heat and chemical hazards by process
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-059.exampleText: Before using a chemical, check its hazards, handling and emergency measures in the SDS. Use hoods and other exposure-control equipment in the specified condition, and check health-examination instructions too. Having had an examination is not a reason to switch off ventilation.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-059.structureTitle: Choose the method, not just whether you can lift it · Manage heat and dust separately
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-059.structureText:
For heavy objects, check weight, shape, gripping points, distance and route. Safety is not decided only by whether someone bends at the waist; ask about specified aids or team-handling methods. Do not force yourself to carry an unmanageable weight. Keep away from suspended loads and restricted areas.

Areas near furnaces may involve heat stress; sand molds and polishing may involve dust. Check rest and hydration measures separately from source control, ventilation and protection. Report changes in physical condition early rather than enduring them. Follow workplace training and emergency procedures for the necessary response.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-060.title: Keep procedures readable and turn improvement ideas into formal changes
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-060.exampleText: After a formal change, check when it takes effect, the target, separation from old versions, and whether training or notification is needed. Altering only your own paper does not inform the next operator. Check the location and update status of procedures at handover as well.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-060.structureTitle: Information must be available when needed · An idea is not an approved change
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-060.structureText:
A procedure states who does what, when and how. Merely possessing a document is insufficient if it cannot be read when needed at the work location. Check the equipment, product and version covered, and report failed displays or unreadable paper. Do not fill in unconfirmed conditions from memory alone.

Even if a step appears possible to shorten, do not change its order or conditions on the spot. Other processes’ quality or safety may be affected. Summarize the proposal’s purpose, expected benefit and possible adverse effects, then submit it through the company’s checks and approval.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-061.title: Connect quality information across departments and QC circles
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-061.exampleText: For repeated incorrect labels, plan the goal and collection method, implement approved measures, compare results and feed them into further improvement. Do not declare completion only in the department taking action. Check that identification is also maintained by the receiving department.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-061.structureTitle: Inspection is not the only department involved · A small team gathers facts
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-061.structureText:
Quality is supported by the whole flow: translating customer requirements into design, procuring materials, manufacturing, inspecting and shipping. When inspection finds the wrong material, do not assume it is only the inspector’s failure. Share information about instructions, identification and handovers as well.

In a QC circle, a small workplace group discusses improvements to work quality and efficiency. Do not decide the cause by a majority vote alone; examine workplace facts and data. A proposal changing equipment or procedures still requires the specified approval.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-062.title: Make inspection-record errors and unjudged items traceable
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-062.exampleTitle: Report errors even in someone else’s records
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-062.exampleText: If an error is found in a past record, report it with the original record and affected target. Do not delete the history; obtain the prescribed correction and impact-scope checks. Also raise hard-to-perform or error-prone points to help prevent future mistakes.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-062.structureTitle: Records represent work actually performed · Ask about cases outside the criteria
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-062.structureText:
Carry out inspection using approved criteria and procedures, and record results promptly. Even when results are usually identical, do not copy the last value without measuring. Link date and time, lot, instrument, value and judgment so the items represented by a result can be identified.

Do not independently pass an item whose condition is absent from the procedure or difficult to judge. Keep unjudged items identified and separated, and tell the quality staff the target and uncertainty. A pass-rate goal does not permit relaxing the criteria.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-063.title: Read DC, AC and equipment ratings separately
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-063.exampleTitle: Withhold use when the supply is unknown
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-063.exampleText: If a relocated machine’s supply marking is unreadable and only an old note remains, withhold connection. Report the machine number and marking condition, and confirm the appropriate ratings and connection. Keep actual energizing and wiring within the authorized work scope.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-063.structureTitle: Diagram the direction difference · Equal voltage does not mean equal conditions
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-063.structureText:
Direct current flows in a consistent direction; alternating current changes direction periodically. Direction and voltage magnitude are separate matters. Both can be dangerous: DC does not mean there is no electric-shock hazard. Compare the directions using arrows and time diagrams on paper.

Numbers such as 100 V or 200 V alone do not identify DC or AC, frequency or equipment compatibility. Read the nameplate together with the specified supply and instructions. Do not connect equipment merely because the connector shape fits.

mfg1-electrical-l057.title: Apply 3R and circular-economy thinking to electrical products
mfg1-electrical-l057.exampleText: DC is basically unidirectional, whereas AC periodically changes direction. DC can vary in magnitude while retaining direction. Do not assume recovered power supplies or batteries are interchangeable from shape or marked voltage alone: check ratings, polarity, and condition.
mfg1-electrical-l057.structureTitle: Reduce, reuse, and recycle · Consider circulation from design onward
mfg1-electrical-l057.structureText:
Reduce limits waste generation, reuse uses products again, and recycle recovers resources. Reducing packaging, reusing returnable boxes, and separating materials have different aims. Do not remove packaging needed for protection.

A circular economy facilitates repair and reuse and keeps products and materials in circulation longer. It also considers pollution prevention, renewable energy, and the natural environment. Identify reused items and inspect suitability; do not unconditionally return safety parts to service.

mfg1-electrical-l058.title: Check laws, technical requirements, and PSE separately
mfg1-electrical-l058.exampleText: Do not unconditionally apply textbook item counts or grounding-omission examples to all current products. Confirm required markings, installation conditions, and qualifications using current public guidance and the responsible person. An earth-leakage breaker does not authorize removing grounding.
mfg1-electrical-l058.structureTitle: Purpose and scope · Different from installation requirements
mfg1-electrical-l058.structureText:
The Electrical Appliances and Materials Safety Act aims to prevent hazards from covered electrical products. PSE marks apply to covered items, with different shapes for specified products and other products. Match classification, notifying business, and ratings with product documents; a mark alone does not prove suitability for every use.

The ministerial ordinance on technical standards for electrical installations concerns installation performance requirements. Its interpretation gives technical details for meeting them. Choosing a product, connecting it to an installation, and verifying workers’ qualifications or training are separate checks.

mfg1-electrical-l059.title: Identify domestic, international, and industry standards
mfg1-electrical-l059.exampleText: Even where JIS and IEC have corresponding standards, check editions and differences before treating them as identical. For drawings with old and new symbols, consult the legend and applicable standard. Record number, edition year, and relevant sections before applying them to assembly conditions.
mfg1-electrical-l059.structureTitle: Issuer and scope · International and overseas requirements
mfg1-electrical-l059.structureText:
JIS are national standards; JEM concerns the electrical manufacturing industry, JEITA electronics and information technology, and JSIA distribution/control systems. Different names have different scopes and issuers. Distinguish basic standards for terms and units, test-method standards, and product standards.

IEC develops international electrical standards, while ISO covers wider international standardization. NEC, VDE, and IEEE differ in region, organization, and scope. Check the requirements of the destination country and contract for exported products.

mfg1-electrical-l060.title: Drawing types, paper sizes, and third-angle projection
mfg1-electrical-l060.exampleText: In third-angle projection, the top view is above the front view, the right-side view to the right, and the left-side view to the left. Relate visible and hidden shapes across views and check the projection symbol. Not every country or drawing uses third-angle projection.
mfg1-electrical-l060.structureTitle: Which drawing to use · Paper and borders
mfg1-electrical-l060.structureText:
Distinguish drawings by purpose such as production, planning, or approval; expression such as outline, exploded view, or connections; and content such as parts, assembly, or layout. A parts list identifies components. Check title block, number, revision, and sheet count, and do not mix another product’s drawing in.

A4 is 210×297 mm and A3 is 297×420 mm. Halving a larger A-series sheet gives the next size. Check borders, title block, and margins, and use written dimensions even on resized printouts. Do not confuse paper size with product dimensions.

mfg1-electrical-l061.title: Dimension, roughness, and fit requirements
mfg1-electrical-l061.exampleText: Clearance, interference, and transition fits depend on the combination of shaft and hole dimensional limits. The same nominal size does not establish the same actual relationship. Do not independently press-fit or heat parts; confirm tolerances and approved assembly methods.
mfg1-electrical-l061.structureTitle: Lines and dimensions · Roughness and manufacturing method
mfg1-electrical-l061.structureText:
Outlines, hidden lines, centerlines, dimension lines, cutting positions, and hatching have different meanings. Dimensions state finished requirements; distinguish radiusR, diameterφ, arc, chord, and angle. Do not infer lengths or angles from appearance.

Ra is arithmetic mean roughness: under comparable conditions, a smaller value describes a smoother surface. Do not confuse roughness inμm with dimensions inmm; check machining notes too. Symbols vary by standard and edition, so do not assume old symbols are current.

mfg1-electrical-l062.title: Electrical symbols and the order of reading a ladder
mfg1-electrical-l062.exampleTitle: A ladder is not a picture of physical wiring
mfg1-electrical-l062.exampleText: Learn basic PLC ladders through evaluating conditions from top to bottom and left to right. Distinguish inputs, internal relays, and outputs, and do not confuse a/b instructions with physical switch wiring. Consult the model specification for actual evaluation order and special instructions.
mfg1-electrical-l062.structureTitle: Identify devices through symbols · Link separated contacts
mfg1-electrical-l062.structureText:
Match resistor, variable resistor, capacitor, coil, diode, LED, transistor, fuse, meter, and contact symbols with names. Light arrows differ between an emitting LED and a receiving photodiode. Also match terminal roles such as A/K and B/C/E.

An expanded connection diagram can place one relay’s coil and contacts apart. Link them through device identifiers and references rather than assuming nearby contacts belong together. Distinguish normal from operated states: a contacts close and b contacts open on operation.

mfg1-electrical-l063.title: Conductive and magnetic materials and thermal classes
