mfg1-electrical-l063.exampleText: The textbook’s thermal-class examples are Y90, A105, E120, B130, F155, H180, and R220°C. These concern materials or insulation systems under specified conditions, not every product’s ambient temperature. Natural rubber is not inorganic insulation: use mica and ceramics as examples. Do not misclassify paper-based materials as inorganic either.
mfg1-electrical-l063.structureTitle: Differences between wire materials · Retaining or changing magnetism
mfg1-electrical-l063.structureText:
Annealed copper has reduced work hardening and differs from hard copper and aluminum in strength, conductivity, mass, and other properties. Material changes resistance even at equal length and cross-section. Not attracting a magnet does not mean not conducting electricity.

Electrical steel uses measures such as thin laminated sheets to reduce losses from changing flux. Select permanent-magnet materials by remanence, coercivity, and use. Do not substitute every magnetic material as the same core or permanent magnet.

mfg1-surface-lesson-057.title: Compare surface treatments by film formation and purpose
mfg1-surface-lesson-057.exampleText: If a part changes from decorative use to an electrical contact, choosing the same color is insufficient. Check conduction and contact, layer structure, wear and corrosion requirements with the responsible person, then choose an approved process.
mfg1-surface-lesson-057.structureTitle: Separate formation methods and functions · Check substrates and applications · Comparison ranges are not specifications
mfg1-surface-lesson-057.structureText:
Plating forms metal coatings; anodizing oxidizes the substrate surface; chemical conversion forms compound films through reactions; painting uses resin and other paints. Their formation mechanisms differ. Thermal spraying, etching, polishing, quenching and nitriding also change surfaces; do not call them all plating.

Methods also exist for applying metal coatings to resins and other nonmetals, but appropriate pretreatment and material conditions are necessary. Anodizing does not work on every metal under identical conditions. Compare material names, underlayers, outermost layers, and electrical and thermal conditions.

Textbook thickness ranges and applications are guides for comparing methods. Do not directly turn general plating, anodizing, conversion or paint thicknesses into acceptance limits or equipment settings for individual products. Link requirements for appearance, corrosion, wear, joining and electrical properties through to inspection.

mfg1-surface-lesson-058.title: Check substrate-specific pretreatment and underlayer compatibility
mfg1-surface-lesson-058.exampleText: If drawing material changes but the process sheet still specifies the old material, past success with the old sheet is insufficient. Ask about the change, underlayer and main coating, pretreatment and inspection requirements. Identify the affected items as awaiting confirmation.
mfg1-surface-lesson-058.structureTitle: A metal name alone does not determine the process · Separate underlayers from the main coating · Light metals and nonconductive substrates
mfg1-surface-lesson-058.structureText:
Steel, stainless steel, copper alloys, aluminium alloys and magnesium alloys have different surfaces and chemical properties. Even if general applications use nickel or chromium, identical pretreatment may not apply. Check item number, material certificate, oxidation or contamination and required quality.

A thin strike underlayer or pretreatment such as zincating relates to adhesion of the later coating. Its role differs from thickening the main coating. Do not invent chemical recipes or electrical conditions from a name; use the process approved for the target material.

For aluminium and similar materials, check the relationship between oxide film and pretreatment. Do not unconditionally transfer a similarly named process to magnesium or another material. Plating resins and other nonconductive substrates also requires checks of pretreatment, catalysts, conductive preparation and material compatibility.

mfg1-surface-lesson-059.title: Read hot-dip plating types and alloy layers
mfg1-surface-lesson-059.exampleText: If zinc-based and aluminium-based process sheets are side by side, the shared immersion method does not make them interchangeable. Check substrate, process number, required performance and dimensions before sending items to the designated process.
mfg1-surface-lesson-059.structureTitle: Identify the molten bath metal · Layers can also form at the interface · Compare corrosion protection and service conditions
mfg1-surface-lesson-059.structureText:
Hot-dip methods include zinc, zinc-aluminium, aluminium and tin systems. Uses include steel corrosion protection, construction materials, heat-resistant applications and containers, according to required properties. Similar bath names do not mean identical composition or processes.

Some substrate and molten-metal combinations form an alloy layer at the interface. Consider that layer, thickness, shape and dimensional requirements as well as the outer surface. Cooling conditions also matter; do not independently set temperatures or times from a principles explanation.

Zinc systems provide sacrificial protection, but thicker does not improve every property. Check threads, fits, edges and the service environment. A general statement that tin is harmless does not guarantee every bath, additive or food-contact application.

mfg1-surface-lesson-060.title: Distinguish pinholes, pits and runs by their shape
mfg1-surface-lesson-060.exampleText: If you find an edge projection, preserve its location diagram, dimensions and lot, identify it separately from conforming items and consult. Even a suspected pinhole must not be enlarged with a needle or tested with chemicals; send it for approved inspection.
mfg1-surface-lesson-060.structureTitle: How far does the hole reach? · Distinguish blisters and unplated areas · Hot-dip runs
mfg1-surface-lesson-060.structureText:
In this electroplating category, a pinhole is a small hole through the coating to the substrate; a pit is a depression that does not reach the substrate. A visible dot alone cannot establish depth; use the specified observation and inspection method. Both can affect quality, so shallow does not mean unconditional acceptance.

A blister is a raised coating separated from the substrate. An unplated area lacks coating where it is required. Preserve location, extent, observation conditions, pretreatment and contact history. Recording every similar appearance as a pinhole makes investigation difficult.

Study a run as excess molten metal attached at an edge or similar location. Temperature, flow, withdrawal and shape can contribute, but appearance alone does not identify one cause. Dimensions, safe handling and quality requirements also matter. A general textbook explanation does not authorize leaving it or grinding it off.

mfg1-surface-lesson-061.title: Explain surface changes and finish types in polishing
mfg1-surface-lesson-061.exampleText: If a hairline-specified part develops near-mirror gloss, few scratches alone do not establish acceptance. Check specified line direction, appearance sample and inspection conditions. Identify affected items and request a decision.
mfg1-surface-lesson-061.structureTitle: Consider how unevenness changes · More gloss is not always better · Do not confuse grit numbers with roughness
mfg1-surface-lesson-061.structureText:
Polishing moves from removing coarse scratches and projections toward finer finishes. The aim is lower surface roughness as processing progresses, but later steps do not remove every scratch. Check prior-process quality and removal amount.

Mirror finishing aims for mirror-like gloss. Satin uses fine short lines and hairline uses aligned fine lines to reduce gloss. Do not accept products with different requirements merely because they are the shiniest.
Stainless-steel and aluminium products are examples where buffing can produce mirror-like gloss. These are possible applications, not a guarantee that every material or product becomes mirror-finished under identical conditions.

Grit numbers indicate abrasive fineness, but results vary with product systems, material and condition. Grit number and measured surface roughness are different quantities. Compare the specified buff and compound, preceding and following processes and measurement conditions.

mfg1-surface-lesson-062.title: Separate polishing dwell marks from edge-coating peeling
mfg1-surface-lesson-062.exampleText: For repeated edge peeling, compile location diagrams, adjacent processes, tool operating time and holding method. Do not assume an operator's increased speed solved it. The responsible person evaluates the issue, and quality is checked under the same conditions after approved measures.
mfg1-surface-lesson-062.structureTitle: Describe appearance defects specifically · Processing concentrates in one place · Edge peeling and rounding
mfg1-surface-lesson-062.structureText:
Record burn as heat discoloration, unevenness as a nonuniform finish, and scratches as linear damage. For insufficient gloss, compare the buff, compound and preceding process. Pressing harder without investigating can create further heat or shape defects.

Continuous polishing at the same location can produce depressions, unevenness and burns. Check holding, feed, pressure and buff wear. Do not confuse the defect name buff dwell mark with electrical power being switched off.

Pressure concentrated at corners or edges can round corners or peel coatings from plated items. Check holding, contact angle, force and required coating thickness. Merely polishing away visible evidence is different from restoring quality.

mfg1-surface-lesson-063.title: Organize thickness-measurement principles and effects on samples
mfg1-surface-lesson-063.exampleText: Two instruments displaying μm may differ in principle and applicability. If old and new methods disagree, do not select only the favorable result. Align samples, positions, calibration, substrates and coatings, and report to the responsible person.
mfg1-surface-lesson-063.structureTitle: What is detected and converted to thickness? · Cross-section and mass-difference methods · Nondestructive does not mean hazard-free
mfg1-surface-lesson-063.structureText:
X-ray fluorescence evaluates element-related X-rays; magnetic and eddy-current methods use electromagnetic properties of substrate and coating. Applicability varies with material, layer structure, shape and surface condition. A method name alone does not establish suitability for every metal coating.

Microscopic cross-section methods prepare and observe a section. Coating-mass methods evaluate the mass difference before and after removal, among other approaches. Conversion to thickness requires checks of area, density and removal conditions. Distinguish measurement locations and the extent of averaging.

Methods evaluating without cutting or dissolving the sample are called nondestructive, but X-ray and other instruments need dedicated controls. Destructive/nondestructive classification alone does not determine operating authority or human safety. Check reference plates, suitable reference samples and calibration too.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-064.title: Check grounding and safe isolation to prevent secondary harm
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-064.exampleTitle: Do not touch a person receiving a shock directly
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-064.exampleText: If a coworker may be receiving an electric shock, do not pull them by hand and expose yourself to shock too. Make the possible report and stop operation from a safe position, then follow emergency medical and workplace procedures. Do not approach an unknown energized state or assume a conveniently available stick is safe for a rescue attempt.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-064.structureTitle: Understand the protective function · A switch position alone does not prove safety
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-064.structureText:
Grounding is part of an equipment protection system and affects current paths during faults such as leakage. Where a grounding conductor is specified, check its connection and report defects. Do not describe grounding as preventing leakage itself or removing every electric-shock hazard.

Cleaning and repair require the equipment-specific procedures for stopping, isolation, residual energy and prevention of restart. Some devices are unplugged; other installations need different isolation and verification. Do not touch electrical wiring without the necessary qualifications and authorization, or omit safety checks on your own.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-065.title: Match the roles of motors, transformers and circuit breakers
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-065.exampleTitle: A name is different from applicability
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-065.exampleText: Apply JIS and other standards or equipment requirements after checking their target and edition. Motors with the same general name can differ in ratings and structure. A conformity marking does not permit improper use or unconfirmed replacement.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-065.structureTitle: Driving equipment and voltage-changing equipment · Check why protection operated
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-065.structureText:
A motor converts electrical energy into mechanical power to drive conveyors, pumps and similar equipment. A transformer changes voltage in suitable AC circuits and related applications. Neither is suitable for use merely because wires can be connected; check ratings and equipment requirements.

A circuit breaker provides protection by interrupting a circuit for overcurrent or other faults, depending on its type. Tripping alone does not identify the fault location. Do not repeatedly reset it to continue operation. Report the equipment number, stop time and conditions, and obtain the responsible person’s check before restarting.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-066.title: Choose conductors, insulators and semiconductors with conditions in mind
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-066.exampleTitle: Use properties that depend on conditions
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-066.exampleText: Semiconductors are materials whose electrical properties under conditions such as heat and light are put to use in diodes, transistors and related parts. The term does not mean a simple mixture of a conductor and an insulator. Select according to the purpose and specified component.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-066.structureTitle: Where current should pass · Where current should not pass
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-066.structureText:
Metals such as copper and aluminum conduct readily and are used in wiring. Good conductivity alone does not establish component suitability: check the required cross-section, temperature, connections and specifications. Do not substitute a similarly colored material without authorization.

Rubber, plastics, glass and ceramics are examples of insulating materials. Their performance has limits depending on contamination, damage, temperature, voltage and other conditions. Do not assume every plastic product is protective equipment for electrical work.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-067.title: Separate resistor and capacitor functions from residual-energy hazards
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-067.exampleTitle: Some parts remain unsafe to touch after stopping
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-067.exampleText: Stored energy may remain even after the supply is switched off. Appearance alone does not prove discharge is complete. Leave the prescribed verification and handling to the responsible personnel. Study the functions using paper diagrams; do not experiment by applying tools to terminals.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-067.structureTitle: A resistor also produces heat · A capacitor stores temporarily
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-067.structureText:
A resistor helps control circuit current and also converts electrical energy into heat. Use components that meet the required ratings as well as the resistance value. Do not decide that a smaller part is an acceptable replacement; report unusual heat or discoloration.

A capacitor uses the ability to temporarily store and release charge and related energy. Applications include voltage stabilization, noise suppression and flashes. Do not describe it as the same mechanism as a resistor or battery. Check the circuit symbol and component specifications.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-068.title: Distinguish diodes and transistors by their circuit roles
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-068.exampleTitle: Do not decide interchangeability by appearance
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-068.exampleText: Two components with similar shapes are not necessarily identical. Check the part numbers and drawing requirements, and report unreadable markings or unknown terminals. Classify functions using paper examples rather than energizing an unknown part to see whether it lights.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-068.structureText:
A diode primarily conducts in one direction under suitable conditions. An LED is a member of this family that emits light when current flows. This does not mean it may be connected without checking direction and ratings, or used without limits in reverse.

A transistor is used to amplify small signals or control current on and off. Do not treat it simply as another part that only passes current one way. Match the circuit role, specified component and terminal identification.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-069.title: Manage the two exam sections’ times and pass conditions separately
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-069.exampleTitle: Check current organizer guidance for eligibility
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-069.exampleText: The overview is information at the time recorded in the source. It says Japanese kanji receive furigana, but current organizer guidance must be checked for application, permitted belongings, eligibility and related rules. Passing a mock is not treated as automatically obtaining a qualification or work authorization.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-069.structureTitle: Practice the formats separately · Separate time and results
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-069.structureText:
The referenced exam overview specifies CBT, with 30 theory true/false questions and 10 practical multiple-choice questions assessing judgment, planning and related skills. Despite the name “practical,” this format is different from operating an actual machine. This app’s mock exams are independently authored, not reproductions of questions that actually appeared.

The source gives 40 minutes for theory and 40 minutes for practical, with pass standards of at least 65% and 60% respectively. A combined average alone does not establish a pass. Where this app gives equal weight to each practice item, it requires at least 20 correct theory answers and 6 correct practical answers independently. This does not guarantee any undisclosed official item weighting.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-070.title: Check work scope and study methods, and protect exam fairness
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-070.exampleTitle: Do not take official exam questions away
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-070.exampleText: The source warns against taking out questions or answers seen in the actual exam, or sharing them through public or private channels. Use independently created general examples in study groups; do not collect or recreate actual exam content. Follow the organizer’s guidance on misconduct and the detailed rules for exam day.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-070.structureTitle: The category name alone does not limit the work · Check words and sentence endings
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-070.structureText:
The source lists many examples in the machining and metalworking category: casting, forging, cutting, sheet metal, maintenance, inspection, assembly, molding, painting, packaging, heat treatment, rolling and extrusion. Experience in one process does not authorize every type of work. Check the assigned job and required training.

Learn technical terms with their targets and situations, not just word translations. Ask the instructor a specific question about unfamiliar language and reread it. Practice reading to the end of phrases such as “may do” and “must not do,” without dropping negation or conditions from the judgment.

mfg1-electrical-l064.title: Identify wire types and connection hardware
mfg1-electrical-l064.exampleText: Nuts, plain washers, spring washers, and captive-washer screws have specified combinations and uses. Trapezoidal threads are used in feed mechanisms and similar applications. If material or fastening target changes, check the drawing; do not omit orientation or quantity on your own judgment.
mfg1-electrical-l064.structureTitle: Compare identifiers with specifications · Select tools by purpose
mfg1-electrical-l064.structureText:
IV, KIV, and KV identify wires with different structures and uses. Check voltage classification, temperature, solid/stranded construction, conductor area, insulation, and destination against specifications. Do not make textbook color or thickness examples mandatory for every installation.

Pliers, long-nose pliers, cutters, and strippers differ in holding, bending, cutting, and insulation removal. Match crimp terminals both to the conductor and mounting screw, and check the tool die profile. Distinguish removal of an outer sheath from conductor insulation.

mfg1-electrical-l065.title: Solder materials, flux, and rework
mfg1-electrical-l065.exampleText: Match tip shape and condition to the component, avoiding lifted lands from prolonged heating or force. Identify bridges, cracks, and insufficient solder, and use approved rework and reinspection. Shine alone does not determine connection quality.
mfg1-electrical-l065.structureTitle: Alloys and conditions · Preparing the surface
mfg1-electrical-l065.structureText:
Leaded and lead-free solders differ in composition, melting point, wetting, and other properties. For example, Sn 63/Pb 37 and Sn-Ag-Cu systems discussed in the textbook may require different conditions. Do not claim every lead-free joint is inferior; use the qualified materials and process conditions for the product.

Flux helps act on oxides and supports wetting. Combine cleaning, suitable heating, restraint, supply, cooling, and inspection. Residue cleaning requirements and solvents depend on flux and specifications; do not wash every product in one liquid.

mfg1-electrical-l066.title: Passive components and devices using temperature or vibration
mfg1-electrical-l066.exampleText: Thermistors use resistance changes with temperature; piezoelectric devices use the relation between force and electricity; quartz resonators use stable vibration properties. Distinguish them from light receivers and emitters; do not swap lookalike parts without authorization.
mfg1-electrical-l066.structureTitle: Resistors also have types · Distinguish what is stored
mfg1-electrical-l066.structureText:
Carbon-film, metal-based, wirewound, chip, variable, and preset resistors differ in structure and use. Even at the same resistance, compare power, temperature coefficient, dimensions, and frequency behavior. Confirm variable-resistor terminals and adjustment range too.

Capacitors and coils are passive components storing energy associated with electric and magnetic fields respectively. Read specified capacitance, inductance, and permissible current. “Passive” does not mean safe to touch: residual charge and heat still require care.

mfg1-electrical-l067.title: Distinguish lathes, milling machines, and NC machines
mfg1-electrical-l067.exampleText: NC is the general term for numerical control, including NC lathes, NC mills, and machining centers. A machining center has automatic tool changing. A program does not remove the need to check datum, tool, fixture, and interference; unattended operation is not unconditionally safe.
mfg1-electrical-l067.structureTitle: Identify what rotates · Drilling and grinding
mfg1-electrical-l067.structureText:
A lathe rotates the workpiece while a cutting tool machines outside and inside diameters, grooves, or threads. A milling machine rotates the cutter and uses relative motion against a secured workpiece to machine planes, sides, steps, and grooves. Product shape alone does not uniquely identify the machine.

A drill press secures the workpiece and machines holes with drills, reamers, or similar tools. A grinder gradually removes material with a grinding wheel. Drills, lathe tools, and end mills differ in cutting-edge location and machine use; do not substitute lookalike tools.

mfg1-electrical-l068.title: Calculate resistance from dimensions, power, and energy
mfg1-electrical-l068.exampleText: At constant voltage, a smaller resistance gives greater power; at constant current, a larger resistance gives greater power. State what is held constant. Do not select equipment from calculated power alone: check rated power, cooling, temperature, and protection.
mfg1-electrical-l068.structureTitle: Wire length and area · Rate of consumption and total amount
mfg1-electrical-l068.structureText:
For the same material and temperature, R=ρℓ/S: resistance increases with length and decreases with cross-sectional area. Ifρ is inΩ·m and length in m, area must be in m². Do not substitute diameter as area; retain material and temperature conditions.

For a uniform wire paper model, hold material and temperature constant and use R=ρℓ/S. With ρ=3.0×10⁻⁸ Ω·m, ℓ=10 m and S=0.5 mm², convert S to0.5×10⁻⁶ m² to obtain R=0.6 Ω. The source image correctly prints m²; losing the superscript2 during text extraction is not a source error. A length of20 m and area1.0 mm² still give0.6 Ω. Doubling a circular diameter quadruples area; if length also doubles, resistance becomes2/4=1/2 of its original value. Do not apply this ratio alone when real material, temperature or contact resistance changes. This is not an instruction to wire or measure equipment.

For a DC resistor, P=VI=I²R=V²/R gives power in W. Energy is power multiplied by time, in Wh or similar units. At 12 V and 60 Ω, I=0.2 A and P=2.4 W; over 30 minutes this is 1.2 Wh. W and Wh are different quantities.

When power changes, calculate energy for each interval and add the results. This is a fictional DC calculation model, not an instruction for operating equipment.
Active interval: constant 18 V and 0.5 A for 20 minutes
Standby interval: constant 3 W for 40 minutes
No other interval or consumption is included. Active power is 18×0.5=9 W; 20/60=1/3 h gives 3 Wh. Standby lasts 40/60=2/3 h and uses 2 Wh. Total energy is 5 Wh=0.005 kWh. Multiply by each interval’s duration before adding Wh; do not just add W.
The whole cycle is 1 hour, so average power is 5 Wh/1 h=5 W, distinct from the maximum 9 W. Two identical cycles use 10 Wh. If standby duration is unknown, total energy is unknown too. Convert minutes to hours and record units and scope. Do not infer tariffs, efficiency, AC power factor or component suitability.

mfg1-electrical-l069.title: AC period and phase, and DC transients
mfg1-electrical-l069.exampleText: Do not apply an ideal coil or capacitor’s DC steady-state description unchanged immediately after connection or interruption. These components are also used in real DC circuits. Consider capacitor charging and residual charge, and voltage associated with changing coil current; do not short components yourself.
mfg1-electrical-l069.structureTitle: A complete repetition is one cycle · Time differences between voltage and current
mfg1-electrical-l069.structureText:
Sine-wave frequency counts complete repetitions per second, not simply direction reversals. One cycle is 20 ms at 50 Hz and about 16.7 ms at 60 Hz. Check nameplate frequency, not location alone.

In an ideal purely resistive sine-wave circuit, voltage and current are in phase. Current lags voltage for an ideal coil and leads it for an ideal capacitor. Compare equivalent phase points; do not confuse different waveform heights with time displacement. Actual circuits include losses and multiple components.

mfg1-electrical-l070.title: Check series-parallel calculations with Kirchhoff’s laws
mfg1-electrical-l070.exampleText: Series components carry the same current; parallel components share terminal voltage. For example,120 Ωparallel to 240 Ωgives 80 Ω; adding 40 Ωin series gives 120 Ω. Find total current, section voltages, and branch currents, then check both laws.
mfg1-electrical-l070.structureTitle: Balance at a node · Add signed potential differences around a loop
mfg1-electrical-l070.structureText:
Kirchhoff’s current law equates total incoming and outgoing current at a node. If 8 mA enters and splits into 3 mA and another branch, the other branch is 5 mA. Keep assumed directions consistent; a negative result indicates the opposite direction.

Check signed balances after normalizing units. In a paper node, 4 mA and 0.002 A enter; 1 mA and X leave. Since 0.002 A=2 mA, X=4+2−1=5 mA. A negative result for an assumed outgoing arrow means actual inflow, not a positive outflow. For a loop, +16−6−X=0 gives X=10 V; reversing the traversal changes every sign to −16+6+10=0. A nonzero residual requires checking signs, units and records, not editing measurements to fit. Two unknown branches need more than one independent equation. Balance alone does not certify fault-free equipment; these are paper calculations.

The voltage law makes the sum of signed potential differences around a loop zero. A12 V rise and drops of 4 V and 8 V give 12−4−8=0. Do not add all voltages as positive: establish traversal direction and polarity.

mfg1-surface-lesson-064.title: Record design, manufacturing and logistics quality separately
mfg1-surface-lesson-064.exampleText: Even a lot with acceptable thickness has a quality problem if specified quantities are missing or transport scratches appear. Record manufacturing results separately from packing and shipping history, and report causes and responses to the responsible person.
mfg1-surface-lesson-064.structureTitle: Consider quality as meeting requirements · Separate three stages · Pass information onward
mfg1-surface-lesson-064.structureText:
Quality concerns how well customer or user expectations and requirements are met. Ease, speed or good appearance is insufficient by itself. Check reliability, safety, necessary performance and intended use. Do not change to high gloss or thick coating while requirements are unclear.

Design quality concerns the intended quality, manufacturing quality realizing the designed performance consistently, and logistics quality the journey to the customer: correct items, quantity, delivery time and transport condition. An inspection-passed item scratched during packing may no longer meet requirements.

When changes occur, connect requirements, drawing editions, processes, inspection and packing conditions. The workplace must not independently reduce inspection items or substitute cheaper materials. Investigate differences using receipt, in-process, storage and shipping records, not only final checks.

mfg1-surface-lesson-065.title: Distinguish water-quality indicators and air impacts
mfg1-surface-lesson-065.exampleText: For changed exhaust flow, unusual smells, leaks or neighborhood complaints, organize time, location, equipment and operating conditions. Reduced smell alone does not establish safety; obtain necessary inspection and measurement.
mfg1-surface-lesson-065.structureTitle: One number does not describe all water quality · Combine treatment methods · Airborne substances and their effects
mfg1-surface-lesson-065.structureText:
pH concerns acidity and alkalinity, metal concentration the amount of a target metal, and SS suspended solids. COD and BOD evaluate water quality as chemical and biochemical oxygen demand respectively. Transparency or pH alone cannot reveal all these indicators.

Wastewater methods include physical separation, chemical and biological treatment, combined according to purpose and composition. Systems containing cyanide, chromium and similar substances require dedicated management. Representative textbook names do not determine neutralizers or mixing order; follow trained personnel's procedures.

Smoke, dust and volatile organic compounds have different sources. SOx and NOx relate to acid rain and other effects; VOC and NOx also participate in photochemical reactions. Do not confuse environmental-condition criteria with equipment-emission criteria. Check the current applicable conditions.

mfg1-surface-lesson-066.title: Read scales and menisci according to conditions
mfg1-surface-lesson-066.exampleText: In a paper burette example, initial 2.6 mL and final 17.4 mL give 14.8 mL used. Check reading and subtraction separately. Do not round actual measurements into tidier numbers that differ from the observed values.
mfg1-surface-lesson-066.structureTitle: Count intervals between numbers · Read the surface appropriate to the instrument · Keep both readings when using a difference
mfg1-surface-lesson-066.structureText:
For analog instruments, check units and range, then divide the difference between two numbered points by the number of intervals to obtain one division. Do not confuse line counts and interval counts. Viewing angle and pointer thickness also matter, so follow the specified reading method.

The curved liquid surface is called a meniscus. Burettes, pipettes and hydrometers may specify different positions, such as the upper or lower edge. Do not transfer one textbook instrument example to every instrument; check the instrument and measurement-method specifications.

Volume used from a burette is the difference between initial and final readings. Check scale direction and units; the final reading alone is not the used volume. Also check temperature, bubbles, contact and leaks that can disturb measurement.

mfg1-surface-lesson-067.title: Separate analytical objectives from deposition phenomena
mfg1-surface-lesson-067.exampleText: If a bath result lists only acid concentration, do not treat metal concentration as already measured. Compare required control items and methods with the responsible person. Do not independently add another reagent to identify a precipitate.
mfg1-surface-lesson-067.structureTitle: What is measured, and how much? · Consider how a solid appears · Record reaction and measurement conditions
mfg1-surface-lesson-067.structureText:
Quantitative analysis determines the amount of a target constituent. Neutralization titration, redox analysis, chelate analysis and separating a precipitate to measure it use different reactions and targets. Even with the same metal name, a method may measure another constituent or acidity.

Precipitation of a sparingly soluble solid in solution, deposition by reducing metal ions at an electrode, and solid separation by cooling or evaporation have different conditions despite all producing solids. The broad word deposition alone does not identify the reaction or composition.

On an analysis sheet, check sample name, target, sampled amount, concentration units, method and pretreatment. Acidity results do not prove all metal constituents are suitable. Before comparing methods, check whether they target the same quantity.

mfg1-surface-lesson-068.title: Compare paint classifications with appearance and durability requirements
mfg1-surface-lesson-068.exampleText: For another product with the same resin name, compare base, hardener, ratio, usable time and curing conditions. Even the same color may require trials or first-piece checks. Follow change procedures and approvals.
mfg1-surface-lesson-068.structureTitle: One label can contain several classifications · Confirm the electrocoating method · Do not rank durability by resin name alone
mfg1-surface-lesson-068.structureText:
Paints can be classified by water-based or solvent-based medium, resin such as acrylic, urethane, silicone or fluororesin, and one- or two-component format. One classification does not determine all conditions. Check formulation, designated undercoat, drying and curing, and service environment together.

Electrocoating includes anionic and cationic methods, with different workpiece electrode roles and material conditions. Using electricity in both does not justify applying metal-plating polarity, equipment or bath conditions. The responsible person checks the designated supply and connections.

A resin described as highly durable in general examples does not unconditionally give the longest life in every environment. Do not infer that water-based means harmless or powder means no dust control. Read the SDS and product specification for required safety controls and evaluations.

mfg1-surface-lesson-069.title: Read anodic-film structure and hard-anodizing conditions
mfg1-surface-lesson-069.exampleTitle: Treat heat and electrical values as representative
mfg1-surface-lesson-069.exampleText: Do not turn representative heat-resistance temperatures or withstand voltages into actual part heating limits or guarantees of shock protection. The responsible person evaluates shape, defects, dyes, thermal-expansion differences and service environment. Do not improvise electrical or high-temperature tests.
mfg1-surface-lesson-069.structureTitle: The film grows from the substrate · Pores and the barrier layer · Tradeoffs in hard films and post-treatment
mfg1-surface-lesson-069.structureText:
In aluminium anodizing the workpiece is on the anode side, and part of its surface becomes oxide to form a film. Do not equate the thin natural oxide with a controlled-process film's thickness. Film thickness and substrate consumption are not simply identical; check process and material conditions.

A typical porous film contains a porous portion and a dense barrier layer next to the substrate. Dye coloring, coloration related to material constituents or electrolysis conditions, and secondary electrolytic coloring have different mechanisms. Some methods use AC or superimposed supplies as well as DC; names alone do not determine settings.

Hard anodizing targets wear resistance and similar properties, but temperature, thickness and sealing depend on required-performance tradeoffs. Do not assume that every hard coating must remain unsealed or that thicker always gives the best insulation. Confirm through specifications and designated tests.

mfg1-surface-lesson-070.title: Check abrasive particles and supply formats by product
mfg1-surface-lesson-070.exampleTitle: Prevent carrying in a different material
mfg1-surface-lesson-070.exampleText: If finishing compound runs short, do not replenish with a similarly colored product. Compare item number, particles, buff, work material and cleaning method, and hold unconfirmed items. When changing supply amounts or methods, follow procedures addressing spray, dust and entanglement.
mfg1-surface-lesson-070.structureTitle: Names and composition are different · Separate coarse removal and finishing · Check supply and cleaning conditions
mfg1-surface-lesson-070.structureText:
Compounds use particles such as alumina, silica and chromium oxide. Names such as Saizer, lime, red bar, white bar and green bar help select products, but color or trade names alone do not establish every product's composition and fineness. Compare label, item number and specified use.

Coarse polishing removes large scratches and burrs; finishing reduces fine scratches to the required appearance. General examples use red, white and green bars at different stages, but there is no fixed sequence for every case. Check substrate, required appearance and buff combination against approved specifications.

Solid compounds bind particles into a solid form; liquid compounds disperse particles in liquid. For liquids, manage spray, contamination and supply method; for solids, application amount and condition. Some nonwoven buffs contain particles. Even soft material can scratch if coarse particles or foreign matter are present.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-071.title: Connect prohibition and warning signs to actions
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-071.exampleText: Tsunami danger areas, landslides and falling-rock signs relate to evacuation or passage decisions, separately from equipment-operation warnings. If a sign is dirty or hidden by goods, report its location and condition. In study, match sign names to necessary actions without independently changing workplace access controls.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-071.structureTitle: Target and role · Principles and distinctions
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-071.structureText:
Prohibition signs identify actions that must not be taken. No smoking and no open flames have different targets: a no-flames area requires attention to ignition sources other than smoking as well. Read the particular action covered by signs such as do not touch, not drinking water, no running or rushing in, and prohibitions on phones or electronic equipment. A sign is not permission to approach and test the hazard.

Warning signs indicate that a hazard exists. Obstacles, upward steps, downward steps, slippery floors, falls, overhead hazards and electric shock are different hazards. Do not identify the hazard from a general warning triangle alone; read the text and check its location. An upward and downward step require different foot movements, so do not assume their pictures mean the same thing.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-072.title: Distinguish chemical labels from emergency-location signs
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-072.exampleText:
An extensive-area evacuation space, a building used for evacuation and a tsunami evacuation site do not necessarily serve the same purpose. Do not confuse evacuation to a broad outdoor space with tsunami evacuation to a tall building or similar place. Confirm routes suitable for the disaster type through the introduction and evacuation plan before work, rather than searching for signs in an emergency.
A wide-area evacuation site is a large open space for temporary protection from major fires following an earthquake. It is used when spreading urban fire makes ordinary evacuation sites unsafe. Check the designated destination and route; do not assume any vacant plot is suitable.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-072.structureTitle: Target and role · Principles and distinctions
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-072.structureText:
The source’s chemical pictograms include a flame for flammability and related hazards; liquid attacking a hand or metal for corrosion; a person with a chest symbol for health hazards; a fish and tree for aquatic environmental hazards; and an exclamation mark for acute toxicity, skin or eye irritation and similar hazards. Pictures help distinguish hazards; they do not identify a substance or a safe concentration by themselves. Read the label and SDS together.

An AED sign identifies the location of an automated external defibrillator. An AED is a medical device supporting electrical treatment of abnormal heart rhythms. Having seen the sign does not mean you have received training. In an emergency, follow reporting procedures, voice guidance and workplace training. Check extinguisher locations together with escape routes in normal conditions too.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-073.title: Connect OSHMS and quality PDCA through records
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-073.exampleTitle: Apply the cycle to environmental goals
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-073.exampleText: A circular economy considers reducing waste and pollution from design, circulating products and materials through repair, reuse and resource recovery, and regenerating nature through renewable energy and ecosystem restoration. In factory improvement plans, separate goals for generation, energy and other factors from recovery quantities, and connect action with results checks. Environmental targets do not authorize omitting safety-related protection or packaging on your own.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-073.structureTitle: Target and role · Principles and distinctions · Records and checks
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-073.structureText:
OSHMS is a company system for managing occupational safety and health. Planning organizes hazards and goals; implementation carries out measures and training; evaluation checks activities and results; improvement reviews causes and the next plan. Writing a countermeasure once does not complete ongoing management.

Quality-management PDCA also cycles through planning, doing, checking or evaluating, and improving. A plan links goals to concrete actions; implementation follows the plan; checking compares results with goals; improvement feeds the next plan. Safety-measure records and product-quality records have different targets, so organize their relationship without mixing them together.

In the three-realities approach, the workplace is where the problem occurs, the actual item is the object concerned, and actual facts are what is verified there. Do not conclude from meeting-room guesses alone; compare records with what can be observed safely. One improved number after action does not rule out other times or remaining hazards. Set the next check date and responsible person.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-074.title: Distinguish variable data, attribute data and actions after sampling
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-074.exampleText: Possible actions for a rejected lot include returning purchased goods, sorting by inspecting all items and separating conforming units, or rework. The choice follows the quality staff’s judgment and procedures. Workers must not remove nonconforming labels and ship; keep the target and its judgment identifiable.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-074.structureTitle: Target and role · Principles and distinctions
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-074.structureText:
Data measured as continuous quantities, such as length or mass, are variable data; counts such as scratches or nonconforming units are attribute data. A measured shaft diameter and the number of shafts whose diameters are out of specification are different information. Match units and record fields; do not put a measurement directly into a count field.

A lot is a group of products made under the same conditions or otherwise managed together. Sampling inspection selects specimens by the specified method and judges using sample size, acceptance number and related conditions. Do not select only convenient good units, or treat sample results as individual guarantees for every uninspected unit.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-075.title: Distinguish tensile properties and five hardness tests
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-075.exampleText: Shore hardness uses the rebound height of a dropped hammer. Separate the measured quantities: depth, diameter, diagonals and rebound height. Equal numbers on different scales are not directly comparable. Check the indentation’s effect, the uses of specimens and products, load and other conditions under the specified method.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-075.structureTitle: Target and role · Principles and distinctions
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-075.structureText:
Tensile strength is the maximum stress in a tensile test. Yield strength is a reference stress associated with the onset of progressive plastic deformation. Elongation after fracture relates to the increase in gauge length after fracture. Young’s modulus expresses the stress–strain relationship in the elastic range. Do not call the elongation at one moment under load the elongation after fracture or tensile strength.

Rockwell hardness uses indentation depth, with a scale following HR. Brinell uses the diameter of a ball indentation, written HBW in the tungsten-carbide-ball example. Vickers hardness HV uses the diagonals of a square-pyramidal indentation; Knoop hardness HK uses the long diagonal of an elongated diamond-shaped indentation. The source gives thin layers as an example where Knoop may be considered.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-076.title: Distinguish the targets of eddy-current and sensory inspection
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-076.exampleText: Even when an inspection uses human senses, use consistent reference samples, lighting, distance and assessment conditions. Assessing quality that is difficult to express numerically does not mean changing pass or fail decisions according to personal preference. In this source passage, magnetic flux leakage is a phenomenon involved in the principle of magnetic particle testing. Distinguish this principle from that of eddy current testing, and confirm the specified inspection method and its applicable conditions with the person responsible.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-076.structureTitle: Target and role · Principles and distinctions
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-076.structureText:
Eddy-current testing, ET, brings a coil carrying alternating current near the object and examines electrical changes in the coil associated with eddy currents in the object. Conductivity, shape and other conditions affect applicability, so this is not a method used identically on every material. Penetrant testing of surface-opening defects and magnetic-particle testing near the surface of magnetizable objects use different principles.

Senses include sight, hearing, smell, touch and taste. The source gives examples of checking scratches or color by sight, sound by hearing and roughness by touch. This does not authorize tasting unknown factory liquids or bringing a nose or hand near chemicals. Perform specified sensory evaluation only on permitted targets under safe conditions.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-077.title: Select measuring aids according to their roles
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-077.exampleText: When selecting an aid, diagram the target shape, reference face, direction of movement and fixing position. Placing a cylinder on a V-block does not mean every dimension has been measured. Check dirt, tilt and loose fixing, and use the specified method to avoid including deformation from excessive clamping in the result.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-077.structureTitle: Target and role · Principles and distinctions
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-077.structureText:
A straightedge has a highly straight reference face and is used for marking or guidance. A square helps check the right-angle relationship between faces. Inside and outside calipers help transfer dimensions such as difficult-to-access internal or external diameters. Calipers of this transfer type alone are not the same as a measuring instrument displaying a number.

A surface gauge has a pointed tip and a holding structure, helping mark parallel lines or check heights. A V-block supports cylindrical and similar objects in a V-shaped groove. A box angle block uses grooves and related features to secure objects; a magnetic base fixes a measuring instrument using a magnet and holding structure. Similar names do not make holding and measurement the same function.

mfg1-electrical-l071.title: Intrinsic, n-type, p-type, and the pn junction
mfg1-electrical-l071.exampleText: Joining p-type and n-type material causes carrier diffusion and recombination near the boundary, forming a depletion layer with few mobile majority carriers and an internal electric field. It is not an empty physical gap or a region without fixed charges. The external voltage direction changes junction behavior.
mfg1-electrical-l071.structureTitle: Atomic bonds and impurities · Donors and acceptors
mfg1-electrical-l071.structureText:
Silicon and germanium are representative intrinsic semiconductors. Adding a small amount of suitable impurity to silicon changes carrier behavior. Electrons are majority carriers in n-type material and holes in p-type; n/p does not simply mean the whole material has negative/positive charge.

Adding a five-valence-electron atom such as phosphorus to silicon is a donor example; a three-valence-electron atom such as boron is an acceptor example. A hole represents a missing electron; movement of surrounding electrons allows us to describe the hole as moving.

mfg1-electrical-l072.title: FETs, IGBTs, and IC function groups
mfg1-electrical-l072.exampleText: Op-amps, A/D, D/A, regulators, logic, memory, and MPUs have different functions. Modulation reflects an information signal into carrier amplitude, frequency, or phase; demodulation retrieves it. Do not confuse amplification, oscillation, and power stabilization as one process.
mfg1-electrical-l072.structureTitle: Three terminals do not imply the same roles · Separate characteristics from ratings
mfg1-electrical-l072.structureText:
Unlike a bipolar transistor’s B/C/E, a FET uses gate-based electric-field control. An IGBT is a power device with an insulated gate. Consult model documents for terminal names, drive conditions, maximum ratings, and static sensitivity; identical shape does not establish interchangeability.

hFE, switching time, and saturation voltage are characteristics dependent on operating conditions. Maximum current, voltage, and dissipation ratings are limits not to exceed. One favorable characteristic does not establish suitability.

mfg1-electrical-l073.title: Analog scales, clamp meters, and measurement error
mfg1-electrical-l073.exampleText: In the R=V/I voltage-drop method, leads, contacts, and instrument resistance affect the result. Voltmeter input and ammeter insertion also change the circuit, so the display is not automatically the true value. Check oscilloscope bandwidth, sample rate, memory, and probe conditions too.
mfg1-electrical-l073.structureTitle: Combine range and scale · Check each model’s capabilities
mfg1-electrical-l073.structureText:
Read an analog meter using the selected range and corresponding scale. A reading of 20 on a 50 full-scale scale with a 25 mA range is 10 mA. Resistance scales are nonlinear and use multipliers; check zero adjustment for each range. Align the pointer with its mirror image to reduce parallax.

Some DMMs directly measure AC current; do not claim all testers cannot. A clamp meter detects current around a conductor: check method, AC/DC capability, which conductor to enclose, and ratings. Current alone does not directly establish power consumption.

mfg1-electrical-l074.title: Tidy up and hand over after assembly
mfg1-electrical-l074.exampleText: Record part number, lot, quantity, completed scope, unfinished work, machine condition, abnormalities and actions, and recipient. If remaining counts disagree, report possible mixing or shortages instead of forcing the numbers to balance. Continue isolation and residual-heat precautions during cleaning.
mfg1-electrical-l074.structureTitle: Preparation and fatigue · Restore quantities and condition
mfg1-electrical-l074.structureText:
Prepare clothing, tools, parts, work surfaces, lighting, instructions, static protection, ventilation, and cooling. Familiar prolonged work can reduce attention through fatigue; follow workplace break plans. Match protection to hazards and avoid items that may be caught in rotation.

Return tools, remaining parts, and documents to designated locations and remove solder scraps and offcuts using specified tools. Check for foreign material inside boards or housings and distinguish held from good items. Do not leave everything simply assuming the next worker will do the same job.

mfg1-electrical-l075.title: Verify logic laws with truth tables
mfg1-electrical-l075.exampleText: De Morgan gives NOT(x+y)=(NOT x)·(NOT y) and NOT(x·y)=(NOT x)+(NOT y). Use parentheses to identify negation scope. Simplifying a logic expression does not replace evaluation of failure behavior or safety.
mfg1-electrical-l075.structureTitle: Order within the same operation · Zero, one, and negation
mfg1-electrical-l075.structureText:
In binary logic, +means OR, ·means AND, and NOT means negation. Commutative and associative laws allow order or parentheses to change within the same operator without changing results. Unlike ordinary arithmetic, x+x=x and x·x=x.

x+0=x, x·1=x, x+1=1, and x·0=0. Also x+NOT x=1, x·NOT x=0, and double negation returns x. Check absorption x+x·y=x and distribution x·(y+z)=x·y+x·z through four or eight input combinations.
The other distributive law is x+(y・z)=(x+y)・(x+z). Here too, x, y and z take values 0 or 1; ＋ means OR and ・ means AND. In the eight-row truth table, both sides equal y・z in the four rows where x=0, and both sides equal 1 in the four rows where x=1. This is not an expression that treats 0 and 1 using ordinary addition and multiplication.

mfg1-electrical-l076.title: Switches, sensors, relays, and SSRs
mfg1-electrical-l076.exampleText: SSRs mainly switch through semiconductors, so not all relays can be explained as mechanical contacts and coils. Check off-state leakage, heating, and load requirements. The shape or contacts of an emergency stop alone do not certify the equipment’s whole safety function.
mfg1-electrical-l076.structureTitle: Components creating inputs · Switching through electromagnetism
mfg1-electrical-l076.structureText:
Pushbuttons can return automatically or retain state. A mechanical limit switch changes contacts through object movement; photoelectric and proximity sensors use different detection principles. For float and pressure detection too, consult specifications for the measured quantity and output form.

An electromagnetic relay moves a mechanism and contacts with coil-generated magnetic force. A contactor switches larger loads but may not itself contain short-circuit or overcurrent protection. Match coil rating, contact capacity, a/b arrangement, and device identifier.

mfg1-electrical-l077.title: State changes of thermal relays and timers
mfg1-electrical-l077.exampleText: A basic off-delay turns on with the input, then off after the set delay from input-off. Retention and power conditions differ by product; do not assume identical behavior on loss of supply. Draw separate input/output lines against time to verify.
mfg1-electrical-l077.structureText:
A thermal relay detects overload using heating from overcurrent and components such as bimetal strips. A bimetal combines metals with different thermal expansion. Do not assume it alone interrupts the main circuit; it is normally combined with a contactor.

A basic on-delay turns the output on after the set time from input-on, and turns it off when the input goes off. In the basic example, an input shorter than the setting produces no output. Check each contact for timed operation and instantaneous return.

mfg1-surface-lesson-071.title: Understand safety-and-health responsibilities and greetings
mfg1-surface-lesson-071.exampleTitle: When you do not know the health contact
mfg1-surface-lesson-071.exampleText: Suppose you wish to discuss how you feel after work but do not know the contact. Use the workplace contact list or supervisor to check health-consultation services and occupational-physician arrangements. Do not assume another factory's arrangements apply. For sudden danger or health abnormalities, request help through emergency procedures without waiting for a routine appointment.
mfg1-surface-lesson-071.structureTitle: A framework for protecting safety and health · Check roles and consultation contacts · Use greetings as a starting point for communication
mfg1-surface-lesson-071.structureText:
The Industrial Safety and Health Act is Japanese law protecting workers' safety and health. The text organizes it into establishing hazard-prevention standards, clarifying responsibilities and promoting voluntary activities. Companies and workers follow the standards and procedures applicable to them.
Voluntary activity does not mean freely omitting laws or safety devices. It means identifying workplace hazards, discussing measures and continuing approved activities.

Safety and health committees and similar bodies discuss safety and health issues. Safety managers handle safety-related management, while occupational physicians contribute specialist expertise to worker health management and related matters.
Appointment or establishment duties and roles vary with industry, establishment size and other conditions. Do not assume every factory needs identical organizations or staffing; check your workplace structure and contacts. Do not wait for a committee meeting during an abnormality: follow emergency communication, stopping and evacuation procedures.
Ask the responsible person about the subjects and timing of special health examinations associated with harmful work and similar conditions. Receive designated examinations and follow health management. Examinations do not replace exposure prevention such as ventilation.

Greet people you pass with situation-appropriate expressions such as good morning, thank you for your work or work safely. Speaking with people in different occupations helps you know one another and makes consultation and communication easier.
A greeting alone does not communicate a hazard or work instruction. Report the location, condition and required response specifically when you notice an abnormality. Do not enter hazardous areas to greet someone or carelessly distract a person operating equipment.

mfg1-surface-lesson-072.title: Compare 21 metals using specific-gravity, property and application references
mfg1-surface-lesson-072.exampleTitle: A paper comparison at equal volume
mfg1-surface-lesson-072.exampleText:
Using only the table, platinum 21.45 has greater specific gravity than aluminium 2.7 and therefore greater mass for the same volume. Actual weight alone cannot identify a material; shape, volume and alloy composition also need checking.
For application scope, buff polishing may also be used on acrylic, polycarbonate, ABS resin and glass, not only metals. Examples include polishing hard chromium plating for corrosion resistance and gloss, and satin or hairline finishes after nickel or copper plating. These are treatment examples; a metal specific-gravity table cannot determine nonmetal polishing conditions.
mfg1-surface-lesson-072.structureTitle: Compare specific gravity without units · The 21-row educational reference · Limits of property and application descriptions
mfg1-surface-lesson-072.structureText:
Specific gravity is the ratio of a material's density to a reference density and is dimensionless. Read the 21 metals in Table 7-1 as educational reference values, distinct from the density unit g/cm³ itself.
The original table does not specify temperature, purity, measurement method or measurement date. Its PDF entries were checked on 26 October 2026; they are not measurements made that day. Do not unconditionally use them as alloy or product guarantees.

1. Lithium / Li: specific gravity 0.534; property lightest; examples batteries, alloys.
2. Magnesium / Mg:1.74; lightweight and high strength; aerospace, electronic equipment.
3. Aluminium / Al:2.7; lightweight, high strength, corrosion resistance; automobiles, construction materials.
4. Sodium / Na:0.971; lightweight, highly reactive; batteries, alloys.
5. Titanium / Ti:4.51; high strength, high corrosion resistance; aerospace, medical equipment.
6. Zinc / Zn:7.13; corrosion resistance; plating on steel, alloys.
7. Iron / Fe:7.87; high strength, good workability; construction materials, machine parts.
8. Copper / Cu:8.93; high conductivity, corrosion resistance; wires, piping.
9. Nickel / Ni:8.9; high strength, corrosion resistance; stainless steel, alloys.
10. Cobalt / Co:8.85; high strength, heat resistance; superalloys, magnets.
11. Silver / Ag:10.49; high conductivity; jewelry, electrical contacts.
12. Lead / Pb:11.36; high density, softness; radiation shielding, batteries.
13. Tin / Sn:7.3; high corrosion resistance, workability; solder, food cans.
14. Molybdenum / Mo:10.22; high strength, heat resistance; superalloys, electronic parts.
15. Platinum / Pt:21.45; high corrosion resistance, heat resistance; jewelry, catalysts.
16. Gold / Au:19.32; high conductivity, corrosion resistance; jewelry, electronic parts.
17. Chromium / Cr:7.19; corrosion resistance, hardness; stainless steel, plating.
18. Beryllium / Be:1.85; lightweight, high strength; alloys.
19. Tungsten / W:19.3; heat resistance; aerospace.
20. Manganese / Mn:7.43; hardness; dry batteries.
21. Bismuth / Bi:9.8; low melting point; solder.

Properties and uses are representative descriptions from the table. High strength or corrosion resistance does not guarantee identical performance across all purities, alloys, shapes and environments. An application example does not mean bare-hand contact or arbitrary substitution is allowed.
Bismuth's low melting point is qualitative; this table gives no numeric melting point. Copper values also differ in another specific-gravity example, so comparisons using this table use 8.93 from Table 7-1. In practice check the conditions of valid material references.

mfg1-surface-lesson-073.title: Refer to conductivity values and units for 15 metals
mfg1-surface-lesson-073.exampleText: Copper 59.6 in the table is 59,600,000 S/m. Silver 62.1 exceeds copper in this table, but a material name alone cannot determine allowable terminal current or heating. Separately check shape, contact, temperature and ratings.
mfg1-surface-lesson-073.structureTitle: Read units and conditions · The 15-row educational reference · Do not confuse multipliers and reference scales
mfg1-surface-lesson-073.structureText:
Conductivity is the reciprocal of electrical resistivity; its SI unit is S/m. Under the same conditions, greater conductivity means easier current flow. The Table 7-2 heading is 10⁶ S/m, so 59.6 means 59.6×10⁶ S/m.
The original table does not state temperature, purity or measurement date. These are educational representative values checked against the PDF on 26 October 2026, not measurements taken that day or values invariant for every alloy and temperature.

1. Silver(Ag):62.1×10⁶ S/m.
2. Copper(Cu):59.6×10⁶ S/m.
3. Gold(Au):44.2×10⁶ S/m.
4. Aluminium(Al):37.7×10⁶ S/m.
5. Magnesium(Mg):22.7×10⁶ S/m.
6. Sodium(Na):21×10⁶ S/m.
7. Tungsten(W):18.2×10⁶ S/m.
8. Zinc(Zn):16.9×10⁶ S/m.
9. Nickel(Ni):14.3×10⁶ S/m.
10. Lithium(Li):11×10⁶ S/m.
11. Cobalt(Co):10.2×10⁶ S/m.
12. Iron(Fe):10×10⁶ S/m.
13. Platinum(Pt):9.4×10⁶ S/m.
14. Tin(Sn):9.1×10⁶ S/m.
15. Titanium(Ti):2.38×10⁶ S/m.

1 mS/m is 0.001 S/m and 1µS/m is 0.000001 S/m. Conductivity units include a length denominator; do not confuse them with conductance units S or mS alone. Check temperature, concentration and other conditions as well as material.
Relative conductivity referenced to annealed copper at 100% is also used. The original text says ACS, but comparison scales such as percent IACS differ from absolute S/m. Do not read the Table 7-2 values directly as percentages.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-078.title: Read information from coordinate and surface-roughness measuring machines
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-078.exampleText: A measurement report links the instrument, reference, measured location and evaluation parameter. Roughness and geometric shape, and coordinate values and acceptance judgments, are different information. Ask the responsible person to confirm the plan for inaccessible areas or surfaces where contact may affect the result.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-078.structureTitle: Target and role · Principles and distinctions
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-078.structureText:
In a contact-type example, a coordinate measuring machine, CMM, reads the coordinates where a probe touches the target, then calculates lengths, angles, geometric tolerances and similar properties. One point of contact does not automatically guarantee the whole part’s shape. Check fixing, coordinate references, measurement points and the plan.

A stylus-type surface-roughness instrument traces the surface and converts vertical stylus motion into a signal describing its unevenness. Values such as Ra require measurement conditions and a specified location. A hole-location result from a CMM cannot simply become a surface-roughness result.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-079.title: Protect gauge-block measuring faces and store them correctly
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-079.exampleText: A master ring is used to set internal-diameter comparison, while plug and ring limit gauges are used for GO/NO-GO judgments. Do not determine use solely from whether the measuring face is inside or outside. Check whether it is a master or limit gauge, its identification and its certification or inspection condition. Keep these roles separate in storage too.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-079.structureTitle: Target and role · Principles and distinctions
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-079.structureText:
In a rectangular gauge-block example, the length between two opposing precision measuring faces provides the reference. Do not assume every visible face has the same role. Joining blocks by close adhesion is also called wringing. This is different from adding lengths with paper or dirt left between them.

After use, remove fingerprints and other contamination, then apply the specified corrosion protection and storage. Do not file away a burr on a measuring face with an ordinary file. Even if the source describes a specialized treatment, confirm the authorized operator and instrument procedure. A damaged reference affects later results set from it.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-080.title: Read line weights and the roles of special lines
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-080.exampleText: Scale is the ratio between drawing size and actual size. Distinguish enlargement examples such as 2:1 or 5:1 from reduction examples such as 1:2 or 1:5. Remembering line-weight ratios or recommended scales does not authorize filling in an unreadable drawing. Request a readable approved drawing when copying has obscured line types.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-080.structureTitle: Target and role · Principles and distinctions
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-080.structureText:
Line weights include thin, thick and extra-thick lines; the source describes their relative ratio as 1:2:4. Even when paper or printing changes, distinguish visible outlines from dimension lines. Read solid, dashed, single-dash-dot and double-dash-dot patterns together with their weight.

A thin double-dash-dot phantom line may show adjacent parts, fixture positions, moved positions, or shapes before and after machining as reference information. A break line marks an omitted boundary; a cutting-plane line identifies the section position and viewing direction; hatching relates to cut material. Do not machine a referenced phantom shape as the part’s current finished outline.
In Table 7-1, the thin double-dashed chain line also indicates reference tool positions, repeated features, and features in front of the section shown. A dimension extension line is a thin continuous line extended from the figure to support dimensioning. In this table, hidden outlines may use thin or thick dashed lines. A break line is a thin, irregular wavy continuous line or a zigzag line. A cutting-plane line uses a thin single-dashed chain line with thickened ends and changes of direction. Hatching consists of regularly spaced thin continuous lines indicating the cut material.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-081.title: Match symbols for spheres, squares, chamfers and holes
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-081.exampleText: Symbols may be omitted where the drawing and dimension line make a radius or diameter clear. A radius obtainable from other dimensions may be given as a reference dimension. Even when a symbol is omitted, check the target. Do not guess unreadable symbols to decide hole depth or seating-face shape; ask about the original drawing.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-081.structureTitle: Target and role · Principles and distinctions
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-081.structureText:
The symbol φ represents diameter, Sφ sphere diameter, R radius, SR sphere radius, and □ a square’s side. CR denotes a controlled radius. For arc length, read the auxiliary arc symbol and dimension-line form, keeping it distinct from straight chord length. Similar symbols do not make a circle and sphere, or radius and diameter, identical.

C indicates a 45-degree chamfer and t indicates thickness. There are also symbols for conical chamfers, spotfaces or counterbores, countersinks and depths. Match the drawing target with nominal tool sizes and machining instructions. For example, C2 cannot be independently changed to an arbitrary rounded R2 feature regardless of direction or angle.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-082.title: Organize the source’s geometric-tolerance types by shape, orientation and position
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-082.exampleText: A tolerance frame combines the characteristic symbol, value and necessary references. An arrow identifying a surface may be attached differently from an axis indication. Follow the drawing’s applicable standard and measurement plan. Do not transfer names or symbols from an older source to a new drawing without confirmation. Show the reference and arrow when asking about an unclear target.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-082.structureTitle: Target and role · Principles and distinctions
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-082.structureText:
The source lists straightness, flatness, roundness, cylindricity, profile of a line and profile of a surface. Separate the targets: a line, plane, circle, cylinder and profile. Checking roundness in one location does not mean the shape of the entire cylinder has been checked.

Parallelism, perpendicularity and angularity concern orientation; position, concentricity, coaxiality and symmetry provide distinctions for position relationships and related requirements. The source also lists circular runout and total runout. Even similarly round symbols differ in target, required references and tolerance zones. Do not substitute one characteristic simply because you remember another symbol’s name.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-083.title: Match metallic luster, thermal conductivity and melting point to use
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-083.exampleText: Melting point relates to the temperature where a solid becomes liquid. Examples include high-melting-point tungsten and low-melting-point tin or solder. Do not determine service temperature from melting point alone; strength and structure can change while a material remains solid. Similar material names do not justify applying the values of a different alloy.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-083.structureTitle: Target and role · Principles and distinctions
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-083.structureText:
Metallic luster concerns reflection of light. Oxidation or other surface changes alter appearance, so shine alone does not identify a material. Thermal conductivity, electrical conductivity and melting point, like density, are physical properties considered in material selection. Keep them distinct from mechanical hardness or toughness.

Thermal conductivity describes how readily heat is transmitted. The source gives examples of copper conducting heat better than aluminum, and stainless steel conducting it poorly. Heat sinks and heat exchangers seek to remove heat, while insulation seeks to retain it. Ease of conducting electricity and the amount of heat transmitted are separate properties.

mfg1-mechanical-lesson-084.title: Distinguish heat-affected zones from forging flow lines
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-084.exampleText: In bending a narrow strip, the source gives an example where a smaller bend radius concentrates the load on the outside and makes cracking more likely. Distinguish elastic recovery, retained plastic deformation, hardness and toughness. A single hardness result does not establish resistance to bend cracking or impact.
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-084.structureTitle: Target and role · Principles and distinctions
mfg1-mechanical-lesson-084.structureText:
Metal properties change when processing or heat treatment changes the structure. Welding can change structure by heat around the melted region too; this is a heat-affected zone. An area that did not melt does not necessarily retain the original properties. Check the required range and evaluation through specified inspection.

Forging flow lines are features related to material flow within a part formed by forging and similar processes. Impact direction and the direction of those lines may affect evaluation; shape alone does not determine strength. Changes to part orientation or stock layout require checking design and process approval.

mfg1-electrical-l078.title: Synchronous speed, mechanical output, and starting methods
mfg1-electrical-l078.exampleText: Full-voltage, star-delta, autotransformer, and reactor starting methods depend on use and installation. Star-delta current-reduction explanations assume suitable windings, connections, and other conditions. Do not rearrange terminals yourself; check starting current, load, and protection.
mfg1-electrical-l078.structureTitle: Field speed and rotor speed · Calculate output from torque
mfg1-electrical-l078.structureText:
The rotating field’s synchronous speed for an AC induction machine is Ns=120 f/p. At 50 Hz and 4 poles it is 1500 min⁻¹, but a loaded induction rotor normally runs slower, with slip. Do not treat this expression as an unconditional guarantee of actual speed.

Mechanical shaft output is P=2πNT/60, with actual speedN in min⁻¹ and torqueT in N·m. At 600 min⁻¹ and 2 N·m it is about 126 W. Distinguish input power from shaft output including losses; calculated output does not permit exceeding ratings.

mfg1-electrical-l079.title: Transformer losses, insulation construction, and the environment
mfg1-electrical-l079.exampleText: Check interrupting media and insulation against equipment specifications. Do not turn textbook overviews into claims that older technologies no longer exist at all; consult actual nameplates and procedures. Solar DC conversion and storage also belong to a system including connection and protection.
mfg1-electrical-l079.structureTitle: How losses grow · Insulation and cooling materials
mfg1-electrical-l079.structureText:
Core losses mainly occur in the core and exist when rated-condition voltage is applied to the primary even without secondary load. Copper loss is winding I²R; doubling current at unchanged resistance quadruples it. Stray load losses also exist, so the ideal ratio alone does not determine efficiency.

Oil-filled, molded, and gas-insulated construction have different maintenance requirements. SF6 is an insulation-gas example with significant environmental impact; do not release it without authorization. Colorless and odorless does not mean safe; use equipment and material information.

mfg1-electrical-l080.title: Inspection stages, reliability, and electrical safety
mfg1-electrical-l080.exampleText: Insulation resistance and withstand-voltage tests differ in purpose and method. Leakage and electromagnetic-immunity checks such as EMS may not be replaceable with an ordinary multimeter. Match test equipment, conditions, criteria, and personnel, and record results and the criteria used.
mfg1-electrical-l080.structureTitle: Components, assembled boards, and finished products · Environment and lifetime
mfg1-electrical-l080.structureText:
Incoming component checks, solder/orientation/electrical checks on assembled boards, and dimensional/function/appearance checks on completed products concern different targets. Supplier records do not authorize skipping your own required checks.

Environmental tests apply defined temperature, humidity, vibration, or shock conditions. Reliability tests may use accelerated conditions to assess continued quality, but a single brief functional check cannot guarantee lifetime.

mfg1-electrical-l081.title: Compare maintenance effects, terminology, and records
mfg1-electrical-l081.exampleText: Compare operating hours, production volume, repair contents, and downtime as well as failure counts. Shorter replacement intervals can prevent failure while increasing cost and waste. Predictive maintenance also needs monitoring equipment and control values.
mfg1-electrical-l081.structureTitle: Make the purpose specific · Do not judge by terminology alone
mfg1-electrical-l081.structureText:
